abstract: This paper describes a technique called Input Reconstruction Reliability Estimation (IRRE) for determining the response reliability of a restricted class of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). The technique uses a network's ability to accurately encode the input pattern in its internal representation as a measure of its reliability. The more accurately a network is able to reconstruct the input pattern from its internal representation, the more reliable the network is considered to be. IRRE is provides a good estimate of the reliability of MLPs trained for autonomous driving. Results are presented in which the reliability estimates provided by IRRE are used to select between networks trained for different driving situations.
originalAbstract: This paper describes a technique called Input Reconstruction Reliability Estimation (IRRE) for determining the response reliability of a restricted class of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). The technique uses a network's ability to accurately encode the input pattern in its internal representation as a measure of its reliability. The more accurately a network is able to reconstruct the input pattern from its internal representation, the more reliable the network is considered to be. paragraphs: Input Reconstruction Reliability Estimation evaluates how dependable a neural network's response is by examining its internal representation. The method applies to a restricted class of multilayer perceptrons. Its central idea is that a network's ability to preserve information about the current input can serve as evidence about the reliability of its response.

The technique reconstructs the input pattern from that internal representation and assesses how accurately the reconstruction matches the original. Better reconstruction is interpreted as greater reliability. This makes the estimate sensitive to the particular input being processed: it asks how well the network represents that pattern, rather than assigning one reliability level to the network as a whole.

The paper reports useful reliability estimates for networks trained for autonomous driving. It also presents results using those estimates to choose among networks trained for different driving situations. The practical contribution is therefore both an assessment method and a way to guide network selection, using reconstruction quality as the signal for deciding which trained network to rely on.
summary.tldr: Input reconstruction quality estimates response reliability and helps select among neural networks trained for different driving situations.

title: Input Reconstruction Reliability Estimation

abstract: We develop a refined mean field approximation for inference and learning in probabilistic neural networks. Our mean field theory, unlike most, does not assume that the units behave as independent degrees of freedom; instead, it exploits in a principled way the existence of large substructures that are computationally tractable. To illustrate the advantages of this framework, we show how to incorporate weak higher order interactions into a first-order hidden Markov model, treating the corrections (but not the first order structure) within mean field theory.
originalAbstract: We develop a refined mean field approximation for inference and learning in probabilistic neural networks. Our mean field theory, unlike most, does not assume that the units behave as independent degrees of freedom; instead, it exploits in a principled way the existence of large substructures that are computationally tractable. To illustrate the advantages of this framework, we show how to incorporate weak higher order interactions into a first-order hidden Markov model, treating the corrections (but not the first order structure) within mean field theory.

paragraphs: The paper develops an approximation for inference and learning in probabilistic neural networks whose full computations are difficult. Its starting point is that a complicated network can contain substantial internal structures that remain computationally manageable. Those structures provide information that an approximation can preserve and use.

The proposed mean field framework avoids treating every unit as an independent degree of freedom. Instead, it incorporates large tractable substructures into the approximation. This matters because assuming complete independence discards relationships even when those relationships could be handled efficiently. The refined approach directs approximation toward the parts responsible for the computational difficulty.

The authors illustrate the framework with a first-order hidden Markov model extended by weak higher-order interactions. The first-order structure remains intact, while mean field theory handles the additional corrections. This example makes the division of labor concrete: retain the manageable dependence structure and approximate the extra interactions. The contribution is a principled way to build an approximation around what can already be computed effectively.
summary.tldr: A refined mean field method preserves tractable network dependencies while approximating the interactions that make computation difficult.

title: Exploiting Tractable Substructures in Intractable Networks

abstract: We provide a model of the standard watermaze task, and of a more challenging task involving novel platform locations, in which rats exhibit one-trial learning after a few days of training. The model uses hippocampal place cells to support reinforcement learning, and also, in an integrated manner, to build and use allocentric coordinates.
originalAbstract: We provide a model of the standard watermaze task, and of a more challenging task involving novel platform locations, in which rats exhibit one-trial learning after a few days of training. The model uses hippocampal place cells to support reinforcement learning, and also, in an integrated manner, to build and use allocentric coordinates.

paragraphs: The paper models spatial behavior in rats using two watermaze tasks. One is the standard task; the other introduces novel platform locations and a more demanding learning requirement. In the latter, rats show learning from a single trial after several days of training. The model therefore addresses rapid learning that emerges after prior experience.

Its central components are hippocampal place cells, used both to support reinforcement learning and to construct and use allocentric coordinates. Allocentric coordinates describe location relative to the surrounding environment. The approach integrates these uses of spatial information, bringing together learning through reinforcement and an environment-based representation of position within the same model.

The title identifies temporal-difference learning as the reinforcement-learning approach. The abstract's main contribution is the integrated account of place-cell-supported learning and coordinates across the two tasks. The novel-platform task makes the relationship especially relevant: the behavior to be modeled includes adapting to a new location after earlier training, alongside performance in the standard watermaze setting.
summary.tldr: A rat navigation model integrates place-cell-supported reinforcement learning with environment-based spatial coordinates.

title: Hippocampal Model of Rat Spatial Abilities Using Temporal Difference Learning

abstract: Stochastic meta-descent (SMD) is a new technique for online adap(cid:173) tation of local learning rates in arbitrary twice-differentiable sys(cid:173) tems. Like matrix momentum it uses full second-order information while retaining O(n) computational complexity by exploiting the efficient computation of Hessian-vector products. Here we apply SMD to independent component analysis, and employ the result(cid:173) ing algorithm for the blind separation of time-varying mixtures. By matching individual learning rates to the rate of change in each source signal's mixture coefficients, our technique is capable of si(cid:173) multaneously tracking sources that move at very different, a priori unknown speeds.

Here we apply SMD to independent component analysis, and employ the result(cid:173) ing algorithm for the blind separation of time-varying mixtures. paragraphs: The paper applies stochastic meta-descent to independent component analysis for separating mixtures that change over time. The underlying challenge is that different sources can change their mixture coefficients at very different speeds. A learning procedure needs to adjust to these differences even when the rates of change are not known beforehand.

Stochastic meta-descent adapts local learning rates online and is presented for arbitrary twice-differentiable systems. It uses full second-order information while retaining linear computational complexity through efficient Hessian-vector products. This gives the adaptation access to curvature information without requiring the computational cost of explicitly manipulating a full Hessian matrix.

In the source-separation application, individual learning rates are matched to how quickly each source's mixture coefficients change. The resulting technique can simultaneously track sources moving at substantially different, initially unknown speeds. The important connection is between local adaptation and uneven change in the signal mixture: different parts of the learning process can respond on different time scales instead of sharing one fixed rate.
summary.tldr: Locally adapted learning rates let online ICA track time-varying mixtures whose sources change at different unknown speeds.

title: Online Independent Component Analysis with Local Learning Rate Adaptation

abstract: Quantitative data on the speed with which animals acquire behav(cid:173) ioral responses during classical conditioning experiments should provide strong constraints on models of learning. However, most models have simply ignored these data; the few that have attempt(cid:173) ed to address them have failed by at least an order of magnitude. We discuss key data on the speed of acquisition, and show how to account for them using a statistically sound model of learning, in which differential reliabilities of stimuli playa crucial role.
originalAbstract: Quantitative data on the speed with which animals acquire behav(cid:173) ioral responses during classical conditioning experiments should provide strong constraints on models of learning. However, most models have simply ignored these data; the few that have attempt(cid:173) ed to address them have failed by at least an order of magnitude. We discuss key data on the speed of acquisition, and show how to account for them using a statistically sound model of learning, in which differential reliabilities of stimuli playa crucial role.

paragraphs: The paper studies how quickly animals acquire responses during classical conditioning. Learning speed is a demanding test for a theory: a model must explain the time course of acquiring a response, as well as the response itself. The authors argue that quantitative measurements of acquisition should therefore place strong constraints on explanations of learning.

According to the abstract, most existing models had overlooked these measurements. Among the few that tried to explain them, discrepancies reached at least an order of magnitude. The paper examines key acquisition-speed data and presents a statistically grounded learning model that accounts for those observations.

A central ingredient is that stimuli differ in reliability. The model's explanation depends on these differences, making reliability an essential part of understanding how quickly learning occurs. The stated result connects a statistical treatment of learning to measured acquisition rates. Its significance is the ability to address a quantitative behavioral pattern that the models discussed by the authors had either ignored or explained poorly.
summary.tldr: A statistical learning model uses differences in stimulus reliability to explain measured rates of conditioning acquisition.

title: Acquisition in Autoshaping

abstract: We investigate data based procedures for selecting the kernel when learn- ing with Support Vector Machines. We provide generalization error bounds by estimating the Rademacher complexities of the corresponding function classes. In particular we obtain a complexity bound for function classes induced by kernels with given eigenvectors, i.e., we allow to vary the spectrum and keep the eigenvectors ﬁx. This bound is only a loga- rithmic factor bigger than the complexity of the function class induced by a single kernel. However, optimizing the margin over such classes leads to overﬁtting. We thus propose a suitable way of constraining the class. We use an efﬁcient algorithm to solve the resulting optimization problem, present preliminary experimental results, and compare them to an alignment-based approach.
originalAbstract: We investigate data based procedures for selecting the kernel when learn- ing with Support Vector Machines. We provide generalization error bounds by estimating the Rademacher complexities of the corresponding function classes. In particular we obtain a complexity bound for function classes induced by kernels with given eigenvectors, i.e., we allow to vary the spectrum and keep the eigenvectors ﬁx. This bound is only a loga- rithmic factor bigger than the complexity of the function class induced by a single kernel. However, optimizing the margin over such classes leads to overﬁtting. We thus propose a suitable way of constraining the class. We use an efﬁcient algorithm to solve the resulting optimization problem, present preliminary experimental results, and compare them to an alignment-based approach.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to choose a support vector machine's kernel from data. Because kernel selection changes the class of functions available to the learner, the authors study its effect on generalization. They derive error bounds by estimating the Rademacher complexity of the relevant function classes, a measure used to control their flexibility.

A particular result concerns kernels with fixed eigenvectors but adjustable spectra. This allows the strength associated with each fixed direction to vary. The resulting complexity bound exceeds the corresponding single-kernel complexity by only a logarithmic factor. However, the authors also find that optimizing the margin over these classes leads to overfitting.

To address that problem, they propose constraining the function class and use an efficient algorithm for the resulting optimization. Preliminary experiments compare the approach with an alignment-based method. The paper thus combines a relatively modest theoretical complexity increase with a practical caution: the margin optimization still needs an appropriate restriction on what kernels it can select.
summary.tldr: Kernel-learning complexity bounds motivate a constrained optimization method after unrestricted margin optimization over adjustable spectra leads to overfitting.

title: On the Complexity of Learning the Kernel Matrix

abstract: Recent algorithms for sparse coding and independent component analy- sis (ICA) have demonstrated how localized features can be learned from natural images. However, these approaches do not take image transfor- mations into account. As a result, they produce image codes that are redundant because the same feature is learned at multiple locations. We describe an algorithm for sparse coding based on a bilinear generative model of images. By explicitly modeling the interaction between im- age features and their transformations, the bilinear approach helps reduce redundancy in the image code and provides a basis for transformation- invariant vision. We present results demonstrating bilinear sparse coding of natural images. We also explore an extension of the model that can capture spatial relationships between the independent features of an ob- ject, thereby providing a new framework for parts-based object recogni- tion.
originalAbstract: Recent algorithms for sparse coding and independent component analy- sis (ICA) have demonstrated how localized features can be learned from natural images. However, these approaches do not take image transfor- mations into account. As a result, they produce image codes that are redundant because the same feature is learned at multiple locations. We describe an algorithm for sparse coding based on a bilinear generative model of images. By explicitly modeling the interaction between im- age features and their transformations, the bilinear approach helps reduce redundancy in the image code and provides a basis for transformation- invariant vision. We present results demonstrating bilinear sparse coding of natural images. We also explore an extension of the model that can capture spatial relationships between the independent features of an ob- ject, thereby providing a new framework for parts-based object recogni- tion.

paragraphs: Sparse coding learns a compact description of an image using a limited set of active features. The paper addresses a source of redundancy in earlier sparse coding and independent component analysis approaches: a feature can be learned repeatedly because it appears at different image locations. Without explicitly accounting for transformations, the representation can treat these appearances as separate features.

The authors introduce a bilinear generative model that represents interactions between image features and their transformations. This gives the coding algorithm a way to describe both a feature and how it appears in an image. The approach helps reduce repeated representations and provides a basis for vision that can recognize features despite transformations.

The paper demonstrates bilinear sparse coding on natural images and explores an extension that captures spatial relationships among an object's independent features. That extension connects the coding problem to recognition based on object parts. The contribution is both a less redundant image representation and a proposed framework for representing how parts belong together.
summary.tldr: A bilinear sparse coding model represents features together with their transformations to reduce redundant image codes.

title: A Bilinear Model for Sparse Coding

abstract: We consider Bayesian mixture approaches, where a predictor is constructed by forming a weighted average of hypotheses from some space of functions. While such procedures are known to lead to optimal predictors in several cases, where sufficiently accurate prior information is available, it has not been clear how they perform when some of the prior assumptions are violated. In this paper we establish data-dependent bounds for such procedures, extending previous randomized approaches such as the Gibbs algorithm to a fully Bayesian setting. The finite-sample guarantees established in this work enable the utilization of Bayesian mixture approaches in agnostic settings, where the usual assumptions of the Bayesian paradigm fail to hold. Moreover, the bounds derived can be directly applied to non-Bayesian mixture approaches such as Bagging and Boosting.

While such procedures are known to lead to optimal predictors in several cases, where sufficiently accurate prior information is available, it has not been clear how they perform when some of the prior assumptions are violated. In this paper we establish data-dependent bounds for such procedures, extending previous randomized approaches such as the Gibbs algorithm to a fully Bayesian setting. The finite-sample guarantees established in this work enable the utilization of Bayesian mixture approaches in agnostic settings, where the usual assumptions of the Bayesian paradigm fail to hold. Moreover, the bounds derived can be directly applied to non-Bayesian mixture approaches such as Bagging and Boosting.

paragraphs: Bayesian mixture methods predict by taking a weighted average of candidate functions. Such methods can be optimal in several settings when the prior information is sufficiently accurate. This paper asks what can still be guaranteed when some prior assumptions are wrong, a situation in which those familiar optimality results do not directly settle performance.

The authors establish bounds that depend on the observed data and apply to a finite training sample. Their analysis extends earlier work on randomized methods, including the Gibbs algorithm, to fully Bayesian mixtures. The focus is therefore on guarantees for the mixture predictor itself, beyond the earlier randomized setting.

These guarantees support using Bayesian mixtures in agnostic settings where the usual Bayesian assumptions fail to hold. They provide a way to assess such procedures without requiring all of those assumptions to be correct. The derived bounds also apply directly to non-Bayesian mixture methods, including bagging and boosting, giving the analysis relevance beyond Bayesian prediction.
summary.tldr: Data-dependent finite-sample bounds give Bayesian mixture predictors guarantees even when usual Bayesian assumptions fail.

title: Data-Dependent Bounds for Bayesian Mixture Methods

abstract: This article addresses the issues of colour classiﬁcation and collision de- tection as they occur in the legged league robot soccer environment of RoboCup. We show how the method of one-class classiﬁcation with sup- port vector machines (SVMs) can be applied to solve these tasks satisfac- torily using the limited hardware capacity of the prescribed Sony AIBO quadruped robots. The experimental evaluation shows an improvement over our previous methods of ellipse ﬁtting for colour classiﬁcation and the statistical approach used for collision detection.
originalAbstract: This article addresses the issues of colour classiﬁcation and collision de- tection as they occur in the legged league robot soccer environment of RoboCup. We show how the method of one-class classiﬁcation with sup- port vector machines (SVMs) can be applied to solve these tasks satisfac- torily using the limited hardware capacity of the prescribed Sony AIBO quadruped robots. The experimental evaluation shows an improvement over our previous methods of ellipse ﬁtting for colour classiﬁcation and the statistical approach used for collision detection.

paragraphs: The paper studies two practical recognition tasks for Sony AIBO robots playing soccer in RoboCup’s legged league: classifying colours and detecting collisions. Both tasks must operate within the limited computing capacity of the prescribed robots. The research question therefore concerns whether a learning method can deliver useful recognition under the hardware constraints of this environment.

The authors apply one-class classification with support vector machines to both problems. This brings the two tasks under the same general classification approach, although they concern different aspects of robot operation. Their stated result is that the method handles both tasks satisfactorily on the available hardware, establishing its practical suitability in the setting studied.

Experimental evaluation compares the approach with the authors’ previous methods: ellipse fitting for colour classification and a statistical method for collision detection. The support vector approach improves on both. The contribution is an application result tied to these tasks and comparisons: a shared learning framework can improve recognition while fitting the computing resources of these soccer robots.
summary.tldr: One-class SVMs improve colour classification and collision detection over the authors’ previous methods while fitting AIBO hardware constraints.

title: Application of SVMs for Colour Classification and Collision Detection with AIBO Robots

abstract: We consider the problem of structured classiﬁcation, where the task is to predict a label y from an input x, and y has meaningful internal struc- ture. Our framework includes supervised training of Markov random ﬁelds and weighted context-free grammars as special cases. We describe an algorithm that solves the large-margin optimization problem deﬁned in [12], using an exponential-family (Gibbs distribution) representation of structured objects. The algorithm is efﬁcient—even in cases where the number of labels y is exponential in size—provided that certain expecta- tions under Gibbs distributions can be calculated efﬁciently. The method for structured labels relies on a more general result, speciﬁcally the ap- plication of exponentiated gradient updates [7, 8] to quadratic programs.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of structured classiﬁcation, where the task is to predict a label y from an input x, and y has meaningful internal struc- ture. Our framework includes supervised training of Markov random ﬁelds and weighted context-free grammars as special cases. We describe an algorithm that solves the large-margin optimization problem deﬁned in [12], using an exponential-family (Gibbs distribution) representation of structured objects. The algorithm is efﬁcient—even in cases where the number of labels y is exponential in size—provided that certain expecta- tions under Gibbs distributions can be calculated efﬁciently. The method for structured labels relies on a more general result, speciﬁcally the ap- plication of exponentiated gradient updates [7, 8] to quadratic programs.

paragraphs: Structured classification predicts an output with meaningful internal organization rather than a single unstructured category. This paper develops an algorithm for a large-margin formulation of that task. Its framework includes supervised training of Markov random fields and weighted context-free grammars, bringing several kinds of structured prediction into a common optimization setting.

The algorithm represents structured objects using an exponential-family, or Gibbs, distribution. Its optimization method comes from a broader result applying exponentiated-gradient updates to quadratic programs. This connects a general numerical update rule with a probabilistic representation that can organize the many candidate outputs arising in structured classification.

The key efficiency claim is conditional: the method can remain efficient even when the number of possible outputs grows exponentially, provided certain expectations under the Gibbs distributions are efficiently computable. The number of labels alone therefore does not determine whether the method is practical. The contribution identifies a route to large-margin learning whose feasibility depends on the required expectation calculations for the particular structured output family.
summary.tldr: Exponentiated-gradient optimization enables efficient large-margin structured learning when the required Gibbs-distribution expectations are tractable.

title: Exponentiated Gradient Algorithms for Large-margin Structured Classification

abstract: Inspired by “Google™ Sets”, we consider the problem of retrieving items from a concept or cluster, given a query consisting of a few items from that cluster. We formulate this as a Bayesian inference problem and de- scribe a very simple algorithm for solving it. Our algorithm uses a model- based concept of a cluster and ranks items using a score which evaluates the marginal probability that each item belongs to a cluster containing the query items. For exponential family models with conjugate priors this marginal probability is a simple function of sufﬁcient statistics. We focus on sparse binary data and show that our score can be evaluated ex- actly using a single sparse matrix multiplication, making it possible to apply our algorithm to very large datasets. We evaluate our algorithm on three datasets: retrieving movies from EachMovie, ﬁnding completions of author sets from the NIPS dataset, and ﬁnding completions of sets of words appearing in the Grolier encyclopedia. We compare to Google™ Sets and show that Bayesian Sets gives very reasonable set completions.

We formulate this as a Bayesian inference problem and de- scribe a very simple algorithm for solving it. Our algorithm uses a model- based concept of a cluster and ranks items using a score which evaluates the marginal probability that each item belongs to a cluster containing the query items. For exponential family models with conjugate priors this marginal probability is a simple function of sufﬁcient statistics. We focus on sparse binary data and show that our score can be evaluated ex- actly using a single sparse matrix multiplication, making it possible to apply our algorithm to very large datasets. We evaluate our algorithm on three datasets: retrieving movies from EachMovie, ﬁnding completions of author sets from the NIPS dataset, and ﬁnding completions of sets of words appearing in the Grolier encyclopedia. We compare to Google™ Sets and show that Bayesian Sets gives very reasonable set completions.

paragraphs: Bayesian Sets addresses retrieval by example: a user supplies a few items belonging to a concept or cluster, and the system seeks additional members. The central challenge is turning those examples into a ranking of candidates. The paper treats this as Bayesian inference using a model-based definition of what constitutes a cluster.

Each candidate receives a score evaluating the marginal probability that it belongs to a cluster containing the query items. For exponential family models with conjugate priors, this calculation reduces to a simple function of sufficient statistics. For the sparse binary data emphasized in the paper, the score can be computed exactly with one sparse matrix multiplication, enabling application to very large datasets.

The evaluation covers movie retrieval from EachMovie, completion of author sets from NIPS data, and completion of word sets from the Grolier encyclopedia. The authors also compare against Google Sets and report very reasonable completions. These results illustrate the use of the same probabilistic retrieval formulation across several kinds of items.
summary.tldr: Bayesian Sets ranks candidates for example-based set completion using a probabilistic cluster score that is especially efficient for sparse binary data.

title: Bayesian Sets

abstract: In this paper we propose a new receiver for digital communications. We focus on the application of Gaussian Processes (GPs) to the multiuser detection (MUD) in code division multiple access (CDMA) systems to solve the near-far problem. Hence, we aim to reduce the interference from other users sharing the same frequency band. While usual approaches minimize the mean square error (MMSE) to linearly retrieve the user of interest, we exploit the same criteria but in the design of a nonlinear MUD. Since the optimal solution is known to be nonlinear, the performance of this novel method clearly improves that of the MMSE detectors. Furthermore, the GP based MUD achieves excellent interference suppression even for short training sequences. We also include some experiments to illustrate that other nonlinear detectors such as those based on Support Vector Machines (SVMs) exhibit a worse performance.

We focus on the application of Gaussian Processes (GPs) to the multiuser detection (MUD) in code division multiple access (CDMA) systems to solve the near-far problem. Hence, we aim to reduce the interference from other users sharing the same frequency band. While usual approaches minimize the mean square error (MMSE) to linearly retrieve the user of interest, we exploit the same criteria but in the design of a nonlinear MUD. Since the optimal solution is known to be nonlinear, the performance of this novel method clearly improves that of the MMSE detectors. Furthermore, the GP based MUD achieves excellent interference suppression even for short training sequences. We also include some experiments to illustrate that other nonlinear detectors such as those based on Support Vector Machines (SVMs) exhibit a worse performance.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a digital communications receiver for separating users who share a frequency band in a CDMA system. Its target is the near-far problem, in which other users interfere with recovery of the user of interest. The authors apply Gaussian processes to multiuser detection to reduce this interference.

Conventional minimum mean-square-error approaches retrieve the desired user through a linear detector. The proposed receiver retains the mean-square-error criterion but uses it to construct a nonlinear detector. This matters because the optimal solution to the detection problem is known to be nonlinear, giving a motivation for moving beyond a linear receiver.

The paper reports improved performance over MMSE detectors and strong interference suppression even with short training sequences. It also presents experiments in which other nonlinear detectors, including support vector machine methods, perform worse. These findings support the Gaussian process receiver in the studied setting. The contribution combines a familiar estimation objective with a nonlinear model and reports that this combination can handle interference effectively with limited training.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process CDMA receiver reports better interference suppression than linear MMSE and tested nonlinear alternatives, even with short training sequences.

title: Gaussian Processes for Multiuser Detection in CDMA receivers

abstract: The increasingly popular independent component analysis (ICA) may only be applied to data following the generative ICA model in order to guarantee algorithmindependent and theoretically valid results. Subspace ICA models generalize the assumption of component independence to independence between groups of components. They are attractive candidates for dimensionality reduction methods, however are currently limited by the assumption of equal group sizes or less general semi-parametric models. By introducing the concept of irreducible independent subspaces or components, we present a generalization to a parameter-free mixture model. Moreover, we relieve the condition of at-most-one-Gaussian by including previous results on non-Gaussian component analysis. After introducing this general model, we discuss joint block diagonalization with unknown block sizes, on which we base a simple extension of JADE to algorithmically perform the subspace analysis. Simulations confirm the feasibility of the algorithm. 1 Independent subspace analysis A random vector Y is called an independent component of the random vector X, if there exists an invertible matrix A and a decomposition X = A(Y, Z) such that Y and Z are stochastically independent. The goal of a general independent subspace analysis (ISA) or multidimensional independent component analysis is the decomposition of an arbitrary random vector X into independent components. If X is to be decomposed into one-dimensional components, this coincides with ordinary independent component analysis (ICA). Similarly, if the independent components are required to be of the same dimension k , then this is denoted by multidimensional ICA of fixed group size k or simply k -ISA. So 1-ISA is equivalent to ICA. 1.1 Why extend ICA? An important structural aspect in the search for decompositions is the knowledge of the number of solutions i.e. the indeterminacies of the problem. Without it, the result of any ICA or ISA algorithm cannot be compared with other solutions, so for instance blind source separation (BSS) would be impossible. Clearly, given an ISA solution, invertible transforms in each component (scaling matrices L) as well as permutations of components of the same dimension (permutation matrices P) give again an ISA of X. And indeed, in the special case of ICA, scaling and permutation are already all indeterminacies given that at most one Gaussian is contained in X [6]. This is one of the key theoretical results in ICA, allowing the usage of ICA for solving BSS problems and hence stimulating many applications. It has been shown that also for k -ISA, scalings and permutations as above are the only indeterminacies [11], given some additional rather weak restrictions to the model. However, a serious drawback of k -ISA (and hence of ICA) lies in the fact that the requirement fixed group-size k does not allow us to apply this analysis to an arbitrary random vector. paragraphs: Independent component analysis seeks a decomposition into independent components, but its theoretical interpretation depends on the data satisfying its generative assumptions. Independent subspace analysis broadens the idea by allowing dependence within groups while requiring independence between groups. This paper develops a more general formulation that avoids requiring every group to have the same size.

The authors introduce irreducible independent subspaces: components that cannot be further decomposed into independent parts within the formulation. This supports a parameter-free mixture model. They also incorporate earlier non-Gaussian component analysis results to relax the usual restriction allowing at most one Gaussian component, expanding the model's treatment of possible independent structure.

For computation, the paper considers joint block diagonalization with unknown block sizes and builds a simple extension of JADE around it. Simulations confirm the algorithm's feasibility. The contribution connects a broader account of independent subspaces with a concrete computational method, addressing the mismatch between fixed-size groups and the potentially unequal independent structures present in a random vector.
summary.tldr: A generalized independent-subspace model removes fixed group-size requirements and motivates a feasible extension of JADE.

title: Towards a general independent subspace analysis

abstract: In many domains, data are distributed among datasets that share only some variables; other recorded variables may occur in only one dataset. There are several asymptotically correct, informative algorithms that search for causal information given a single dataset, even with missing values and hidden variables. There are, however, no such reliable procedures for distributed data with overlapping variables, and only a single heuristic procedure (Structural EM). This paper describes an asymptotically correct procedure, ION, that provides all the information about structure obtainable from the marginal independence relations. Using simulated and real data, the accuracy of ION is compared with that of Structural EM, and with inference on complete, unified data.

paragraphs: Causal analysis becomes difficult when separate datasets record overlapping but different sets of variables. Some variables may connect datasets, while others appear in only one. The paper addresses how to combine causal information learned locally without requiring every dataset to contain the same complete collection of measurements.

The authors introduce ION, a procedure with an asymptotic correctness guarantee. It extracts all structural information obtainable from the marginal independence relations. These relations describe independence within the observed subsets of variables, so the contribution concerns how much causal structure can be recovered by bringing those pieces of information together.

The scope of the guarantee matters: it is about information supported by those independence relations, and correctness is stated asymptotically. It does not assert that any collection of overlapping datasets uniquely identifies a complete causal structure. The authors compare ION’s accuracy with Structural EM and with inference using complete, unified data on simulated and real examples. These comparisons examine both an existing heuristic and the setting where the variables are observed together.
summary.tldr: ION combines causal information across overlapping datasets with an asymptotic guarantee covering structure supported by marginal independences.

title: Integrating Locally Learned Causal Structures with Overlapping Variables

abstract: We study the problem of decision-theoretic online learning (DTOL). Motivated by practical applications, we focus on DTOL when the number of actions is very large. Previous algorithms for learning in this framework have a tunable learning rate parameter, and a major barrier to using online-learning in practical applications is that it is not understood how to set this parameter optimally, particularly when the number of actions is large. In this paper, we offer a clean solution by proposing a novel and completely parameter-free algorithm for DTOL. In addition, we introduce a new notion of regret, which is more natural for applications with a large number of actions. We show that our algorithm achieves good performance with respect to this new notion of regret; in addition, it also achieves performance close to that of the best bounds achieved by previous algorithms with optimally-tuned parameters, according to previous notions of regret.

Earlier algorithms require a learning rate, a parameter whose choice affects performance. The authors identify setting that parameter well as an important practical obstacle, especially with a large action set.

Their contribution is a completely parameter-free algorithm for decision-theoretic online learning. They also introduce a new definition of regret, the criterion used to assess how well an online decision maker performs relative to alternatives. The new definition is intended to be more natural for applications involving many possible actions.

The algorithm performs well under the proposed regret criterion. Under earlier regret definitions, it also comes close to the best bounds available for previous algorithms with optimally chosen parameters. The significance is the combination: removing parameter tuning does not require abandoning strong comparisons with established methods, while the new evaluation criterion addresses the large-action setting directly.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free online learning algorithm approaches optimally tuned regret bounds while introducing a regret criterion suited to large action sets.

title: A Parameter-free Hedging Algorithm

abstract: This paper is concerned with the consistency analysis on listwise ranking methods. Among various ranking methods, the listwise methods have competitive performances on benchmark datasets and are regarded as one of the state-of-the-art approaches. Most listwise ranking methods manage to optimize ranking on the whole list (permutation) of objects, however, in practical applications such as information retrieval, correct ranking at the top k positions is much more important. This paper aims to analyze whether existing listwise ranking methods are statistically consistent in the top-k setting. For this purpose, we define a top-k ranking framework, where the true loss (and thus the risks) are defined on the basis of top-k subgroup of permutations. This framework can include the permutation-level ranking framework proposed in previous work as a special case. Based on the new framework, we derive sufficient conditions for a listwise ranking method to be consistent with the top-k true loss, and show an effective way of modifying the surrogate loss functions in existing methods to satisfy these conditions. Experimental results show that after the modifications, the methods can work significantly better than their original versions.

paragraphs: Listwise ranking methods optimize an ordering of an entire set of objects, while applications such as information retrieval often care most about the first few positions. This paper asks whether existing listwise methods are statistically consistent for that top-k objective. The issue is whether optimizing their training losses aligns with the desired ranking risk.

The authors define a framework whose true loss and associated risks are based on top-k subgroups of permutations. It includes the earlier whole-permutation framework as a special case. Within this formulation, they derive sufficient conditions for consistency and describe how to modify existing surrogate losses so that they meet those conditions.

The contribution is both analytical and practical. It provides a way to assess whether a listwise training objective fits a top-k goal, then offers a constructive route to improving that fit. Experiments show that the modified methods can perform significantly better than their original versions. The theoretical conditions are sufficient guarantees, while the performance gains are findings from the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: A top-k ranking framework yields sufficient consistency conditions and loss modifications that improve existing methods in experiments.

title: Statistical Consistency of Top-k Ranking

abstract: While many advances have already been made on the topic of hierarchical classi- ﬁcation learning, we take a step back and examine how a hierarchical classiﬁca- tion problem should be formally deﬁned. We pay particular attention to the fact that many arbitrary decisions go into the design of the the label taxonomy that is provided with the training data, and that this taxonomy is often unbalanced. We correct this problem by using the data distribution to calibrate the hierarchical classiﬁcation loss function. This distribution-based correction must be done with care, to avoid introducing unmanagable statstical dependencies into the learning problem. This leads us off the beaten path of binomial-type estimation and into the uncharted waters of geometric-type estimation. We present a new calibrated deﬁnition of statistical risk for hierarchical classiﬁcation, an unbiased geometric estimator for this risk, and a new algorithmic reduction from hierarchical classiﬁ- cation to cost-sensitive classiﬁcation.

paragraphs: Hierarchical classification organizes labels within a taxonomy, making the hierarchy part of how prediction errors are judged. This paper questions how that judgment should be defined. Taxonomies reflect many arbitrary design decisions and are often unbalanced, so their structure can influence the loss assigned to a prediction in ways that warrant correction.

The authors propose calibrating the classification loss using the data distribution. This leads to a revised definition of statistical risk, the expected loss that a learning method aims to control. Incorporating distributional information requires care because the correction can create difficult statistical dependencies. The proposed analysis therefore moves from binomial-type estimation to a geometric-type approach.

The resulting contributions are a calibrated risk definition, an unbiased geometric estimator of that risk, and a reduction to cost-sensitive classification. Unbiasedness means the estimator targets the defined risk correctly in expectation. The reduction connects the revised objective to a classification setting that explicitly handles different error costs. Together, these results address both what hierarchical classification should optimize and how that objective can be estimated and pursued.
summary.tldr: The paper calibrates hierarchical classification loss to the data distribution and supplies an unbiased risk estimator and a cost-sensitive learning reduction.

title: Distribution-Calibrated Hierarchical Classification

abstract: Estimating 3D pose from monocular images is a highly ambiguous problem. Physical constraints can be exploited to restrict the space of feasible configurations. In this paper we propose an approach to constraining the prediction of a discriminative predictor. We first show that the mean prediction of a Gaussian process implicitly satisfies linear constraints if those constraints are satisfied by the training examples. We then show how, by performing a change of variables, a GP can be forced to satisfy quadratic constraints. As evidenced by the experiments, our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the tasks of rigid and non-rigid pose estimation.

We then show how, by performing a change of variables, a GP can be forced to satisfy quadratic constraints. As evidenced by the experiments, our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the tasks of rigid and non-rigid pose estimation.

paragraphs: Recovering a three-dimensional pose from a single image is ambiguous because the image does not uniquely specify the underlying configuration. Physical constraints can narrow the set of plausible poses. This paper studies how to make the output of a learned predictor respect such constraints, using Gaussian process regression as its predictive model.

The first result concerns linear constraints: if the training examples satisfy them, the Gaussian process mean prediction implicitly satisfies them as well. This connects a property of the training outputs directly to the structure of the prediction. The result specifically concerns the predicted mean, so its scope is more precise than a claim about every possible output of the probabilistic model.

The authors then show how a change of variables can force a Gaussian process to satisfy quadratic constraints. Together, these results provide ways to incorporate physical feasibility into discriminative pose prediction. Experiments on rigid and non-rigid pose estimation report better performance than state-of-the-art approaches, supporting the practical usefulness of the constrained formulation.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how Gaussian process pose predictions can inherit linear constraints and satisfy quadratic constraints through a change of variables.

title: Implicitly Constrained Gaussian Process Regression for Monocular Non-Rigid Pose Estimation

abstract: In discrete undirected graphical models, the conditional independence of node labels Y is specified by the graph structure. We study the case where there is another input random vector X (e.g. observed features) such that the distribution P (Y | X) is determined by functions of X that characterize the (higher-order) interactions among the Y ’s. The main contribution of this paper is to learn the graph structure and the functions conditioned on X at the same time. We prove that discrete undirected graphical models with feature X are equivalent to mul- tivariate discrete models. The reparameterization of the potential functions in graphical models by conditional log odds ratios of the latter offers advantages in representation of the conditional independence structure. The functional spaces can be flexibly determined by kernels. Additionally, we impose a Structure Lasso (SLasso) penalty on groups of functions to learn the graph structure. These groups with overlaps are designed to enforce hierarchical function selection. In this way, we are able to shrink higher order interactions to obtain a sparse graph structure.

These groups with overlaps are designed to enforce hierarchical function selection. In this way, we are able to shrink higher order interactions to obtain a sparse graph structure.

paragraphs: In a discrete undirected graphical model, graph structure expresses which labels are conditionally independent. This paper studies models where observed features also influence the interactions among labels, including interactions involving more than two labels. The task is to learn both those feature-dependent functions and the graph structure at the same time.

The authors prove an equivalence between these graphical models and multivariate discrete models. They use that connection to express potential functions through conditional log odds ratios, giving a representation better suited to describing conditional independence. Kernels provide flexibility in choosing the spaces of functions that relate observed features to label interactions.

A Structure Lasso penalty then acts on overlapping groups of functions. The groups enforce hierarchical selection, while shrinking higher-order interactions encourages a sparse graph. The approach therefore combines flexible feature dependence with structured control over interaction complexity. Its main contribution is a formulation for jointly learning relationships and their dependence on observed inputs.
summary.tldr: Structure Lasso jointly learns feature-dependent label interactions and sparse graph structure through hierarchical penalties on overlapping function groups.

title: Learning Higher-Order Graph Structure with Features by Structure Penalty

abstract: The exploration-exploitation trade-off is among the central challenges of reinforcement learning. The optimal Bayesian solution is intractable in general. This paper studies to what extent analytic statements about optimal learning are possible if all beliefs are Gaussian processes. A first order approximation of learning of both loss and dynamics, for nonlinear, time-varying systems in continuous time and space, subject to a relatively weak restriction on the dynamics, is described by an infinite-dimensional partial differential equation. An approximate finite-dimensional projection gives an impression for how this result may be helpful.
originalAbstract: The exploration-exploitation trade-off is among the central challenges of reinforcement learning. The optimal Bayesian solution is intractable in general. This paper studies to what extent analytic statements about optimal learning are possible if all beliefs are Gaussian processes. An approximate finite-dimensional projection gives an impression for how this result may be helpful.

paragraphs: An optimal learning agent must weigh immediate performance against the value of acquiring information. The general Bayesian solution to this exploration-exploitation problem is intractable. This paper asks how much analytical progress is possible when all beliefs are represented by Gaussian processes, providing a particular setting in which to study optimal learning.

The analysis covers learning both the loss and the dynamics of nonlinear, time-varying systems evolving in continuous time and space. Under a relatively weak restriction on the dynamics, a first-order approximation to that learning problem is described by an infinite-dimensional partial differential equation. The approximation and the restriction are part of the result's scope.

The authors also consider an approximate finite-dimensional projection to illustrate how the analytical result might become useful. This is presented as an indication of potential applicability. The contribution is therefore a mathematical characterization within a specified belief model, together with an illustrative approximation, rather than an exact finite-dimensional solution to the general Bayesian reinforcement-learning problem.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-process beliefs enable a first-order analytical description of learning loss and dynamics through an infinite-dimensional differential equation.

title: Optimal Reinforcement Learning for Gaussian Systems

abstract: One of the enduring challenges in Markov chain Monte Carlo methodology is the development of proposal mechanisms to make moves distant from the current point, that are accepted with high probability and at low computational cost. The recent introduction of locally adaptive MCMC methods based on the natural underlying Riemannian geometry of such models goes some way to alleviating these problems for certain classes of models for which the metric tensor is analytically tractable, however computational efficiency is not assured due to the necessity of potentially high-dimensional matrix operations at each iteration. In this paper we firstly investigate a sampling-based approach for approximating the metric tensor and suggest a valid MCMC algorithm that extends the applicability of Riemannian Manifold MCMC methods to statistical models that do not admit an analytically computable metric tensor. Secondly, we show how the approximation scheme we consider naturally motivates the use of l1 regularisation to improve estimates and obtain a sparse approximate inverse of the metric, which enables stable and sparse approximations of the local geometry to be made. We demonstrate the application of this algorithm for inferring the parameters of a realistic system of ordinary differential equations using a biologically motivated robust student-t error model, for which the expected Fisher Information is analytically intractable.

paragraphs: Geometry-aware Markov chain Monte Carlo methods use local model structure to guide sampling moves. Their promise is to make substantial moves that are often accepted, but computing the required geometry can be difficult or expensive. This paper addresses both unavailable analytic metric tensors and the cost of high-dimensional matrix operations.

The authors investigate estimating the metric tensor through sampling and propose a valid MCMC algorithm using that approximation. This extends Riemannian manifold methods to models without analytically computable metrics. The approximation also motivates l1 regularization, which improves estimates and yields a sparse approximation to the inverse metric, supporting stable representations of local geometry.

The method is demonstrated by inferring parameters of a realistic system of ordinary differential equations with a biologically motivated, robust Student-t error model. In this example, the expected Fisher information is analytically intractable. The application illustrates the intended benefit: approximate geometric information can make this class of sampling methods usable when the exact metric needed by the original approach is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Sampling-based metric estimates and sparse regularization extend geometric MCMC to models with analytically intractable local geometry.

title: Sparse Approximate Manifolds for Differential Geometric MCMC

abstract: Automatic translation from natural language descriptions into programs is a long-standing challenging problem. In this work, we consider a simple yet important sub-problem: translation from textual descriptions to If-Then programs. We devise a novel neural network architecture for this task which we train end-to-end. Specifically, we introduce Latent Attention, which computes multiplicative weights for the words in the description in a two-stage process with the goal of better leveraging the natural language structures that indicate the relevant parts for predicting program elements. Our architecture reduces the error rate by 28.57% compared to prior art. We also propose a one-shot learning scenario of If-Then program synthesis and simulate it with our existing dataset. We demonstrate a variation on the training procedure for this scenario that outperforms the original procedure, significantly closing the gap to the model trained with all data.

paragraphs: Translating natural-language requests into programs requires identifying which words specify the relevant program elements. This paper focuses on the restricted but useful task of producing If-Then programs from textual descriptions. It introduces a neural architecture trained end to end, with an attention mechanism designed to make better use of the structure in those descriptions.

Latent Attention assigns multiplicative weights to words through a two-stage process. The purpose is to identify the parts of the description that matter for predicting particular program elements. The resulting architecture reduces the error rate by 28.57% compared with prior work, providing the paper’s main reported improvement for the standard synthesis setting.

The authors also introduce a one-shot learning scenario and simulate it using their existing dataset. They modify the training procedure for this scenario and find that the variation outperforms the original procedure. It significantly narrows the gap to a model trained on all available data, indicating that training design can help the architecture work in the proposed limited-example setting.
summary.tldr: Two-stage Latent Attention improves translation from text to If-Then programs, with an adapted training procedure also helping in a simulated one-shot setting.

title: Latent Attention For If-Then Program Synthesis

abstract: Designing optimal treatment plans for patients with comorbidities requires accurate cause-specific mortality prognosis. Motivated by the recent availability of linked electronic health records, we develop a nonparametric Bayesian model for survival analysis with competing risks, which can be used for jointly assessing a patient's risk of multiple (competing) adverse outcomes. The model views a patient's survival times with respect to the competing risks as the outputs of a deep multi-task Gaussian process (DMGP), the inputs to which are the patients' covariates. Unlike parametric survival analysis methods based on Cox and Weibull models, our model uses DMGPs to capture complex non-linear interactions between the patients' covariates and cause-specific survival times, thereby learning flexible patient-specific and cause-specific survival curves, all in a data-driven fashion without explicit parametric assumptions on the hazard rates. We propose a variational inference algorithm that is capable of learning the model parameters from time-to-event data while handling right censoring. Experiments on synthetic and real data show that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art survival models.

paragraphs: Patients with multiple conditions may face several competing adverse outcomes, making cause-specific prognosis important for treatment planning. This paper develops a Bayesian survival model that jointly assesses these risks. It uses patient characteristics as inputs and represents survival times for the competing outcomes through a deep multi-task Gaussian process.

The approach is designed to capture complex nonlinear relationships between patient characteristics and cause-specific survival times. It learns survival curves that vary both by patient and by outcome, without imposing explicit parametric forms on hazard rates. This flexibility is the main distinction drawn from the Cox- and Weibull-based parametric approaches discussed in the abstract.

The authors introduce a variational inference algorithm for learning from time-to-event records while accounting for right censoring, where observation ends before the event occurs. Experiments on synthetic and real data show better performance than the state-of-the-art survival models considered. The findings support flexible joint prognosis for competing risks; the reported evaluation concerns prediction rather than demonstrated improvements in treatment outcomes.
summary.tldr: A deep multi-task Gaussian process learns flexible patient-specific survival curves for competing risks while handling censored observations.

title: Deep Multi-task Gaussian Processes for Survival Analysis with Competing Risks

abstract: Machine learning systems trained on user-provided data are susceptible to data poisoning attacks, whereby malicious users inject false training data with the aim of corrupting the learned model. While recent work has proposed a number of attacks and defenses, little is understood about the worst-case loss of a defense in the face of a determined attacker. We address this by constructing approximate upper bounds on the loss across a broad family of attacks, for defenders that first perform outlier removal followed by empirical risk minimization. Our approximation relies on two assumptions: (1) that the dataset is large enough for statistical concentration between train and test error to hold, and (2) that outliers within the clean (non-poisoned) data do not have a strong effect on the model. Our bound comes paired with a candidate attack that often nearly matches the upper bound, giving us a powerful tool for quickly assessing defenses on a given dataset. Empirically, we find that even under a simple defense, the MNIST-1-7 and Dogfish datasets are resilient to attack, while in contrast the IMDB sentiment dataset can be driven from 12% to 23% test error by adding only 3% poisoned data.

paragraphs: Data poisoning corrupts a learned model by inserting malicious examples into its training data. This paper asks how much damage an attacker could cause against a particular defense. It constructs approximate upper bounds on loss over a broad family of attacks for defenses that remove outliers and then perform empirical risk minimization.

The approximation depends on two assumptions: the dataset must be large enough for training and test errors to concentrate, and outliers in the clean data must not strongly influence the model. Each bound is accompanied by a candidate attack that often comes close to it. A close match helps assess how much room remains between demonstrated damage and the estimated worst case.

The empirical results show substantial differences across datasets. MNIST-1-7 and Dogfish remain resilient under a simple defense, whereas adding 3% poisoned data raises IMDB sentiment test error from 12% to 23%. These findings make the assessment dataset-specific: the same broad defensive approach can face very different levels of vulnerability.
summary.tldr: Approximate loss bounds paired with candidate attacks help assess poisoning defenses under explicit assumptions.

title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks

abstract: Policy-gradient approaches to reinforcement learning have two common and undesirable overhead procedures, namely warm-start training and sample variance reduction. In this paper, we describe a reinforcement learning method based on a softmax value function that requires neither of these procedures. Our method combines the advantages of policy-gradient methods with the efficiency and simplicity of maximum-likelihood approaches. We apply this new cold-start reinforcement learning method in training sequence generation models for structured output prediction problems. Empirical evidence validates this method on automatic summarization and image captioning tasks.

We apply this new cold-start reinforcement learning method in training sequence generation models for structured output prediction problems. Empirical evidence validates this method on automatic summarization and image captioning tasks.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient reinforcement learning commonly involves preliminary warm-start training and procedures for reducing sampling variance. The paper treats these as undesirable overhead and proposes a method that requires neither. Its goal is to retain advantages of policy-gradient learning while making the training procedure simpler to use.

The method is built around a softmax value function. The authors describe it as combining policy-gradient benefits with the efficiency and simplicity of maximum-likelihood approaches. The cold-start property concerns the training setup: the proposed method does not depend on a separate warm-start phase. Likewise, dispensing with a variance-reduction procedure is a claim about what the method requires, rather than a claim that sampling has no variability.

The application is sequence generation for structured output prediction, where a model must produce an entire organized output. The authors provide empirical evidence from automatic summarization and image captioning. These results support the proposed training approach in two sequence-generation tasks and connect its procedural simplification to concrete prediction problems.
summary.tldr: A softmax-value reinforcement learning method trains sequence generators without requiring warm-start training or a separate sampling-variance reduction procedure.

title: Cold-Start Reinforcement Learning with Softmax Policy Gradient

abstract: We consider the problem of improving kernel approximation via randomized feature maps. These maps arise as Monte Carlo approximation to integral representations of kernel functions and scale up kernel methods for larger datasets. Based on an efficient numerical integration technique, we propose a unifying approach that reinterprets the previous random features methods and extends to better estimates of the kernel approximation. We derive the convergence behavior and conduct an extensive empirical study that supports our hypothesis.

Based on an efficient numerical integration technique, we propose a unifying approach that reinterprets the previous random features methods and extends to better estimates of the kernel approximation. We derive the convergence behavior and conduct an extensive empirical study that supports our hypothesis.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to improve randomized feature maps used to approximate kernels. Such maps help scale kernel methods to larger datasets. The starting point is that these approximations arise by applying Monte Carlo estimation to integral representations of kernel functions.

The authors approach the problem through numerical integration. They propose a unifying method based on an efficient integration technique that both reinterprets earlier random-feature approaches and extends them toward better kernel estimates. This perspective links feature construction to the problem of approximating an integral: improving the integration procedure provides a route to improving the resulting kernel approximation.

The paper derives the method's convergence behavior and reports an extensive empirical study supporting its hypothesis. The theoretical analysis addresses how the approximation converges, while the experiments supply evidence for the proposed improvement. The stated contribution combines an explanation of existing random-feature methods with a way to extend them. Its focus is the quality of kernel approximation within the broader effort to make kernel methods practical for larger datasets.
summary.tldr: A numerical-integration framework unifies earlier random-feature methods and develops improved kernel approximations supported by convergence analysis and experiments.

title: Quadrature-based features for kernel approximation

abstract: We propose a simple, tractable lower bound on the mutual information contained in the joint generative density of any latent variable generative model: the GILBO (Generative Information Lower BOund). It offers a data-independent measure of the complexity of the learned latent variable description, giving the log of the effective description length. It is well-defined for both VAEs and GANs. We compute the GILBO for 800 GANs and VAEs each trained on four datasets (MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10 and CelebA) and discuss the results.

Mutual information captures how much the generated observation and its latent description reveal about one another, giving the metric a specific information-based interpretation.

Because it is a lower bound, its value provides a bounded assessment of the underlying information quantity rather than an assertion that the quantity has been calculated exactly.

The measure is defined for both variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks, allowing the same construction to be applied across these model types. The authors compute it for 800 GANs and VAEs trained on MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA, and discuss the results. The stated contribution is a common, computable measure of latent-description complexity across different generative modeling approaches.
summary.tldr: GILBO provides a tractable, data-independent information lower bound for assessing latent-description complexity in both VAEs and GANs.

title: GILBO: One Metric to Measure Them All

abstract: We study the general problem of testing whether an unknown discrete distribution belongs to a specified family of distributions. More specifically, given a distribution family P and sample access to an unknown discrete distribution D , we want to distinguish (with high probability) between the case that D in P and the case that D is ε-far, in total variation distance, from every distribution in P . This is the prototypical hypothesis testing problem that has received significant attention in statistics and, more recently, in computer science. The main contribution of this work is a simple and general testing technique that is applicable to all distribution families whose Fourier spectrum satisfies a certain approximate sparsity property. We apply our Fourier-based framework to obtain near sample-optimal and computationally efficient testers for the following fundamental distribution families: Sums of Independent Integer Random Variables (SIIRVs), Poisson Multinomial Distributions (PMDs), and Discrete Log-Concave Distributions. For the first two, ours are the first non-trivial testers in the literature, vastly generalizing previous work on testing Poisson Binomial Distributions. For the third, our tester improves on prior work in both sample and time complexity.

The testing goal is to distinguish, with high probability, a distribution inside the family from one at least ε away from every member in total variation distance. This formulation asks for a reliable distinction between membership and substantial departure.

That structural condition is central: it identifies the families for which the framework can yield efficient tests, rather than asserting a method for every possible family.

For the first two families, the paper provides the first nontrivial testers, extending earlier Poisson-binomial testing work. For discrete log-concave distributions, it improves both sample and time complexity over previous methods.
summary.tldr: Approximate sparsity in the Fourier domain enables efficient, nearly sample-optimal membership tests for several important discrete distribution families.

title: Testing for Families of Distributions via the Fourier Transform

abstract: Multiplicative noise, including dropout, is widely used to regularize deep neural networks (DNNs), and is shown to be effective in a wide range of architectures and tasks. From an information perspective, we consider injecting multiplicative noise into a DNN as training the network to solve the task with noisy information pathways, which leads to the observation that multiplicative noise tends to increase the correlation between features, so as to increase the signal-to-noise ratio of information pathways. However, high feature correlation is undesirable, as it increases redundancy in representations. In this work, we propose non-correlating multiplicative noise (NCMN), which exploits batch normalization to remove the correlation effect in a simple yet effective way. We show that NCMN significantly improves the performance of standard multiplicative noise on image classification tasks, providing a better alternative to dropout for batch-normalized networks. Additionally, we present a unified view of NCMN and shake-shake regularization, which explains the performance gain of the latter.

The paper examines a side effect of that process: features tend to become more correlated as the network increases the signal-to-noise ratio of those pathways. The proposed non-correlating multiplicative noise method, NCMN, uses batch normalization to remove this correlation effect. Its aim is to change how noise influences learned features while retaining a noise-based regularization approach. The design therefore targets a specific consequence of multiplicative noise rather than treating its effect on representations as uniformly beneficial.

The authors report significant image-classification improvements over standard multiplicative noise and present NCMN as a better alternative to dropout for batch-normalized networks. They also give a unified interpretation of NCMN and shake-shake regularization that explains the latter's performance gains. The contribution combines a practical regularization method with an account of how feature correlation helps explain differences between these training approaches.
summary.tldr: NCMN uses batch normalization to remove multiplicative noise's feature-correlation effect and improves reported image-classification performance.

title: Removing the Feature Correlation Effect of Multiplicative Noise

abstract: Mapping structural brain connectomes for living human brains typically requires expert analysis and rule-based models on diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging. A data-driven approach, however, could overcome limitations in such rule-based approaches and improve precision mappings for individuals. In this work, we explore a framework that facilitates applying learning algorithms to automatically extract brain connectomes. Using a tensor encoding, we design an objective with a group-regularizer that prefers biologically plausible fascicle structure. We show that the objective is convex and has unique solutions, ensuring identifiable connectomes for an individual. We develop an efficient optimization strategy for this extremely high-dimensional sparse problem, by reducing the number of parameters using a greedy algorithm designed specifically for the problem. We show that this greedy algorithm significantly improves on a standard greedy algorithm, called Orthogonal Matching Pursuit. We conclude with an analysis of the solutions found by our method, showing we can accurately reconstruct the diffusion information while maintaining contiguous fascicles with smooth direction changes.

Its aim is to fit the measured diffusion information while favoring structures that are biologically plausible.

The framework uses a tensor encoding and an objective with group regularization to encourage plausible fascicles, or bundles of fibers. The authors show that the objective is convex and has a unique solution, giving identifiability within the proposed formulation. This mathematical property makes the inferred solution well defined for an individual under the model.

Because the sparse optimization problem is extremely high dimensional, the authors design a specialized greedy algorithm to reduce the number of parameters. It significantly improves on Orthogonal Matching Pursuit in the reported comparison. Analysis of the resulting solutions shows accurate reconstruction of diffusion information alongside contiguous fascicles with smooth directional changes. These findings connect computational tractability, a unique optimization solution, and the structural preferences built into the objective.
summary.tldr: A convex, group-regularized framework learns individual brain connectomes while encouraging contiguous fascicles with smooth directional changes.

title: Learning Macroscopic Brain Connectomes via Group-Sparse Factorization

abstract: Recent breakthroughs in AI for multi-agent games like Go, Poker, and Dota, have seen great strides in recent years. Yet none of these games address the real-life challenge of cooperation in the presence of unknown and uncertain teammates. This challenge is a key game mechanism in hidden role games. Here we develop the DeepRole algorithm, a multi-agent reinforcement learning agent that we test on "The Resistance: Avalon", the most popular hidden role game. DeepRole combines counterfactual regret minimization (CFR) with deep value networks trained through self-play. Our algorithm integrates deductive reasoning into vector-form CFR to reason about joint beliefs and deduce partially observable actions. We augment deep value networks with constraints that yield interpretable representations of win probabilities. These innovations enable DeepRole to scale to the full Avalon game. Empirical game-theoretic methods show that DeepRole outperforms other hand-crafted and learned agents in five-player Avalon. DeepRole played with and against human players on the web in hybrid human-agent teams. We find that DeepRole outperforms human players as both a cooperator and a competitor.
