paragraphs: Hidden-role games require cooperation without knowing who is genuinely on the same side. This uncertainty adds a challenge beyond choosing strong actions against known opponents. The paper develops DeepRole for The Resistance: Avalon, where reasoning about other players' roles and partially observed behavior is central to effective play.

DeepRole combines counterfactual regret minimization with deep value networks trained through self-play. Deductive reasoning is incorporated into the regret-minimization procedure so the agent can reason about joint beliefs and infer partially observable actions. Constraints on the value networks produce interpretable representations of winning probabilities. Together, these components allow the approach to handle the full game.

Empirical game-theoretic evaluation shows that DeepRole outperforms the tested handcrafted and learned agents in five-player Avalon. The authors also evaluate it in online teams mixing humans and agents, where it outperforms human players in both cooperative and competitive roles. These findings demonstrate effective hidden-role play in the evaluated game, including situations where success depends on working with uncertain teammates.
summary.tldr: DeepRole combines game-theoretic learning and deductive reasoning to cooperate and compete successfully in five-player Avalon.

title: Finding Friend and Foe in Multi-Agent Games

abstract: Perception and reasoning are two representative abilities of intelligence that are integrated seamlessly during human problem-solving processes. In the area of artificial intelligence (AI), the two abilities are usually realised by machine learning and logic programming, respectively. However, the two categories of techniques were developed separately throughout most of the history of AI. In this paper, we present the abductive learning targeted at unifying the two AI paradigms in a mutually beneficial way, where the machine learning model learns to perceive primitive logic facts from data, while logical reasoning can exploit symbolic domain knowledge and correct the wrongly perceived facts for improving the machine learning models. Furthermore, we propose a novel approach to optimise the machine learning model and the logical reasoning model jointly. We demonstrate that by using abductive learning, machines can learn to recognise numbers and resolve unknown mathematical operations simultaneously from images of simple hand-written equations. Moreover, the learned models can be generalised to longer equations and adapted to different tasks, which is beyond the capability of state-of-the-art deep learning models.

paragraphs: The paper connects two capabilities that are often developed separately: learning to recognize information in raw data and reasoning with symbolic knowledge. In abductive learning, a machine learning model converts observations into primitive logical facts. A reasoning component then uses domain knowledge to identify and correct facts that were perceived incorrectly.

Those corrections feed back into learning, so symbolic reasoning helps improve perception rather than simply consuming its outputs. The authors also propose a method for jointly optimizing the learning and reasoning models. This mutual interaction matters because errors in recognizing an input need not remain fixed before reasoning begins.

The demonstration uses images of simple handwritten equations. The system learns both to recognize numbers and to resolve unknown mathematical operations, bringing visual interpretation and reasoning into the same learning process. The authors report that the learned models generalize to longer equations and adapt to different tasks, beyond the capabilities of the state-of-the-art deep learning models considered. These results illustrate how domain knowledge can guide learning when recognizing symbols and understanding their relationships must happen together.
summary.tldr: Abductive learning jointly develops perception and logical reasoning, using symbolic knowledge to correct learned interpretations of handwritten equations.

title: Bridging Machine Learning and Logical Reasoning by Abductive Learning

abstract: Sequential modelling with self-attention has achieved cutting edge performances in natural language processing. With advantages in model flexibility, computation complexity and interpretability, self-attention is gradually becoming a key component in event sequence models. However, like most other sequence models, self-attention does not account for the time span between events and thus captures sequential signals rather than temporal patterns. Without relying on recurrent network structures, self-attention recognizes event orderings via positional encoding. To bridge the gap between modelling time-independent and time-dependent event sequence, we introduce a functional feature map that embeds time span into high-dimensional spaces. By constructing the associated translation-invariant time kernel function, we reveal the functional forms of the feature map under classic functional function analysis results, namely Bochner's Theorem and Mercer's Theorem. We propose several models to learn the functional time representation and the interactions with event representation. These methods are evaluated on real-world datasets under various continuous-time event sequence prediction tasks. The experiments reveal that the proposed methods compare favorably to baseline models while also capture useful time-event interactions.

paragraphs: Event order and elapsed time carry different information. Positional encoding lets self-attention distinguish where events occur in a sequence, but does not itself account for the gaps between them. This paper introduces a representation of time spans to help attention-based models capture temporal patterns alongside sequential order.

The method maps time spans into high-dimensional feature spaces. The authors construct an associated translation-invariant time kernel and use Bochner’s and Mercer’s theorems to derive functional forms for the feature map. This supplies a mathematical basis for representing elapsed time within the model, connecting the time features to kernel-based descriptions of temporal relationships.

The paper proposes several models that learn these time representations and their interactions with event representations. Evaluations use real-world datasets and multiple continuous-time event prediction tasks. The methods compare favorably with baseline models and capture useful interactions between timing and events. The findings support explicitly representing elapsed time when event sequences contain predictive temporal structure beyond their ordering.
summary.tldr: Kernel-derived time features help self-attention model elapsed time and useful time-event interactions in continuous-time prediction tasks.

title: Self-attention with Functional Time Representation Learning

abstract: We study nonzero-sum hypothesis testing games that arise in the context of adversarial classification, in both the Bayesian as well as the Neyman-Pearson frameworks. We first show that these games admit mixed strategy Nash equilibria, and then we examine some interesting concentration phenomena of these equilibria. Our main results are on the exponential rates of convergence of classification errors at equilibrium, which are analogous to the well-known Chernoff-Stein lemma and Chernoff information that describe the error exponents in the classical binary hypothesis testing problem, but with parameters derived from the adversarial model. The results are validated through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Hypothesis testing concerns deciding which explanation is supported by observations. In adversarial classification, that decision occurs in the presence of another participant with strategic interests. This paper studies nonzero-sum versions of such games, where the participants' objectives need not be exact opposites, under both Bayesian and Neyman–Pearson formulations.

The authors first establish the existence of mixed-strategy Nash equilibria. These are stable combinations of potentially randomized strategies, in which neither participant gains by changing strategy alone. They then investigate concentration phenomena associated with those equilibria, examining structure in the strategic behavior rather than only proving that equilibria exist.

The main results characterize exponential rates of convergence for classification errors at equilibrium. They parallel classical error-exponent results associated with the Chernoff–Stein lemma and Chernoff information, but use parameters determined by the adversarial model. Numerical experiments validate the results. The contribution connects strategic classification with precise descriptions of how its error behavior compares structurally with classical binary testing.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes equilibria and characterizes classification-error exponents for nonzero-sum adversarial hypothesis-testing games.

title: Nonzero-sum Adversarial Hypothesis Testing Games

abstract: Long-term temporal credit assignment is an important challenge in deep reinforcement learning (RL). It refers to the ability of the agent to attribute actions to consequences that may occur after a long time interval. Existing policy-gradient and Q-learning algorithms typically rely on dense environmental rewards that provide rich short-term supervision and help with credit assignment. However, they struggle to solve tasks with delays between an action and the corresponding rewarding feedback. To make credit assignment easier, recent works have proposed algorithms to learn dense "guidance" rewards that could be used in place of the sparse or delayed environmental rewards. This paper is in the same vein -- starting with a surrogate RL objective that involves smoothing in the trajectory-space, we arrive at a new algorithm for learning guidance rewards. We show that the guidance rewards have an intuitive interpretation, and can be obtained without training any additional neural networks. Due to the ease of integration, we use the guidance rewards in a few popular algorithms (Q-learning, Actor-Critic, Distributional-RL) and present results in single-agent and multi-agent tasks that elucidate the benefit of our approach when the environmental rewards are sparse or delayed.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when an action's useful consequences appear much later. The learner must determine which earlier decisions deserve credit despite sparse or delayed feedback. This paper studies learned guidance rewards, which supply denser feedback that can be used in place of the environment's original rewards to make that assignment easier.

The authors begin with a substitute reinforcement learning objective that smooths over trajectory space, the space of sequences of interaction. From this objective they derive an algorithm for learning guidance rewards. They show that the resulting rewards have an intuitive interpretation and can be obtained without training additional neural networks, making the construction easier to integrate into existing methods.

The contribution therefore combines an objective-based derivation with a practical integration strategy: improving the feedback used for learning can help established algorithms address long-term credit assignment without adding another neural network to train.
summary.tldr: Trajectory-space smoothing yields learned guidance rewards that help existing reinforcement learning algorithms handle sparse or delayed feedback.

title: Learning Guidance Rewards with Trajectory-space Smoothing

abstract: We extend randomized smoothing to cover parameterized transformations (e.g., rotations, translations) and certify robustness in the parameter space (e.g., rotation angle). This is particularly challenging as interpolation and rounding effects mean that image transformations do not compose, in turn preventing direct certification of the perturbed image (unlike certification with $\ell^p$ norms). We address this challenge by introducing three different defenses, each with a different guarantee (heuristic, distributional and individual) stemming from the method used to bound the interpolation error. Importantly, in the individual case, we show how to efficiently compute the inverse of an image transformation, enabling us to provide individual guarantees in the online setting. We provide an implementation of all methods at https://github.com/eth-sri/transformation-smoothing.

This is particularly challenging as interpolation and rounding effects mean that image transformations do not compose, in turn preventing direct certification of the perturbed image (unlike certification with $\ell^p$ norms). We address this challenge by introducing three different defenses, each with a different guarantee (heuristic, distributional and individual) stemming from the method used to bound the interpolation error. Importantly, in the individual case, we show how to efficiently compute the inverse of an image transformation, enabling us to provide individual guarantees in the online setting. paragraphs: This paper extends randomized smoothing to image transformations described by parameters, such as rotation angles or translation amounts. The goal is to certify robustness with respect to changes in those parameters. This connects robustness guarantees to geometric alterations of an image, with the transformation's parameter space defining the changes being considered.

A central obstacle comes from how digital images are transformed. Interpolation and rounding mean that applying transformations in sequence does not necessarily behave like their mathematical composition. As a result, certification cannot simply be transferred directly to a perturbed image using the reasoning available for standard pixel-norm perturbations. The authors address this issue by bounding the interpolation error.

Different ways of handling that error lead to three defenses with distinct guarantee types: heuristic, distributional, and individual. These distinctions matter because the methods provide different levels or forms of assurance. For the individual case, the paper develops an efficient way to compute an image transformation's inverse, enabling guarantees in an online setting. The contribution combines an extension of smoothing with explicit treatment of the digital effects that complicate transformation-based certification.
summary.tldr: The paper extends randomized smoothing to geometric image transformations through three defenses with different forms of assurance.

title: Certified Defense to Image Transformations via Randomized Smoothing

abstract: Deep Gaussian Processes learn probabilistic data representations for supervised learning by cascading multiple Gaussian Processes. While this model family promises flexible predictive distributions, exact inference is not tractable. Approximate inference techniques trade off the ability to closely resemble the posterior distribution against speed of convergence and computational efficiency. We propose a novel Gaussian variational family that allows for retaining covariances between latent processes while achieving fast convergence by marginalising out all global latent variables. After providing a proof of how this marginalisation can be done for general covariances, we restrict them to the ones we empirically found to be most important in order to also achieve computational efficiency. We provide an efficient implementation of our new approach and apply it to several benchmark datasets. It yields excellent results and strikes a better balance between accuracy and calibrated uncertainty estimates than its state-of-the-art alternatives.

Their appeal includes rich predictive uncertainty, but exact inference is computationally intractable. Practical methods therefore approximate the posterior, balancing how faithfully they represent it against how quickly and efficiently they can learn.

This paper introduces a Gaussian variational approximation that retains covariances between latent processes. These covariances represent dependencies that would otherwise be discarded by a more restrictive approximation. The method also integrates out all global latent variables to achieve fast convergence. The authors prove that this marginalization is possible for general covariance structures, providing a theoretical foundation for the approach.

To make the method computationally efficient, the implementation retains the covariances that the authors empirically identify as most important. This combines a more expressive approximation with a selective use of its additional dependencies. Across several benchmark datasets, the method achieves a better balance between predictive accuracy and calibrated uncertainty than the leading alternatives considered. The result supports preserving selected posterior dependencies when reliable uncertainty is an important part of prediction.
summary.tldr: Retaining selected dependencies in deep Gaussian process inference improves the benchmark balance between predictive accuracy and calibrated uncertainty.

title: Beyond the Mean-Field: Structured Deep Gaussian Processes Improve the Predictive Uncertainties

abstract: Neural Coding analyses often reflect an assumption that neural populations respond uniquely and consistently to particular stimuli. For example, analyses of spatial remapping in hippocampal populations often assume that each environment has one unique representation and that remapping occurs over long time scales as an animal traverses between distinct environments. However, as neuroscience experiments begin to explore more naturalistic tasks and stimuli, and reflect more ambiguity in neural representations, methods for analyzing population neural codes must adapt to reflect these features. In this paper, we develop a new state-space modeling framework to address two important issues related to remapping. First, neurons may exhibit significant trial-to-trial or moment-to-moment variability in the firing patterns used to represent a particular environment or stimulus. Second, in ambiguous environments and tasks that involve cognitive uncertainty, neural populations may rapidly fluctuate between multiple representations. The state-space model addresses these two issues by integrating an observation model, which allows for multiple representations of the same stimulus or environment, with a state model, which characterizes the moment-by-moment probability of a shift in the neural representation. These models allow us to compute instantaneous estimates of the stimulus or environment currently represented by the population. We demonstrate the application of this approach to the analysis of population activity in the CA1 region of hippocampus of a mouse moving through ambiguous virtual environments. Our analyses demonstrate that many hippocampal cells express significant trial-to-trial variability in their representations and that the population representation can fluctuate rapidly between environments within a single trial when spatial cues are most ambiguous.

Second, in ambiguous environments and tasks that involve cognitive uncertainty, neural populations may rapidly fluctuate between multiple representations. The state-space model addresses these two issues by integrating an observation model, which allows for multiple representations of the same stimulus or environment, with a state model, which characterizes the moment-by-moment probability of a shift in the neural representation. These models allow us to compute instantaneous estimates of the stimulus or environment currently represented by the population. We demonstrate the application of this approach to the analysis of population activity in the CA1 region of hippocampus of a mouse moving through ambiguous virtual environments. Our analyses demonstrate that many hippocampal cells express significant trial-to-trial variability in their representations and that the population representation can fluctuate rapidly between environments within a single trial when spatial cues are most ambiguous.

The authors develop a state-space framework with two complementary components. An observation model permits multiple activity patterns for the same stimulus or environment. A state model describes the moment-by-moment probability that the representation changes. Together, these components produce instantaneous estimates of which stimulus or environment the population currently represents, while allowing both variable firing patterns and changing represented content.

The framework is applied to activity in the CA1 region of a mouse's hippocampus during movement through ambiguous virtual environments. The analysis finds substantial trial-to-trial representational variation in many cells. It also finds that population representations can switch rapidly between environments within a trial when spatial cues are most ambiguous. These findings show why a model that permits both variability and rapid switching can reveal structure obscured by a single stable representation.
summary.tldr: A state-space model reveals variable and rapidly switching hippocampal representations in a mouse navigating ambiguous virtual environments.

title: Estimating Fluctuations in Neural Representations of Uncertain Environments

abstract: We develop a framework that leverages the smoothed complexity analysis by Spielman and Teng to circumvent paradoxes and impossibility theorems in social choice, motivated by modern applications of social choice powered by AI and ML. For Condrocet’s paradox, we prove that the smoothed likelihood of the paradox either vanishes at an exponential rate as the number of agents increases, or does not vanish at all. For the ANR impossibility on the non-existence of voting rules that simultaneously satisfy anonymity, neutrality, and resolvability, we characterize the rate for the impossibility to vanish, to be either polynomially fast or exponentially fast. We also propose a novel easy-to-compute tie-breaking mechanism that optimally preserves anonymity and neutrality for even number of alternatives in natural settings. Our results illustrate the smoothed possibility of social choice—even though the paradox and the impossibility theorem hold in the worst case, they may not be a big concern in practice.

paragraphs: Social-choice impossibility results establish that desirable voting properties can conflict in the worst case. This paper uses smoothed analysis to investigate how persistently those problems arise beyond a purely worst-case perspective. The aim is to characterize when classical obstacles may become less concerning as the number of voters grows.

For Condorcet's paradox, the authors prove a dichotomy: its smoothed likelihood either decreases exponentially with the number of agents or fails to vanish. They also study the incompatibility of anonymity, neutrality, and resolvability, characterizing cases where the impossibility vanishes at polynomial or exponential rates. These are rate and regime results, so they retain the possibility that some problems remain prevalent.

The paper additionally proposes an easily computed tie-breaking mechanism that optimally preserves anonymity and neutrality for an even number of alternatives in natural settings. Together, the results show how worst-case impossibilities can coexist with more favorable behavior under smoothed analysis. They support a conditional practical possibility for social choice while leaving the underlying impossibility theorems intact.
summary.tldr: Smoothed analysis characterizes when voting paradoxes and impossibilities diminish, showing why worst-case obstacles may be less severe in some settings.

title: The Smoothed Possibility of Social Choice

abstract: One of the common ways children learn is by mimicking adults. Imitation learning focuses on learning policies with suitable performance from demonstrations generated by an expert, with an unspecified performance measure, and unobserved reward signal. Popular methods for imitation learning start by either directly mimicking the behavior policy of an expert (behavior cloning) or by learning a reward function that prioritizes observed expert trajectories (inverse reinforcement learning). However, these methods rely on the assumption that covariates used by the expert to determine her/his actions are fully observed. In this paper, we relax this assumption and study imitation learning when sensory inputs of the learner and the expert differ. First, we provide a non-parametric, graphical criterion that is complete (both necessary and sufficient) for determining the feasibility of imitation from the combinations of demonstration data and qualitative assumptions about the underlying environment, represented in the form of a causal model. We then show that when such a criterion does not hold, imitation could still be feasible by exploiting quantitative knowledge of the expert trajectories. Finally, we develop an efficient procedure for learning the imitating policy from experts' trajectories.

Common approaches copy the expert's behavior or infer a reward that favors expert trajectories. These methods rely on observing the variables the expert uses to choose actions. This paper studies what happens when the learner and expert receive different sensory information.

The authors develop a graphical criterion using demonstration data and qualitative assumptions about the environment expressed as a causal model. The criterion is complete: it is both necessary and sufficient for establishing imitation feasibility from that combination of information. This gives a precise way to assess whether available observations and causal knowledge support learning an imitating policy.

Failure of that criterion does not settle every possible case. The paper shows that additional quantitative knowledge of expert trajectories can still make imitation feasible. It also develops an efficient procedure for learning the policy from those trajectories. The distinction matters because feasibility depends on both what is observed and what kind of knowledge about the expert and environment is available.
summary.tldr: A causal framework characterizes when imitation is feasible with unequal expert and learner observations and provides a policy-learning procedure.

title: Causal Imitation Learning With Unobserved Confounders

abstract: Normalizing flows and variational autoencoders are powerful generative models that can represent complicated density functions. However, they both impose constraints on the models: Normalizing flows use bijective transformations to model densities whereas VAEs learn stochastic transformations that are non-invertible and thus typically do not provide tractable estimates of the marginal likelihood. In this paper, we introduce SurVAE Flows: A modular framework of composable transformations that encompasses VAEs and normalizing flows. SurVAE Flows bridge the gap between normalizing flows and VAEs with surjective transformations, wherein the transformations are deterministic in one direction -- thereby allowing exact likelihood computation, and stochastic in the reverse direction -- hence providing a lower bound on the corresponding likelihood. We show that several recently proposed methods, including dequantization and augmented normalizing flows, can be expressed as SurVAE Flows. Finally, we introduce common operations such as the max value, the absolute value, sorting and stochastic permutation as composable layers in SurVAE Flows.

SurVAE Flows provide a modular framework that encompasses both kinds of generative model.

The connecting ingredient is a surjective transformation, which can map multiple inputs to the same output. In the framework described by the authors, the transformation is deterministic in one direction, allowing exact likelihood computation, and stochastic in the reverse direction, yielding a likelihood lower bound. This directional distinction explains how the framework links exact and variational treatments.

The authors show that existing methods, including dequantization and augmented normalizing flows, can be expressed within SurVAE Flows. They also introduce composable layers based on maximum values, absolute values, sorting, and stochastic permutations. The contribution is a common language for combining transformations with different invertibility properties while tracking the appropriate likelihood computation or bound for the resulting construction.
summary.tldr: SurVAE Flows unify flows and VAEs through composable transformations that connect exact likelihood computation with variational lower bounds.

title: SurVAE Flows: Surjections to Bridge the Gap between VAEs and Flows

abstract: We study the problem of sampling from a probability distribution on $\mathbb R^p$ defined via a convex and smooth potential function. We first consider a continuous-time diffusion-type process, termed Penalized Langevin dynamics (PLD), the drift of which is the negative gradient of the potential plus a linear penalty that vanishes when time goes to infinity. An upper bound on the Wasserstein-2 distance between the distribution of the PLD at time $t$ and the target is established. This upper bound highlights the influence of the speed of decay of the penalty on the accuracy of approximation. As a consequence, in the case of low-temperature limit we infer a new result on the convergence of the penalized gradient flow for the optimization problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies sampling from a distribution on a Euclidean space whose potential function is smooth and convex. Its proposed process modifies continuous-time Langevin dynamics by adding a linear penalty to the drift associated with the negative potential gradient. The penalty decreases over time and eventually vanishes.

The central analysis bounds the Wasserstein-2 distance between the process's distribution at a given time and the target distribution. This measures approximation error between distributions in a way that accounts for geometry. The bound explicitly reveals how the speed at which the penalty disappears affects accuracy, connecting a design choice in the dynamics to a quantitative guarantee.

The authors also examine the low-temperature limit, obtaining a convergence result for penalized gradient flow in optimization. Thus, the same construction links a noisy sampling process with an optimization flow in that limit. The contribution is an analysis of a time-varying penalty under the stated smoothness and convexity assumptions, showing how its decay enters sampling accuracy and yields a related optimization result.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds sampling error for Langevin dynamics with a vanishing linear penalty and derives a related gradient-flow convergence result.

title: Penalized Langevin dynamics with vanishing penalty for smooth and log-concave targets

abstract: Many practical tasks involve sampling sequentially without replacement (WoR) from a finite population of size $N$, in an attempt to estimate some parameter $\theta^\star$. Accurately quantifying uncertainty throughout this process is a nontrivial task, but is necessary because it often determines when we stop collecting samples and confidently report a result. We present a suite of tools for designing \textit{confidence sequences} (CS) for $\theta^\star$. A CS is a sequence of confidence sets $(C_n)_{n=1}^N$, that shrink in size, and all contain $\theta^\star$ simultaneously with high probability. We present a generic approach to constructing a frequentist CS using Bayesian tools, based on the fact that the ratio of a prior to the posterior at the ground truth is a martingale. We then present Hoeffding- and empirical-Bernstein-type time-uniform CSs and fixed-time confidence intervals for sampling WoR, which improve on previous bounds in the literature and explicitly quantify the benefit of WoR sampling.

paragraphs: When sampling sequentially from a finite population without replacement, uncertainty changes as more distinct items are observed. That uncertainty may determine when to stop collecting data. The paper develops confidence sequences: successive confidence sets that become smaller while simultaneously containing the target parameter with high probability across the sampling process.

The simultaneous guarantee is central. It addresses uncertainty throughout data collection, rather than only at one predetermined sample size. The authors give a general construction that uses Bayesian quantities to obtain a frequentist confidence sequence. The key mathematical property is that the ratio of the prior to the posterior, evaluated at the true parameter, forms a martingale.

The paper also develops Hoeffding-type and empirical-Bernstein-type bounds, including both time-uniform confidence sequences and fixed-time intervals. These improve on previous bounds and explicitly measure the advantage of sampling without replacement. Together, the results provide tools for reporting uncertainty as observations accumulate, with guarantees that account for the finite population and the fact that previously sampled items cannot be drawn again.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs tighter uncertainty bounds that remain valid throughout sequential sampling without replacement.

title: Confidence sequences for sampling without replacement

abstract: We aim at the problem named One-Shot Unsupervised Domain Adaptation. Unlike traditional Unsupervised Domain Adaptation, it assumes that only one unlabeled target sample can be available when learning to adapt. This setting is realistic but more challenging, in which conventional adaptation approaches are prone to failure due to the scarce of unlabeled target data. To this end, we propose a novel Adversarial Style Mining approach, which combines the style transfer module and task-specific module into an adversarial manner. Specifically, the style transfer module iteratively searches for harder stylized images around the one-shot target sample according to the current learning state, leading the task model to explore the potential styles that are difficult to solve in the almost unseen target domain, thus boosting the adaptation performance in a data-scarce scenario. The adversarial learning framework makes the style transfer module and task-specific module benefit each other during the competition. Extensive experiments on both cross-domain classification and segmentation benchmarks verify that ASM achieves state-of-the-art adaptation performance under the challenging one-shot setting.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation aims to help a model handle data from a different environment. This paper studies an especially restrictive version: only one unlabeled example from the target environment is available during adaptation. That single example provides little evidence about the range of appearances the model may later encounter, making conventional adaptation approaches prone to failure.

Adversarial Style Mining couples a style-transfer module with the model performing the actual task. The style-transfer module repeatedly searches for stylized images around the available target example that are difficult for the current task model. As the task model changes, the search changes too, directing training toward styles that remain challenging.

This competitive interaction is intended to make both modules improve together while exposing the task model to potential variation in the largely unseen target domain. Experiments on cross-domain classification and segmentation benchmarks report state-of-the-art adaptation performance in the one-shot setting. The findings support using actively mined style variation to make more effective use of an extremely small amount of target data.
summary.tldr: Adversarial Style Mining improves one-shot domain adaptation by generating stylized examples that challenge the current task model.

title: Adversarial Style Mining for One-Shot Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: Mathematically characterizing the implicit regularization induced by gradient-based optimization is a longstanding pursuit in the theory of deep learning. A widespread hope is that a characterization based on minimization of norms may apply, and a standard test-bed for studying this prospect is matrix factorization (matrix completion via linear neural networks). It is an open question whether norms can explain the implicit regularization in matrix factorization. The current paper resolves this open question in the negative, by proving that there exist natural matrix factorization problems on which the implicit regularization drives all norms (and quasi-norms) towards infinity. Our results suggest that, rather than perceiving the implicit regularization via norms, a potentially more useful interpretation is minimization of rank. We demonstrate empirically that this interpretation extends to a certain class of non-linear neural networks, and hypothesize that it may be key to explaining generalization in deep learning.

paragraphs: Gradient-based training can favor particular solutions even without an explicit regularization penalty. A common hope is that this implicit preference can be described as minimizing a norm. This paper tests that idea in matrix factorization, a standard setting that represents matrix completion through linear neural networks.

The authors prove that natural matrix-factorization problems exist where the implicit regularization sends every norm and quasi-norm toward infinity. This rules out norm minimization as a general explanation for the behavior in that setting. The force of the result comes from these counterexamples, rather than a claim that norms are uninformative for every learning problem.

The paper suggests minimizing rank as a potentially more useful interpretation of the optimization bias. Experiments provide evidence that this interpretation also applies to a particular class of nonlinear neural networks. The authors further hypothesize that it could help explain generalization more broadly. That broader possibility remains distinct from the proved counterexamples and the empirical extension to the specified network class.
summary.tldr: Matrix-factorization counterexamples rule out norm minimization as a general account of implicit regularization and motivate a rank-based interpretation.

title: Implicit Regularization in Deep Learning May Not Be Explainable by Norms

abstract: We initiate the work towards a comprehensive picture of the worst average-case satisfaction of voting axioms in semi-random models, to provide a finer and more realistic foundation for comparing voting rules. We adopt the semi-random model and formulation in [Xia 2020], where an adversary chooses arbitrarily correlated ``ground truth'' preferences for the agents, on top of which random noises are added. We focus on characterizing the semi-random satisfaction of two well-studied voting axioms: Condorcet criterion and participation. We prove that for any fixed number of alternatives, when the number of voters $n$ is sufficiently large, the semi-random satisfaction of the Condorcet criterion under a wide range of voting rules is $1$, $1-\exp(-\Theta(n))$, $\Theta(n^{-0.5})$, $ \exp(-\Theta(n))$, or being $\Theta(1)$ and $1-\Theta(1)$ at the same time; and the semi-random satisfaction of participation is $1-\Theta(n^{-0.5})$. Our results address open questions by Berg and Lepelley in 1994, and also confirm the following high-level message: the Condorcet criterion is a bigger concern than participation under realistic models.

paragraphs: Voting rules can be compared by how often they satisfy desirable principles, rather than only whether a counterexample exists. This paper studies a worst-average-case setting: an adversary chooses potentially correlated underlying voter preferences, after which random noise is added. The framework combines unfavorable preference structure with randomness to analyze the reliability of voting axioms.

The analysis focuses on the Condorcet criterion and participation. For a fixed number of alternatives and sufficiently many voters, the authors classify several possible behaviors for Condorcet satisfaction across a wide range of voting rules. Satisfaction can be certain, approach certainty exponentially, decay at an inverse-square-root or exponential rate, or remain bounded away from both zero and one.

For participation, the satisfaction probability instead approaches one with a shortfall of order one over the square root of the voter count. These asymptotic results distinguish the frequency of violations under the semi-random model, rather than merely their possibility. They support the authors' conclusion that Condorcet satisfaction is the larger concern in the models studied, while also resolving previously open questions.
summary.tldr: Semi-random voting analysis shows that Condorcet satisfaction can behave much less favorably than participation as the electorate grows.

title: The Semi-Random Satisfaction of Voting Axioms

abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) powered by neural net approximation of the Q function has had enormous empirical success. While the theory of RL has traditionally focused on linear function approximation (or eluder dimension) approaches, little is known about nonlinear RL with neural net approximations of the Q functions. This is the focus of this work, where we study function approximation with two-layer neural networks (considering both ReLU and polynomial activation functions). Our first result is a computationally and statistically efficient algorithm in the generative model setting under completeness for two-layer neural networks. Our second result considers this setting but under only realizability of the neural net function class. Here, assuming deterministic dynamics, the sample complexity scales linearly in the algebraic dimension. In all cases, our results significantly improve upon what can be attained with linear (or eluder dimension) methods.

paragraphs: Neural networks have been successful at approximating action-value functions in reinforcement learning, but theoretical understanding has focused heavily on linear approximations. This paper studies what efficiency guarantees are possible when the approximating functions are two-layer neural networks. It considers both ReLU and polynomial activation functions.

The first result provides an algorithm that is efficient in both computation and samples in a generative-model setting, under a completeness assumption for the neural function class. Completeness is a substantive requirement on the class, so the result establishes efficiency within that setting rather than for arbitrary neural reinforcement learning problems.

The second result replaces completeness with realizability of the neural function class, while additionally assuming deterministic dynamics. Under these conditions, sample complexity grows linearly with the algebraic dimension. Across the analyzed cases, the guarantees significantly improve on what linear or eluder-dimension methods can attain. Together, the results show how analyzing nonlinear neural structure directly can yield stronger efficiency guarantees under explicitly stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes efficient reinforcement learning with two-layer neural approximations under distinct completeness or realizability-and-deterministic-dynamics assumptions.

title: Going Beyond Linear RL: Sample Efficient Neural Function Approximation

abstract: Gaussian Processes (GPs) have been widely used in machine learning to model distributions over functions, with applications including multi-modal regression, time-series prediction, and few-shot learning. GPs are particularly useful in the last application since they rely on Normal distributions and enable closed-form computation of the posterior probability function. Unfortunately, because the resulting posterior is not flexible enough to capture complex distributions, GPs assume high similarity between subsequent tasks - a requirement rarely met in real-world conditions. In this work, we address this limitation by leveraging the flexibility of Normalizing Flows to modulate the posterior predictive distribution of the GP. This makes the GP posterior locally non-Gaussian, therefore we name our method Non-Gaussian Gaussian Processes (NGGPs). More precisely, we propose an invertible ODE-based mapping that operates on each component of the random variable vectors and shares the parameters across all of them. We empirically tested the flexibility of NGGPs on various few-shot learning regression datasets, showing that the mapping can incorporate context embedding information to model different noise levels for periodic functions. As a result, our method shares the structure of the problem between subsequent tasks, but the contextualization allows for adaptation to dissimilarities. NGGPs outperform the competing state-of-the-art approaches on a diversified set of benchmarks and applications.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes are useful for regression with few examples because their Gaussian structure permits closed-form posterior computation. The paper argues that this structure can also restrict predictive flexibility when successive tasks differ substantially. It proposes Non-Gaussian Gaussian Processes, or NGGPs, to retain shared problem structure while allowing richer, context-sensitive predictions.

NGGPs use normalizing flows to transform the Gaussian process's posterior predictive distribution. The transformation is an invertible mapping defined through an ordinary differential equation. It acts on each component of the random variable vectors while sharing parameters across components. This makes the posterior locally non-Gaussian and provides a way to incorporate contextual information into its shape.

Shared structure transfers between tasks, while contextualization adapts predictions to their differences. NGGPs outperform the competing methods on the reported collection of benchmarks and applications, supporting the value of making Gaussian process predictions more flexible for varied tasks.
summary.tldr: NGGPs transform Gaussian process predictions with context-sensitive normalizing flows to improve flexibility and few-shot regression performance.

title: Non-Gaussian Gaussian Processes for Few-Shot Regression

abstract: Recently, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) frameworks have shown potential for solving NP-hard routing problems such as the traveling salesman problem (TSP) without problem-specific expert knowledge. Although DRL can be used to solve complex problems, DRL frameworks still struggle to compete with state-of-the-art heuristics showing a substantial performance gap. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical problem-solving strategy, termed learning collaborative policies (LCP), which can effectively find the near-optimum solution using two iterative DRL policies: the seeder and reviser. The seeder generates as diversified candidate solutions as possible (seeds) while being dedicated to exploring over the full combinatorial action space (i.e., sequence of assignment action). To this end, we train the seeder's policy using a simple yet effective entropy regularization reward to encourage the seeder to find diverse solutions. On the other hand, the reviser modifies each candidate solution generated by the seeder; it partitions the full trajectory into sub-tours and simultaneously revises each sub-tour to minimize its traveling distance. Thus, the reviser is trained to improve the candidate solution's quality, focusing on the reduced solution space (which is beneficial for exploitation). Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed two-policies collaboration scheme improves over single-policy DRL framework on various NP-hard routing problems, including TSP, prize collecting TSP (PCTSP), and capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP).
originalAbstract: Recently, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) frameworks have shown potential for solving NP-hard routing problems such as the traveling salesman problem (TSP) without problem-specific expert knowledge. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical problem-solving strategy, termed learning collaborative policies (LCP), which can effectively find the near-optimum solution using two iterative DRL policies: the seeder and reviser. The seeder generates as diversified candidate solutions as possible (seeds) while being dedicated to exploring over the full combinatorial action space (i.e., sequence of assignment action). To this end, we train the seeder's policy using a simple yet effective entropy regularization reward to encourage the seeder to find diverse solutions. On the other hand, the reviser modifies each candidate solution generated by the seeder; it partitions the full trajectory into sub-tours and simultaneously revises each sub-tour to minimize its traveling distance. Thus, the reviser is trained to improve the candidate solution's quality, focusing on the reduced solution space (which is beneficial for exploitation). Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed two-policies collaboration scheme improves over single-policy DRL framework on various NP-hard routing problems, including TSP, prize collecting TSP (PCTSP), and capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP).

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can tackle difficult routing problems without problem-specific expert knowledge, but existing approaches still trail strong heuristics. This paper proposes learning collaborative policies, or LCP, which divides route construction and improvement between two policies. Their collaboration separates broad exploration of possible solutions from focused refinement of promising candidates.

The seeder generates diverse candidate routes while exploring the full combinatorial action space. An entropy regularization reward encourages it to avoid concentrating on a narrow range of solutions. The reviser then splits each candidate into subtours and revises those pieces simultaneously to reduce travel distance. Its learning focuses on a smaller solution space, making local improvement its dedicated role.

The policies work iteratively to find near-optimal solutions. Experiments show that the collaboration improves on single-policy deep reinforcement learning for the traveling salesman problem, prize-collecting traveling salesman problem, and capacitated vehicle routing problem. The findings support a division of labor between generating varied starting points and improving their parts, with the reported comparison specifically establishing gains over single-policy frameworks.
summary.tldr: LCP pairs a policy that generates diverse routes with one that refines subtours, improving on single-policy reinforcement learning across evaluated routing problems.

abstract: We consider interactive learning in the realizable setting and develop a general framework to handle problems ranging from best arm identification to active classification. We begin our investigation with the observation that agnostic algorithms \emph{cannot} be minimax-optimal in the realizable setting. Hence, we design novel computationally efficient algorithms for the realizable setting that match the minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors and are general-purpose, accommodating a wide variety of function classes including kernel methods, H{\"o}lder smooth functions, and convex functions. The sample complexities of our algorithms can be quantified in terms of well-known quantities like the extended teaching dimension and haystack dimension. However, unlike algorithms based directly on those combinatorial quantities, our algorithms are computationally efficient. To achieve computational efficiency, our algorithms sample from the version space using Monte Carlo ``hit-and-run'' algorithms instead of maintaining the version space explicitly. Our approach has two key strengths. First, it is simple, consisting of two unifying, greedy algorithms. Second, our algorithms have the capability to seamlessly leverage prior knowledge that is often available and useful in practice. In addition to our new theoretical results, we demonstrate empirically that our algorithms are competitive with Gaussian process UCB methods.

paragraphs: Interactive learning lets an algorithm choose what information to request, as in active classification or identifying the best available arm. This paper studies the realizable setting, where the target is represented by the assumed function class. It begins by showing that agnostic algorithms cannot attain minimax-optimal performance in this setting, motivating methods that explicitly use realizability.

The authors develop two general-purpose greedy algorithms whose sample requirements match minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. Its sample complexity can be expressed through established quantities such as extended teaching dimension and haystack dimension, connecting the algorithms to theoretical measures of interactive learning difficulty.

The methods can also incorporate prior knowledge. Experiments show performance competitive with Gaussian process UCB approaches. Together, the results connect near-optimal information use with a computationally efficient implementation, with the realizability assumption central to both the motivation and the guarantees.
summary.tldr: Two efficient interactive learning algorithms exploit realizability to achieve near-minimax sample complexity while supporting broad function classes and prior knowledge.

title: Practical, Provably-Correct Interactive Learning in the Realizable Setting: The Power of True Believers

abstract: Most conventional Neural Architecture Search (NAS) approaches are limited in that they only generate architectures without searching for the optimal parameters. While some NAS methods handle this issue by utilizing a supernet trained on a large-scale dataset such as ImageNet, they may be suboptimal if the target tasks are highly dissimilar from the dataset the supernet is trained on. To address such limitations, we introduce a novel problem of Neural Network Search (NNS), whose goal is to search for the optimal pretrained network for a novel dataset and constraints (e.g. number of parameters), from a model zoo. Then, we propose a novel framework to tackle the problem, namely Task-Adaptive Neural Network Search (TANS). Given a model-zoo that consists of network pretrained on diverse datasets, we use a novel amortized meta-learning framework to learn a cross-modal latent space with contrastive loss, to maximize the similarity between a dataset and a high-performing network on it, and minimize the similarity between irrelevant dataset-network pairs. We validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method on ten real-world datasets, against existing NAS/AutoML baselines. The results show that our method instantly retrieves networks that outperform models obtained with the baselines with significantly fewer training steps to reach the target performance, thus minimizing the total cost of obtaining a task-optimal network. Our code and the model-zoo are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TANS-33D6

paragraphs: Architecture search often selects a network structure without also searching for suitable pretrained parameters. This paper introduces Neural Network Search, which chooses a pretrained network from a model zoo for a new dataset and constraints such as parameter count. The formulation makes the network's learned parameters part of the selection problem alongside its architecture.

Task-Adaptive Neural Network Search, or TANS, learns a shared latent space for datasets and networks through amortized meta-learning. A contrastive objective brings a dataset close to networks that perform well on it and separates irrelevant dataset-network pairs. The model zoo contains networks pretrained on diverse datasets, supporting selection across different target tasks.

Across ten real-world datasets, the authors report immediate retrieval of networks that outperform models obtained through the compared NAS and AutoML baselines. The retrieved networks also require substantially fewer training steps to reach target performance. These findings support learning the relationship between task characteristics and pretrained networks as a way to reduce the total cost of obtaining a suitable model.
summary.tldr: TANS learns dataset-network compatibility to quickly retrieve effective pretrained models from a diverse model zoo.

title: Task-Adaptive Neural Network Search with Meta-Contrastive Learning

abstract: Thompson sampling and other Bayesian sequential decision-making algorithms are among the most popular approaches to tackle explore/exploit trade-offs in (contextual) bandits. The choice of prior in these algorithms offers flexibility to encode domain knowledge but can also lead to poor performance when misspecified. In this paper, we demonstrate that performance degrades gracefully with misspecification. We prove that the expected reward accrued by Thompson sampling (TS) with a misspecified prior differs by at most $\tilde{O}(H^2 \epsilon)$ from TS with a well-specified prior, where $\epsilon$ is the total-variation distance between priors and $H$ is the learning horizon. Our bound does not require the prior to have any parametric form. For priors with bounded support, our bound is independent of the cardinality or structure of the action space, and we show that it is tight up to universal constants in the worst case.Building on our sensitivity analysis, we establish generic PAC guarantees for algorithms in the recently studied Bayesian meta-learning setting and derive corollaries for various families of priors. Our results generalize along two axes: (1) they apply to a broader family of Bayesian decision-making algorithms, including a Monte-Carlo implementation of the knowledge gradient algorithm (KG), and (2) they apply to Bayesian POMDPs, the most general Bayesian decision-making setting, encompassing contextual bandits as a special case. Through numerical simulations, we illustrate how prior misspecification and the deployment of one-step look-ahead (as in KG) can impact the convergence of meta-learning in multi-armed and contextual bandits with structured and correlated priors.

paragraphs: Bayesian decision algorithms use prior beliefs to guide exploration, but those beliefs can be wrong. This paper quantifies how much that mismatch can affect Thompson sampling. It compares the expected accumulated reward obtained with a misspecified prior against the reward obtained with a correctly specified one.

The reward difference is bounded by a quantity scaling roughly as H squared times epsilon, up to logarithmic factors. Here H is the learning horizon, and epsilon measures total-variation distance between the priors. The result requires no parametric form for the prior. For bounded-support priors, the bound does not depend on the action space's size or structure, and the authors establish worst-case tightness up to universal constants.

The sensitivity analysis also yields probabilistic learning guarantees for Bayesian meta-learning. Extensions cover a broader family of decision algorithms, including a Monte Carlo knowledge-gradient implementation, and Bayesian partially observable decision processes. Simulations illustrate how prior mismatch and one-step look-ahead influence meta-learning convergence with structured and correlated priors.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds how prior misspecification affects Bayesian decision-making and uses that analysis to establish meta-learning guarantees.

title: Bayesian decision-making under misspecified priors with applications to meta-learning

abstract: Multi-label classification (MLC) allows complex dependencies among labels, making it more suitable to model many real-world problems. However, data annotation for training MLC models becomes much more labor-intensive due to the correlated (hence non-exclusive) labels and a potential large and sparse label space. We propose to conduct multi-label active learning (ML-AL) through a novel integrated Gaussian Process-Bayesian Bernoulli Mixture model (GP-B$^2$M) to accurately quantify a data sample's overall contribution to a correlated label space and choose the most informative samples for cost-effective annotation. In particular, the B$^2$M encodes label correlations using a Bayesian Bernoulli mixture of label clusters, where each mixture component corresponds to a global pattern of label correlations. To tackle highly sparse labels under AL, the B$^2$M is further integrated with a predictive GP to connect data features as an effective inductive bias and achieve a feature-component-label mapping. The GP predicts coefficients of mixture components that help to recover the final set of labels of a data sample. A novel auxiliary variable based variational inference algorithm is developed to tackle the non-conjugacy introduced along with the mapping process for efficient end-to-end posterior inference. The model also outputs a predictive distribution that provides both the label prediction and their correlations in the form of a label covariance matrix. A principled sampling function is designed accordingly to naturally capture both the feature uncertainty (through GP) and label covariance (through B$^2$M) for effective data sampling. Experiments on real-world multi-label datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art AL performance of the proposed GP-B$^2$M model.

paragraphs: When an example can have several labels, deciding what to annotate requires more than finding uncertainty about a single category. Labels may occur together, and many possible labels may be rare. This paper develops an active learning model that uses those dependencies to select examples whose annotation should be informative across the label space.

The model combines a Bayesian Bernoulli mixture with a Gaussian process. Each mixture component represents a broad pattern of labels occurring together. The Gaussian process connects an example’s features to the mixture components, helping predict labels even when label observations are sparse. The authors also develop a variational inference algorithm to make inference across this combined model practical.

The resulting predictions include both label probabilities and a covariance matrix describing label relationships. The sampling rule uses this covariance alongside uncertainty from the Gaussian process when choosing examples for annotation. Experiments on real multi-label datasets report state-of-the-art active learning performance, supporting the value of considering correlated labels jointly during sample selection.
summary.tldr: A combined probabilistic model selects informative examples for multi-label annotation by accounting for feature uncertainty and correlations among labels.

title: A Gaussian Process-Bayesian Bernoulli Mixture Model for Multi-Label Active Learning

abstract: The ratio of two probability densities, called a density-ratio, is a vital quantity in machine learning. In particular, a relative density-ratio, which is a bounded extension of the density-ratio, has received much attention due to its stability and has been used in various applications such as outlier detection and dataset comparison. Existing methods for (relative) density-ratio estimation (DRE) require many instances from both densities. However, sufficient instances are often unavailable in practice. In this paper, we propose a meta-learning method for relative DRE, which estimates the relative density-ratio from a few instances by using knowledge in related datasets. Specifically, given two datasets that consist of a few instances, our model extracts the datasets' information by using neural networks and uses it to obtain instance embeddings appropriate for the relative DRE. We model the relative density-ratio by a linear model on the embedded space, whose global optimum solution can be obtained as a closed-form solution. The closed-form solution enables fast and effective adaptation to a few instances, and its differentiability enables us to train our model such that the expected test error for relative DRE can be explicitly minimized after adapting to a few instances. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method by using three problems: relative DRE, dataset comparison, and outlier detection.

paragraphs: Density-ratio estimation compares two probability densities directly. A relative density ratio is a bounded version valued for its stability in tasks such as dataset comparison and outlier detection. This paper addresses the difficulty of estimating it when only a few examples from each distribution are available.

The proposed method learns from related datasets so that it can adapt to a new pair of small datasets. Neural networks extract information about the pair and construct suitable embeddings of individual examples. Within that learned space, a linear model represents the relative density ratio, and its global optimum can be computed in closed form.

That closed-form step supports fast adaptation and is differentiable, allowing training to explicitly minimize expected test error after adaptation to a few examples. The global-optimum claim applies to the linear estimation problem in the embedding space. Experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness for relative density-ratio estimation, dataset comparison, and outlier detection, supporting the use of knowledge from related datasets when observations are scarce.
summary.tldr: Meta-learned embeddings and a closed-form linear estimator enable relative density-ratio estimation from a few examples using knowledge from related datasets.

title: Meta-Learning for Relative Density-Ratio Estimation

abstract: In many practical applications of AI, an AI model is used as a decision aid for human users. The AI provides advice that a human (sometimes) incorporates into their decision-making process. The AI advice is often presented with some measure of "confidence" that the human can use to calibrate how much they depend on or trust the advice. In this paper, we present an initial exploration that suggests showing AI models as more confident than they actually are, even when the original AI is well-calibrated, can improve human-AI performance (measured as the accuracy and confidence of the human's final prediction after seeing the AI advice). We first train a model to predict human incorporation of AI advice using data from thousands of human-AI interactions. This enables us to explicitly estimate how to transform the AI's prediction confidence, making the AI uncalibrated, in order to improve the final human prediction. We empirically validate our results across four different tasks---dealing with images, text and tabular data---involving hundreds of human participants. We further support our findings with simulation analysis. Our findings suggest the importance of jointly optimizing the human-AI system as opposed to the standard paradigm of optimizing the AI model alone.

paragraphs: When AI advises a person, the final outcome depends on how that person uses the advice. Confidence displays can influence this decision. This paper offers an initial exploration suggesting that presenting greater confidence than a model actually has can improve human-AI performance, even when the original model is well calibrated.

The authors first train a model of how people incorporate AI advice, using thousands of human-AI interactions. They then use that model to estimate transformations of displayed prediction confidence that could improve the human's final prediction. The optimization therefore explicitly considers the person's response to the advice, including the confidence attached to it.

Experiments involve hundreds of participants across four tasks using images, text, and tabular data, with additional simulation analysis supporting the findings. Performance is assessed through the accuracy and confidence of the human's final prediction. The results suggest benefits from optimizing the combined human-AI system. They support a possibility demonstrated in the studied settings, rather than a universal claim that inflated confidence improves decisions.
summary.tldr: An initial study finds that adjusting displayed AI confidence upward can improve human-AI outcomes when the adjustment accounts for how people use advice.

title: Uncalibrated Models Can Improve Human-AI Collaboration

abstract: Supervised learning with deep models has tremendous potential for applications in materials science. Recently, graph neural networks have been used in this context, drawing direct inspiration from models for molecules. However, materials are typically much more structured than molecules, which is a feature that these models do not leverage. In this work, we introduce a class of models that are equivariant with respect to crystalline symmetry groups. We do this by defining a generalization of the message passing operations that can be used with more general permutation groups, or that can alternatively be seen as defining an expressive convolution operation on the crystal graph. Empirically, these models achieve competitive results with state-of-the-art on the Materials Project dataset.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks used in materials science often borrow their structure from models of molecules. This paper argues that crystals have additional organization that these models do not exploit. It introduces networks designed around crystalline symmetry groups, so the model's computations respond consistently to the transformations described by those groups.

The central change is a generalization of message passing, the operation through which nodes in a graph exchange information. The proposed operation can work with more general permutation groups, allowing the architecture to incorporate crystal-specific symmetry. The authors also describe it as an expressive convolution on the crystal graph, providing another way to understand how local information is combined within the structured material.

On the Materials Project dataset, the models achieve results competitive with state-of-the-art approaches. This empirical finding supports incorporating crystalline structure directly into a learning architecture. The contribution connects a mathematical description of crystal symmetries to practical graph computations, showing that such structure can be used in models that remain competitive on materials prediction.
summary.tldr: Crystal-aware message passing builds symmetry-equivariant networks that achieve competitive results on the Materials Project dataset.

title: Equivariant Networks for Crystal Structures

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a new powerful alternative for multivariate time series forecasting, demonstrating remarkable success in a variety of spatio-temporal applications, from urban flow monitoring systems to health care informatics to financial analytics. Yet, such GNN models pre-dominantly capture only lower order interactions, that is, pairwise relations among nodes, and also largely ignore intrinsic time-conditioned information on the underlying topology of multivariate time series. To address these limitations, we propose a new time-aware GNN architecture which amplifies the power of the recently emerged simplicial neural networks with a time-conditioned topological knowledge representation in a form of zigzag persistence. That is, our new approach, Zigzag Filtration Curve based Supra-Hodge Convolution Networks (ZFC-SHCN) is built upon the two main components: (i) a new highly computationally efficientzigzag persistence curve which allows us to systematically encode time-conditioned topological information, and (ii) a new temporal multiplex graph representation module for learning higher-order network interactions. We discuss theoretical properties of the proposed time-conditioned topological knowledge representation and extensively validate the new time-aware ZFC-SHCN model in conjunction with time series forecasting on a broad range of synthetic and real-world datasets: traffic flows, COVID-19 biosurveillance, Ethereum blockchain, surface air temperature, wind energy, and vector autoregressions. Our experiments demonstrate that the ZFC-SHCN achieves the state-of-the-art performance with lower requirements on computational costs.

paragraphs: Forecasting several related time series requires understanding how their relationships evolve. The paper argues that common graph neural networks emphasize pairwise connections and often overlook time-dependent topology. Its proposed architecture, ZFC-SHCN, combines temporal structural information with interactions involving more than two nodes.

The first component is a computationally efficient zigzag persistence curve that encodes topological information conditioned on time. The experiments report state-of-the-art forecasting performance with lower computational requirements. summary.tldr: ZFC-SHCN combines time-dependent topology and higher-order interactions, reporting improved time-series forecasting with lower computational costs.

title: Time-Conditioned Dances with Simplicial Complexes: Zigzag Filtration Curve based Supra-Hodge Convolution Networks for Time-series Forecasting

abstract: Embodied AI agents continue to become more capable every year with the advent of new models, environments, and benchmarks, but are still far away from being performant and reliable enough to be deployed in real, user-facing, applications. In this paper, we ask: can we bridge this gap by enabling agents to ask for assistance from an expert such as a human being? To this end, we propose the Ask4Help policy that augments agents with the ability to request, and then use expert assistance. Ask4Help policies can be efficiently trained without modifying the original agent's parameters and learn a desirable trade-off between task performance and the amount of requested help, thereby reducing the cost of querying the expert. We evaluate Ask4Help on two different tasks -- object goal navigation and room rearrangement and see substantial improvements in performance using minimal help. On object navigation, an agent that achieves a $52\%$ success rate is raised to $86\%$ with $13\%$ help and for rearrangement, the state-of-the-art model with a $7\%$ success rate is dramatically improved to $90.4\%$ using $39\%$ help. Human trials with Ask4Help demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in practical scenarios.

paragraphs: An embodied agent may complete many tasks independently yet still struggle often enough to need assistance. Ask4Help treats requesting expert help as something an agent can learn. The aim is to improve task completion while controlling how much assistance the expert must provide.

The proposed policy augments an existing agent with the ability to request and use help. Training does not require changing the original agent’s parameters. Instead, the added policy learns a trade-off between performance and assistance, making the cost of querying an expert part of the problem. This allows help-seeking behavior to be developed around an already trained agent.

The authors evaluate object goal navigation and room rearrangement. Navigation success rises from 52% to 86% with a reported 13% help, while rearrangement success rises from 7% to 90.4% with 39% help. Human trials also support the approach’s practical effectiveness. These findings show substantial benefits from learned assistance in the evaluated tasks, with different amounts of help accompanying the two improvements.
summary.tldr: Ask4Help learns when to request expert assistance, substantially improving embodied task success without changing the original agent’s parameters.

title: Ask4Help: Learning to Leverage an Expert for Embodied Tasks

abstract: World models learn the consequences of actions in vision-based interactive systems. However, in practical scenarios such as autonomous driving, there commonly exists noncontrollable dynamics independent of the action signals, making it difficult to learn effective world models. Naturally, therefore, we need to enable the world models to decouple the controllable and noncontrollable dynamics from the entangled spatiotemporal data. To this end, we present a reinforcement learning approach named Iso-Dream, which expands the Dream-to-Control framework in two aspects. First, the world model contains a three-branch neural architecture. By solving the inverse dynamics problem, it learns to factorize latent representations according to the responses to action signals. Second, in the process of behavior learning, we estimate the state values by rolling-out a sequence of noncontrollable states (less related to the actions) into the future and associate the current controllable state with them. In this way, the isolation of mixed dynamics can greatly facilitate long-horizon decision-making tasks in realistic scenes, such as avoiding potential future risks by predicting the movement of other vehicles in autonomous driving. Experiments show that Iso-Dream is effective in decoupling the mixed dynamics and remarkably outperforms existing approaches in a wide range of visual control and prediction domains.
