paragraphs: Visual environments contain both changes caused by an agent’s actions and changes that happen independently, such as other vehicles moving. A world model that entangles them can make planning difficult. Iso-Dream explicitly separates controllable and noncontrollable dynamics in a learned latent representation.

The model uses a three-branch architecture and an inverse-dynamics task to factor representations according to their response to actions. During behavior learning, it rolls noncontrollable states forward and associates those predictions with the current controllable state when estimating value.

Experiments across visual-control and prediction domains show effective separation of the mixed dynamics and substantial improvements over existing methods. The abstract does not provide benchmark scores or demonstrate deployment in autonomous driving; that example motivates the method’s potential. The supported result is improved planning and prediction within the evaluated domains through explicit treatment of motion that the agent does not control.
summary.tldr: Iso-Dream separates action-controlled dynamics from independent motion to improve visual planning.

title: Iso-Dream: Isolating and Leveraging Noncontrollable Visual Dynamics in World Models

abstract: Diffusion-based Deep Generative Models (DDGMs) offer state-of-the-art performance in generative modeling. Their main strength comes from their unique setup in which a model (the backward diffusion process) is trained to reverse the forward diffusion process, which gradually adds noise to the input signal. Although DDGMs are well studied, it is still unclear how the small amount of noise is transformed during the backward diffusion process. Here, we focus on analyzing this problem to gain more insight into the behavior of DDGMs and their denoising and generative capabilities. We observe a fluid transition point that changes the functionality of the backward diffusion process from generating a (corrupted) image from noise to denoising the corrupted image to the final sample. Based on this observation, we postulate to divide a DDGM into two parts: a denoiser and a generator. The denoiser could be parameterized by a denoising auto-encoder, while the generator is a diffusion-based model with its own set of parameters. We experimentally validate our proposition, showing its pros and cons.

paragraphs: Diffusion models learn to reverse a process that progressively adds noise to data. Their reverse process ultimately produces a sample, but the role played by small amounts of noise during that process is less clear. This paper studies that behavior to better understand how image generation and denoising relate.

The authors observe a fluid transition in the reverse process. One part behaves as though it is generating a still-corrupted image from noise; another behaves as though it is cleaning that image into the final sample. Describing the transition as fluid matters: the observation motivates a functional distinction without asserting a rigid, universal boundary between the two roles.

Based on this finding, the authors propose separating a diffusion model into a generator and a denoiser. The generator remains diffusion-based with its own parameters, while a denoising autoencoder could implement the cleanup component. Experiments validate the proposal and examine both advantages and disadvantages. The contribution is an experimentally investigated decomposition of diffusion behavior, rather than a claim that the split is uniformly better.
summary.tldr: An observed transition from generation to cleanup motivates splitting diffusion models into separate generator and denoiser components.

title: On Analyzing Generative and Denoising Capabilities of Diffusion-based Deep Generative Models

abstract: In offline RL, constraining the learned policy to remain close to the data is essential to prevent the policy from outputting out-of-distribution (OOD) actions with erroneously overestimated values. In principle, generative adversarial networks (GAN) can provide an elegant solution to do so, with the discriminator directly providing a probability that quantifies distributional shift. However, in practice, GAN-based offline RL methods have not outperformed alternative approaches, perhaps because the generator is trained to both fool the discriminator and maximize return - two objectives that are often at odds with each other. In this paper, we show that the issue of conflicting objectives can be resolved by training two generators: one that maximizes return, with the other capturing the "remainder" of the data distribution in the offline dataset, such that the mixture of the two is close to the behavior policy. We show that not only does having two generators enable an effective GAN-based offline RL method, but also approximates a support constraint, where the policy does not need to match the entire data distribution, but only the slice of the data that leads to high long term performance. We name our method DASCO, for Dual-Generator Adversarial Support Constrained Offline RL. On benchmark tasks that require learning from sub-optimal data, DASCO significantly outperforms prior methods that enforce distribution constraint.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from a fixed dataset, making unsupported actions a concern: their values can be mistakenly overestimated. Adversarial methods can encourage a learned policy to remain close to the recorded behavior. However, asking one generator both to reproduce the data distribution and to maximize return can create conflicting objectives, especially when the data contains suboptimal behavior.

DASCO divides these responsibilities between two generators. One seeks high returns, while the other captures the remaining parts of the dataset’s distribution. Their mixture is trained to stay close to the behavior policy. This lets the return-seeking generator concentrate on useful behavior without requiring that generator alone to reproduce every kind of action in the dataset.

The authors show that this arrangement approximates a support constraint: the policy can focus on high-performing behavior supported by the data rather than matching the entire distribution. On benchmark tasks requiring learning from suboptimal data, DASCO significantly outperforms earlier methods imposing distribution constraints. The result supports separating distribution coverage from the objective of finding a strong policy.
summary.tldr: DASCO uses two adversarial generators to pursue high-return behavior while their mixture remains close to the offline data distribution.

title: DASCO: Dual-Generator Adversarial Support Constrained Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper presents a simple, self-supervised method for magnifying subtle motions in video: given an input video and a magnification factor, we manipulate the video such that its new optical flow is scaled by the desired amount. To train our model, we propose a loss function that estimates the optical flow of the generated video and penalizes how far if deviates from the given magnification factor. Thus, training involves differentiating through a pretrained optical flow network. Since our model is self-supervised, we can further improve its performance through test-time adaptation, by finetuning it on the input video. It can also be easily extended to magnify the motions of only user-selected objects. Our approach avoids the need for synthetic magnification datasets that have been used to train prior learning-based approaches. Instead, it leverages the existing capabilities of off-the-shelf motion estimators. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through evaluations of both visual quality and quantitative metrics on a range of real-world and synthetic videos, and we show our method works for both supervised and unsupervised optical flow methods.

paragraphs: Motion magnification makes subtle movements in video easier to see. This paper learns to produce a video whose optical flow—the estimated motion between frames—is scaled by a requested magnification factor. The central idea is to supervise the desired change through motion estimates, allowing training without a synthetic dataset of magnified target videos.

A pretrained optical-flow network estimates motion in the generated video. The training loss penalizes disagreement with the requested motion scaling, and gradients pass through that flow estimator to train the magnification model. This turns an existing motion-estimation capability into a learning signal for changing motion. The approach works with both supervised and unsupervised optical-flow methods in the reported evaluations.

Because the objective is self-supervised, the model can also be fine-tuned on the input video at test time to improve performance. The method can be extended to magnify only user-selected objects. Evaluations of visual quality and quantitative metrics on real and synthetic videos demonstrate effectiveness, supporting optical flow as a practical source of supervision for controlled motion amplification.
summary.tldr: A self-supervised model magnifies video motion by learning through a pretrained optical-flow estimator, with optional adaptation to the input video.

title: Self-Supervised Motion Magnification by Backpropagating Through Optical Flow

abstract: Few-Shot 3D Point Cloud Object Detection (FS3D) is a challenging task, aiming to detect 3D objects of novel classes using only limited annotated samples for training. Considering that the detection performance highly relies on the quality of the latent features, we design a VAE-based prototype learning scheme, named prototypical VAE (P-VAE), to learn a probabilistic latent space for enhancing the diversity and distinctiveness of the sampled features. The network encodes a multi-center GMM-like posterior, in which each distribution centers at a prototype. For regularization, P-VAE incorporates a reconstruction task to preserve geometric information. To adopt P-VAE for the detection framework, we formulate Geometric-informative Prototypical VAE (GP-VAE) to handle varying geometric components and Class-specific Prototypical VAE (CP-VAE) to handle varying object categories. In the first stage, we harness GP-VAE to aid feature extraction from the input scene. In the second stage, we cluster the geometric-informative features into per-instance features and use CP-VAE to refine each instance feature with category-level guidance. Experimental results show the top performance of our approach over the state of the arts on two FS3D benchmarks. Quantitative ablations and qualitative prototype analysis further demonstrate that our probabilistic modeling can significantly boost prototype learning for FS3D.

paragraphs: Detecting unfamiliar object categories in 3D point clouds is difficult when only a few labeled examples are available. This paper focuses on improving the latent features used by the detector. Its prototypical variational autoencoder, P-VAE, learns a probabilistic feature space intended to make sampled features both diverse and distinguishable.

The model uses a posterior resembling a mixture of Gaussian distributions, with each component centered on a prototype. A reconstruction task helps preserve geometric information. The detector applies this idea at two levels: a geometry-focused version assists feature extraction from the scene, then a category-focused version refines object-instance features after the geometry-informed features have been clustered.

This sequence gives geometric structure and object-category information distinct roles in the detection process. On two few-shot 3D detection benchmarks, the authors report performance above the compared state-of-the-art approaches. Ablation experiments and qualitative prototype analysis further support the contribution of probabilistic modeling to prototype learning. The results connect richer prototype-based features with improved detection when annotations for new categories are scarce.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic prototypes enrich geometry and category features, improving few-shot 3D object detection on two benchmarks.

title: Prototypical Variational Autoencoder for 3D Few-shot Object Detection

abstract: Policy gradient lies at the core of deep reinforcement learning (RL) in continuous domains. Despite much success, it is often observed in practice that RL training with policy gradient can fail for many reasons, even on standard control problems with known solutions. We propose a framework for understanding one inherent limitation of the policy gradient approach: the optimization landscape in the policy space can be extremely non-smooth or fractal for certain classes of MDPs, such that there does not exist gradient to be estimated in the first place. We draw on techniques from chaos theory and non-smooth analysis, and analyze the maximal Lyapunov exponents and H\"older exponents of the policy optimization objectives. Moreover, we develop a practical method that can estimate the local smoothness of objective function from samples to identify when the training process has encountered fractal landscapes. We show experiments to illustrate how some failure cases of policy optimization can be explained by such fractal landscapes.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods improve a reinforcement-learning policy by estimating how changes to it affect performance. The paper examines a fundamental obstacle to this approach: for certain classes of decision processes, the objective over policies can be so irregular that a gradient does not exist. In those settings, improving the gradient estimate alone cannot resolve the underlying problem.

The authors use ideas from chaos theory and nonsmooth analysis to characterize these landscapes. Their analysis considers maximal Lyapunov exponents and Hölder exponents, connecting the behavior of the underlying system with the smoothness of the policy objective. This provides a framework for studying when policy optimization encounters extremely rough or fractal structure.

They also introduce a practical procedure for estimating local objective smoothness from samples. Such an estimate can help identify when training has reached a fractal region. Experiments illustrate how this phenomenon explains some policy-optimization failures. The claim is specifically about certain problem classes and failure cases, providing one explanation for unsuccessful training rather than a universal account of reinforcement-learning difficulties.
summary.tldr: Some policy objectives have fractal landscapes without usable gradients, and the paper provides analysis and a sample-based diagnostic for this failure mode.

title: Fractal Landscapes in Policy Optimization

abstract: Hand-crafted image quality metrics, such as PSNR and SSIM, are commonly used to evaluate model privacy risk under reconstruction attacks. Under these metrics, reconstructed images that are determined to resemble the original one generally indicate more privacy leakage. Images determined as overall dissimilar, on the other hand, indicate higher robustness against attack. However, there is no guarantee that these metrics well reflect human opinions, which offers trustworthy judgement for model privacy leakage. In this paper, we comprehensively study the faithfulness of these hand-crafted metrics to human perception of privacy information from the reconstructed images. On 5 datasets ranging from natural images, faces, to fine-grained classes, we use 4 existing attack methods to reconstruct images from many different classification models and, for each reconstructed image, we ask multiple human annotators to assess whether this image is recognizable. Our studies reveal that the hand-crafted metrics only have a weak correlation with the human evaluation of privacy leakage and that even these metrics themselves often contradict each other. These observations suggest risks of current metrics in the community. To address this potential risk, we propose a learning-based measure called SemSim to evaluate the Semantic Similarity between the original and reconstructed images. SemSim is trained with a standard triplet loss, using an original image as an anchor, one of its recognizable reconstructed images as a positive sample, and an unrecognizable one as a negative. By training on human annotations, SemSim exhibits a greater reflection of privacy leakage on the semantic level. We show that SemSim has a significantly higher correlation with human judgment compared with existing metrics. Moreover, this strong correlation generalizes to unseen datasets, models and attack methods. We envision this work as a milestone for image quality evaluation closer to the human level. The project webpage can be accessed at https://sites.google.com/view/semsim.

paragraphs: Reconstruction attacks can reveal private information by recovering recognizable images from a model. Privacy assessments often use image-quality measures such as PSNR and SSIM to compare reconstructions with originals. This paper asks whether those measures agree with what people can actually recognize, which is central to the privacy interpretation of a reconstructed image.

The authors study five datasets, four attack methods, and multiple classification models. Several human annotators judge whether each reconstruction is recognizable. The existing hand-crafted measures correlate only weakly with these judgments and often disagree with one another, showing that overall image similarity can be an unreliable proxy for the assessed privacy leakage.

The proposed alternative, SemSim, learns semantic similarity from the human annotations. Its triplet training uses an original image, a recognizable reconstruction, and an unrecognizable reconstruction. SemSim correlates substantially better with human judgments, and this relationship generalizes in the reported evaluations to unseen datasets, models, and attacks. The findings support evaluating recognizable semantic information more directly when assessing reconstruction-based privacy risk.
summary.tldr: Human-trained SemSim tracks recognizable information in reconstructed images more closely than the hand-crafted metrics evaluated in the paper.

title: Privacy Assessment on Reconstructed Images: Are Existing Evaluation Metrics Faithful to Human Perception?

abstract: As the use of large embedding models in recommendation systems and language applications increases, concerns over user data privacy have also risen. DP-SGD, a training algorithm that combines differential privacy with stochastic gradient descent, has been the workhorse in protecting user privacy without compromising model accuracy by much. However, applying DP-SGD naively to embedding models can destroy gradient sparsity, leading to reduced training efficiency. To address this issue, we present two new algorithms, DP-FEST and DP-AdaFEST, that preserve gradient sparsity during the private training of large embedding models. Our algorithms achieve substantial reductions ($10^6 \times$) in gradient size, while maintaining comparable levels of accuracy, on benchmark real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Large embedding models are widely used in recommendation and language applications, making private training increasingly important. Differentially private stochastic gradient descent is a standard approach, but applying it naively can destroy gradient sparsity. When a gradient no longer retains its sparse structure, training loses an efficiency advantage that is particularly relevant for large embedding models.

The paper introduces DP-FEST and DP-AdaFEST to preserve that structure during differentially private training. The central objective is to keep private learning compatible with compact gradient updates. This addresses an implementation-level obstacle to using privacy-preserving training at scale, alongside the familiar concern of maintaining useful predictive accuracy.

On benchmark datasets drawn from real-world settings, the authors report gradient-size reductions of a million-fold while retaining comparable accuracy. The stated reduction concerns gradient size, so it should not be read as an equal reduction in total training time. The findings show that preserving sparsity can dramatically reduce the size of the gradient representation without sacrificing comparable model accuracy in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: DP-FEST and DP-AdaFEST preserve sparse gradients during private embedding-model training, reporting million-fold gradient-size reductions with comparable accuracy.

title: Sparsity-Preserving Differentially Private Training of Large Embedding Models

abstract: Neural Temporal Point Processes (TPPs) are the prevalent paradigm for modeling continuous-time event sequences, such as user activities on the web and financial transactions. In real world applications, the event data typically comes in a streaming manner, where the distribution of the patterns may shift over time. Under the privacy and memory constraints commonly seen in real scenarios, how to continuously monitor a TPP to learn the streaming event sequence is an important yet under-investigated problem. In this work, we approach this problem by adopting Continual Learning (CL), which aims to enable a model to continuously learn a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting. While CL for event sequence is less well studied, we present a simple yet effective framework, PromptTPP, by integrating the base TPP with a continuous-time retrieval prompt pool. In our proposed framework, prompts are small learnable parameters, maintained in a memory space and jointly optimized with the base TPP so that the model is properly instructed to learn event streams arriving sequentially without buffering past examples or task-specific attributes. We formalize a novel and realistic experimental setup for modeling event streams, where PromptTPP consistently sets state-of-the-art performance across two real user behavior datasets.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model events occurring in continuous time, such as web activity or transactions. In streaming applications, new events arrive continually and their patterns can change. The paper studies how a model can keep learning under memory and privacy constraints while addressing the tendency to forget previously learned patterns.

PromptTPP combines a base temporal point process with a continuous-time retrieval prompt pool. The prompts are small learnable parameters stored in memory and optimized together with the base model. They guide learning as event streams arrive sequentially, without requiring a buffer of previous examples or task-specific attributes.

The authors frame this as a continual-learning problem and define an experimental setup for streaming event modeling. On two real user-behavior datasets, PromptTPP consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance in that setup. The findings support learned prompts as a way to adapt event-sequence models over time while avoiding storage of past training examples, a concrete constraint central to the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: PromptTPP uses a learned prompt pool to help temporal point processes learn changing event streams without storing past examples.

title: Prompt-augmented Temporal Point Process for Streaming Event Sequence

abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to address the issue of class imbalance in graph neural networks (GNNs) for learning on graph-structured data. Our approach integrates imbalanced node classification and Bias-Variance Decomposition, establishing a theoretical framework that closely relates data imbalance to model variance. We also leverage graph augmentation technique to estimate the variance and design a regularization term to alleviate the impact of imbalance. Exhaustive tests are conducted on multiple benchmarks, including naturally imbalanced datasets and public-split class-imbalanced datasets, demonstrating that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in various imbalanced scenarios. This work provides a novel theoretical perspective for addressing the problem of imbalanced node classification in GNNs.

paragraphs: This paper examines class imbalance in graph neural networks used to classify nodes. When classes are represented unevenly, learning must cope with differences in the available evidence for each class. The authors approach this problem through bias-variance decomposition, developing a theoretical framework that closely connects imbalance with model variance.

That connection motivates a concrete training method. The approach uses graph augmentation to estimate variance, then introduces a regularization term intended to reduce the effects of imbalance. Variance therefore serves both as an explanatory concept and as a quantity used to shape learning, connecting the theoretical perspective to the proposed intervention.

The evaluation covers multiple benchmarks, including naturally imbalanced datasets and class-imbalanced datasets using public splits. The authors report performance above state-of-the-art methods across the tested imbalance scenarios. These findings support treating variance as a useful target when designing graph classifiers for uneven class distributions. The contribution combines a perspective on why imbalance matters with an augmentation-based way to estimate and address its effects.
summary.tldr: A bias-variance view of imbalanced graph classification motivates augmentation-based variance estimation and a regularizer that improves benchmark performance.

title: Rethinking Semi-Supervised Imbalanced Node Classification from Bias-Variance Decomposition

abstract: Unsupervised multi-object segmentation has shown impressive results on images by utilizing powerful semantics learned from self-supervised pretraining. An additional modality such as depth or motion is often used to facilitate the segmentation in video sequences. However, the performance improvements observed in synthetic sequences, which rely on the robustness of an additional cue, do not translate to more challenging real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose the first fully unsupervised method for segmenting multiple objects in real-world sequences. Our object-centric learning framework spatially binds objects to slots on each frame and then relates these slots across frames. From these temporally-aware slots, the training objective is to reconstruct the middle frame in a high-level semantic feature space. We propose a masking strategy by dropping a significant portion of tokens in the feature space for efficiency and regularization. Additionally, we address over-clustering by merging slots based on similarity. Our method can successfully segment multiple instances of complex and high-variety classes in YouTube videos.

The authors propose a fully unsupervised approach that builds object representations from semantic features and their relationships over time.

The authors demonstrate segmentation of multiple instances from complex and varied classes in YouTube videos, supporting the approach’s usefulness on real-world sequences rather than only synthetic scenes.
summary.tldr: The method learns object slots across video frames and reconstructs semantic features to segment real-world videos without supervision.

title: Self-supervised Object-Centric Learning for Videos

abstract: Cookies are designed to enable more accurate identification and tracking of user behavior, in turn allowing for more personalized ads and better performing ad campaigns. Given the additional information that is recorded, questions related to privacy and fairness naturally arise. How does a user's consent decision influence how much the system can learn about their demographic and tastes? Is the impact of a user's consent decision on the recommender system's ability to learn about their latent attributes uniform across demographics? We investigate these questions in the context of an engagement-driven recommender system using simulation. We empirically demonstrate that when consent rates exhibit demographic-dependence, user consent has a disparate impact on the recommender agent's ability to estimate users' latent attributes. In particular, we find that when consent rates are demographic-dependent, a user disagreeing to share their cookie may counter-intuitively cause the recommender agent to know more about the user than if the user agreed to share their cookie. Furthermore, the gap in base consent rates across demographics serves as an amplifier: users from the lower consent rate demographic who agree to cookie sharing generally experience higher estimation errors than the same users from the higher consent rate demographic, and conversely for users who choose to disagree to cookie sharing, with these differences increasing in consent rate gap. We discuss the need for new notions of fairness that encourage consistency between a user's privacy decisions and the system's ability to estimate their latent attributes.

paragraphs: Cookie consent changes the information available to a recommender, but the consequences may depend on how consent choices differ across demographic groups. This paper investigates that relationship in simulations of a recommender driven by user engagement. It asks how accurately the system can estimate hidden user characteristics, including demographics and tastes.

When consent rates depend on demographics, the simulations show unequal effects on estimation accuracy. Counterintuitively, refusing cookie sharing can sometimes let the recommender estimate a user's attributes more accurately than accepting would. The finding is conditional on the demographic dependence of consent rates; it does not establish that refusal generally reveals more information.

The gap between groups' consent rates amplifies these differences. Among users who consent, those in the lower-consent group generally face larger estimation errors than comparable users in the higher-consent group; the direction reverses among those who refuse. These results motivate fairness criteria that consider whether privacy choices correspond consistently to what a system can infer about people.
summary.tldr: Simulations show that demographic differences in cookie consent rates can produce unequal inference accuracy and sometimes make refusal more revealing than consent.

title: Cookie Consent Has Disparate Impact on Estimation Accuracy

abstract: Enabling machine learning classifiers to defer their decision to a downstream expert when the expert is more accurate will ensure improved safety and performance. This objective can be achieved with the learning-to-defer framework which aims to jointly learn how to classify and how to defer to the expert. In recent studies, it has been theoretically shown that popular estimators for learning to defer parameterized with softmax provide unbounded estimates for the likelihood of deferring which makes them uncalibrated. However, it remains unknown whether this is due to the widely used softmax parameterization and if we can find a softmax-based estimator that is both statistically consistent and possesses a valid probability estimator. In this work, we first show that the cause of the miscalibrated and unbounded estimator in prior literature is due to the symmetric nature of the surrogate losses used and not due to softmax. We then propose a novel statistically consistent asymmetric softmax-based surrogate loss that can produce valid estimates without the issue of unboundedness. We further analyze the non-asymptotic properties of our proposed method and empirically validate its performance and calibration on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Learning to defer trains a classifier to decide both what to predict and when to pass a decision to an expert. Reliable deferral requires meaningful estimates of when that handoff is appropriate. Earlier analyses found that popular softmax-based estimators could produce unbounded estimates of deferral likelihood, leaving open whether softmax itself caused the problem.

This paper locates the cause in the symmetry of the surrogate training losses used by those estimators. That distinction matters because it separates the parameterization from the objective used to train it. The authors then construct an asymmetric softmax-based surrogate loss that is statistically consistent and produces valid estimates without the earlier unboundedness issue.

The work also analyzes non-asymptotic properties, addressing behavior beyond a purely limiting statistical description, and evaluates performance and calibration on benchmark datasets. The result supports retaining softmax while changing the loss structure. More broadly, it shows that a calibration failure in a learning-to-defer system can arise from how the learning objective is designed, rather than being an unavoidable property of softmax.
summary.tldr: An asymmetric loss makes softmax-based learning to defer statistically consistent while avoiding unbounded probability estimates.

title: In Defense of Softmax Parametrization for Calibrated and Consistent Learning to Defer

abstract: Individual preference (IP) stability, introduced by Ahmadi et al. (ICML 2022), is a natural clustering objective inspired by stability and fairness constraints. A clustering is $\alpha$-IP stable if the average distance of every data point to its own cluster is at most $\alpha$ times the average distance to any other cluster. Unfortunately, determining if a dataset admits a $1$-IP stable clustering is NP-Hard. Moreover, before this work, it was unknown if an $o(n)$-IP stable clustering always exists, as the prior state of the art only guaranteed an $O(n)$-IP stable clustering. We close this gap in understanding and show that an $O(1)$-IP stable clustering always exists for general metrics, and we give an efficient algorithm which outputs such a clustering. We also introduce generalizations of IP stability beyond average distance and give efficient near optimal algorithms in the cases where we consider the maximum and minimum distances within and between clusters.

Moreover, before this work, it was unknown if an $o(n)$-IP stable clustering always exists, as the prior state of the art only guaranteed an $O(n)$-IP stable clustering. paragraphs: Individual preference stability asks whether each point is reasonably well served by its assigned cluster. Specifically, its average distance to its own cluster must be at most a factor alpha times its average distance to any alternative cluster. A smaller factor gives a stronger guarantee for every point, connecting clustering quality with individual preferences.

Determining whether a dataset admits a clustering with factor one is NP-hard. Before this work, the available general guarantee allowed a factor growing linearly with the number of points. The paper proves that a constant-factor stable clustering always exists in general metric spaces and provides an efficient algorithm to construct one.

This changes the guarantee from one that weakens with dataset size to one bounded by a constant. It does not claim to efficiently solve exact factor-one stability. The authors also extend the objective beyond average distances, considering maximum and minimum distances within and between clusters, and provide efficient, nearly optimal algorithms for those variants.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that constant-factor individually stable clusterings exist in general metric spaces and gives an efficient construction algorithm.

title: Constant Approximation for Individual Preference Stable Clustering

abstract: This paper focuses on graph-level representation learning that aims to represent graphs as vectors that can be directly utilized in downstream tasks such as graph classification. We propose a novel graph-level representation learning principle called Lovász principle, which is motivated by the Lovász number in graph theory. The Lovász number of a graph is a real number that is an upper bound for graph Shannon capacity and is strongly connected with various global characteristics of the graph. Specifically, we show that the handle vector for computing the Lovász number is potentially a suitable choice for graph representation, as it captures a graph's global properties, though a direct application of the handle vector is difficult and problematic. We propose to use neural networks to address the problems and hence provide the Lovász principle. Moreover, we propose an enhanced Lovász principle that is able to exploit the subgraph Lovász numbers directly and efficiently. The experiments demonstrate that our Lovász principles achieve competitive performance compared to the baselines in unsupervised and semi-supervised graph-level representation learning tasks. The code of our Lovász principles is publicly available on GitHub.

We propose to use neural networks to address the problems and hence provide the Lovász principle. Moreover, we propose an enhanced Lovász principle that is able to exploit the subgraph Lovász numbers directly and efficiently. The experiments demonstrate that our Lovász principles achieve competitive performance compared to the baselines in unsupervised and semi-supervised graph-level representation learning tasks. The code of our Lovász principles is publicly available on GitHub.

paragraphs: Graph-level representation learning converts an entire graph into a vector usable for tasks such as classification. This paper develops a learning principle inspired by the Lovász number, a graph-theoretic quantity related to global graph characteristics and providing an upper bound on graph Shannon capacity. The goal is to bring that global structural information into learned representations.

The authors examine the handle vector used in computing the Lovász number and argue that it is potentially suitable as a graph representation. Directly using this vector is difficult and problematic, so they introduce a neural-network approach to address those obstacles. This produces their proposed Lovász principle.

An enhanced version also uses Lovász numbers of subgraphs directly and efficiently. Experiments report competitive performance against baselines in both unsupervised and semi-supervised graph-level learning. The findings support this mathematical quantity as a useful source of guidance for representation learning, with neural networks providing a practical route from the graph-theoretic motivation to vectors used in downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: The Lovász principle uses graph-theoretic global structure to guide neural graph representations, achieving competitive unsupervised and semi-supervised results.

title: Lovász Principle for Unsupervised Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Mixup refers to interpolation-based data augmentation, originally motivated as a way to go beyond empirical risk minimization (ERM). Its extensions mostly focus on the definition of interpolation and the space (input or feature) where it takes place, while the augmentation process itself is less studied. In most methods, the number of generated examples is limited to the mini-batch size and the number of examples being interpolated is limited to two (pairs), in the input space.We make progress in this direction by introducing MultiMix, which generates an arbitrarily large number of interpolated examples beyond the mini-batch size and interpolates the entire mini-batch in the embedding space. Effectively, we sample on the entire convex hull of the mini-batch rather than along linear segments between pairs of examples.On sequence data, we further extend to Dense MultiMix. We densely interpolate features and target labels at each spatial location and also apply the loss densely. To mitigate the lack of dense labels, we inherit labels from examples and weight interpolation factors by attention as a measure of confidence.Overall, we increase the number of loss terms per mini-batch by orders of magnitude at little additional cost. This is only possible because of interpolating in the embedding space. We empirically show that our solutions yield significant improvement over state-of-the-art mixup methods on four different benchmarks, despite interpolation being only linear. By analyzing the embedding space, we show that the classes are more tightly clustered and uniformly spread over the embedding space, thereby explaining the improved behavior.

paragraphs: Mixup creates training examples by interpolating existing examples. Many variants change where or how interpolation happens while still mixing pairs and generating relatively few samples. MultiMix changes the augmentation process itself: it interpolates across an entire mini-batch in embedding space and can generate arbitrarily many interpolated examples beyond the batch size.

Geometrically, this samples throughout the mini-batch's convex hull rather than only along lines joining pairs. Dense MultiMix extends the approach to sequence data by mixing features and targets at individual spatial locations and applying the loss there. Because dense labels may be unavailable, it inherits example-level labels and uses attention to weight interpolation factors according to confidence.

Working in embedding space lets the methods increase the number of loss terms by orders of magnitude at little additional cost. Across four benchmarks, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art mixup methods despite using linear interpolation. Their analysis finds tighter class clusters and a more uniform spread of classes in embedding space, offering an explanation for the observed improvements.
summary.tldr: MultiMix expands mixup to whole mini-batches in embedding space, producing many more training loss terms at little additional cost.

title: Embedding Space Interpolation Beyond Mini-Batch, Beyond Pairs and Beyond Examples

abstract: In image recovery problems, one seeks to infer an image from distorted, incomplete, and/or noise-corrupted measurements.Such problems arise in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography, deblurring, super-resolution, inpainting, phase retrieval, image-to-image translation, and other applications. Given a training set of signal/measurement pairs, we seek to do more than just produce one good image estimate. Rather, we aim to rapidly and accurately sample from the posterior distribution. To do this,we propose a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN that generates dozens of high-quality posterior samples per second. Our regularization comprises an $\ell_1$ penalty and an adaptively weighted standard-deviation reward. Using quantitative evaluation metrics like conditional Fréchet inception distance, we demonstrate that our method produces state-of-the-art posterior samples in both multicoil MRI and large-scale inpainting applications. The code for our model can be found here: https://github.com/matt-bendel/rcGAN.

paragraphs: Recovering an image from incomplete or corrupted measurements can leave uncertainty about what the original image contained. This paper targets that uncertainty directly: given training pairs of images and measurements, it aims to generate samples from the posterior distribution. The goal is therefore a collection of plausible reconstructions conditioned on the measurements, rather than a single image estimate.

The proposed method uses a conditional Wasserstein generative adversarial network with additional regularization. Its training objective combines an L1 penalty with a reward for standard deviation whose weight adjusts adaptively. This introduces an explicit incentive related to variation among outputs alongside the image-recovery penalty, making the sampling behavior part of the training design.

The authors report generating dozens of high-quality posterior samples per second. Evaluations on multicoil MRI and large-scale inpainting, including conditional Fréchet inception distance, show state-of-the-art posterior sampling performance. The significance is the combination of reconstruction quality, distributional evaluation, and rapid sampling: the method is designed to provide multiple plausible answers efficiently in these recovery applications.
summary.tldr: A regularized conditional GAN rapidly generates plausible image reconstructions, with state-of-the-art posterior sampling results in MRI and inpainting.

title: A Regularized Conditional GAN for Posterior Sampling in Image Recovery Problems

abstract: Pre-trained multimodal foundation models have demonstrated remarkable generalizability but pose challenges for deployment due to their large sizes. One effective approach to reducing their sizes is layerwise distillation, wherein small student models are trained to match the hidden representations of large teacher models at each layer. Motivated by our observation that certain architecture components, referred to as modules, contribute more significantly to the student's performance than others, we propose to track the contributions of individual modules by recording the loss decrement after distillation each module and choose the module with a greater contribution to distill more frequently. Such an approach can be naturally formulated as a multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem, where modules and loss decrements are considered as arms and rewards, respectively. We then develop a modified-Thompson sampling algorithm named OPTIMA to address the nonstationarity of module contributions resulting from model updating. Specifically, we leverage the observed contributions in recent history to estimate the changing contribution of each module and select modules based on these estimations to maximize the cumulative contribution. We evaluate the effectiveness of OPTIMA through distillation experiments on various multimodal understanding and image captioning tasks, using the CoCa-Large model \citep{yu2022coca} as the teacher model.

paragraphs: Distillation compresses a large teacher model into a smaller student by training the student to reproduce aspects of the teacher's behavior. Layerwise distillation matches internal representations at different layers. This paper observes that individual architectural modules do not contribute equally to student performance, motivating a training schedule that allocates more attention to productive modules.

The method records how much the loss decreases after distilling each module. It treats module selection as a multi-armed bandit problem: modules are the available choices, and their measured loss reductions are rewards. OPTIMA, a modified Thompson sampling algorithm, selects modules using estimates of these contributions rather than assigning every module the same fixed emphasis.

Because updating the student can change which modules are most helpful, OPTIMA bases its estimates on recent observations. This explicitly addresses contributions that vary during training and aims to maximize their cumulative benefit. The authors evaluate the method using CoCa-Large as the teacher on multimodal understanding and image-captioning tasks. The contribution is an adaptive allocation strategy for distillation effort.
summary.tldr: OPTIMA adaptively chooses which multimodal model modules to distill based on their recent contributions to reducing the student's loss.

title: Module-wise Adaptive Distillation for Multimodality Foundation Models

abstract: Trajectory prediction plays a vital role in the performance of autonomous driving systems, and prediction accuracy, such as average displacement error (ADE) or final displacement error (FDE), is widely used as a performance metric. However, a significant disparity exists between the accuracy of predictors on fixed datasets and driving performance when the predictors are used downstream for vehicle control, because of a dynamics gap. In the real world, the prediction algorithm influences the behavior of the ego vehicle, which, in turn, influences the behaviors of other vehicles nearby. This interaction results in predictor-specific dynamics that directly impacts prediction results. In fixed datasets, since other vehicles' responses are predetermined, this interaction effect is lost, leading to a significant dynamics gap. This paper studies the overlooked significance of this dynamics gap. We also examine several other factors contributing to the disparity between prediction performance and driving performance. The findings highlight the trade-off between the predictor's computational efficiency and prediction accuracy in determining real-world driving performance. In summary, an interactive, task-driven evaluation protocol for trajectory prediction is crucial to capture its effectiveness for autonomous driving. Source code along with experimental settings is available online (https://whatmatters23.github.io/).

paragraphs: The paper examines why accurate trajectory prediction on a fixed dataset can fail to translate into good autonomous driving performance. Common prediction measures assess how closely a forecast matches recorded movement. Yet a predictor used for vehicle control participates in an interaction that a fixed recording cannot reproduce.

The authors call this mismatch a dynamics gap. Predictions influence the ego vehicle’s behavior, that behavior changes how nearby vehicles respond, and those responses affect subsequent predictions. Each predictor can therefore induce different dynamics. In a fixed dataset, other vehicles’ responses are already determined, so this feedback between prediction, control, and surrounding traffic is absent.

The study examines this gap alongside other contributors to the disparity between prediction and driving performance. Its findings highlight a trade-off between prediction accuracy and computational efficiency in downstream driving. The authors argue for interactive evaluation tied to the driving task, so that assessment captures the consequences of using a predictor for control as well as its ability to match recorded trajectories.
summary.tldr: Trajectory predictors need interactive driving evaluation because their control decisions alter surrounding traffic, creating dynamics absent from fixed datasets.

title: What Truly Matters in Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving?

abstract: We present a method for controlling a simulated humanoid to grasp an object and move it to follow an object's trajectory. Due to the challenges in controlling a humanoid with dexterous hands, prior methods often use a disembodied hand and only consider vertical lifts or short trajectories. This limited scope hampers their applicability for object manipulation required for animation and simulation. To close this gap, we learn a controller that can pick up a large number (>1200) of objects and carry them to follow randomly generated trajectories. Our key insight is to leverage a humanoid motion representation that provides human-like motor skills and significantly speeds up training. Using only simplistic reward, state, and object representations, our method shows favorable scalability on diverse objects and trajectories. For training, we do not need a dataset of paired full-body motion and object trajectories. At test time, we only require the object mesh and desired trajectories for grasping and transporting. To demonstrate the capabilities of our method, we show state-of-the-art success rates in following object trajectories and generalizing to unseen objects. Code and models will be released.

paragraphs: Omnigrasp studies how a simulated humanoid can grasp an object and carry it along a desired trajectory. This requires coordinating a full body with dexterous hands over an extended movement. Earlier approaches often simplified the problem to a detached hand performing a vertical lift or following a short path, limiting their usefulness for broader animation and simulation tasks.

The method builds on a humanoid motion representation that supplies human-like motor skills and substantially accelerates training. With this representation, the controller learns to pick up more than 1,200 objects and follow randomly generated trajectories. The authors report that simple reward, state, and object representations are sufficient for favorable scaling across diverse objects and paths.

Training does not require paired examples of full-body motion and object trajectories. At test time, the controller needs the object's mesh and the desired trajectory for grasping and transport. Reported results show state-of-the-art success rates for trajectory following and generalization to unseen objects, supporting the approach's ability to extend manipulation beyond narrowly specified lifts.
summary.tldr: Omnigrasp uses a humanoid motion representation to train simulated full-body controllers that grasp diverse objects and transport them along desired trajectories.

title: Omnigrasp: Grasping Diverse Objects with Simulated Humanoids

abstract: Data valuation is a class of techniques for quantitatively assessing the value of data for applications like pricing in data marketplaces. Existing data valuation methods define a value for a discrete dataset. However, in many use cases, users are interested in not only the value of the dataset, but that of the distribution from which the dataset was sampled. For example, consider a buyer trying to evaluate whether to purchase data from different vendors. The buyer may observe (and compare) only a small preview sample from each vendor, to decide which vendor's data distribution is most useful to the buyer and purchase. The core question is how should we compare the values of data distributions from their samples? Under a Huber characterization of the data heterogeneity across vendors, we propose a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)-based valuation method which enables theoretically principled and actionable policies for comparing data distributions from samples. We empirically demonstrate that our method is sample-efficient and effective in identifying valuable data distributions against several existing baselines, on multiple real-world datasets (e.g., network intrusion detection, credit card fraud detection) and downstream applications (classification, regression).
originalAbstract: Data valuation is a class of techniques for quantitatively assessing the value of data for applications like pricing in data marketplaces. Existing data valuation methods define a value for a discrete dataset. However, in many use cases, users are interested in not only the value of the dataset, but that of the distribution from which the dataset was sampled. For example, consider a buyer trying to evaluate whether to purchase data from different vendors. The buyer may observe (and compare) only a small preview sample from each vendor, to decide which vendor's data distribution is most useful to the buyer and purchase. The core question is how should we compare the values of data distributions from their samples? Under a Huber characterization of the data heterogeneity across vendors, we propose a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)-based valuation method which enables theoretically principled and actionable policies for comparing data distributions from samples. We empirically demonstrate that our method is sample-efficient and effective in identifying valuable data distributions against several existing baselines, on multiple real-world datasets (e.g., network intrusion detection, credit card fraud detection) and downstream applications (classification, regression).

paragraphs: A small preview of a dataset may need to support a much larger purchasing decision. The buyer wants to know whether the vendor's underlying data source will be useful, not merely what the preview itself is worth. This paper reframes data valuation around the distributions that generate datasets, using observed samples to compare those distributions.

The proposed method uses maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, as the basis of its valuation. Its theoretical treatment assumes a Huber characterization of differences between vendors' data. Under that model of heterogeneity, the method supports principled and actionable comparison policies. This assumption is part of the foundation for the theory, rather than an unrestricted claim about every possible collection of data sources.

The experiments evaluate whether useful distributions can be identified efficiently from samples. Across real-world datasets, including intrusion and credit-card-fraud detection, and across classification and regression applications, the method performs effectively against existing baselines. The reported sample efficiency matters for settings where only limited previews are available before committing to acquiring more data.
summary.tldr: The paper uses MMD to compare the value of data-generating distributions from samples under a specified model of vendor heterogeneity.

title: Data Distribution Valuation

abstract: Driving systems often rely on high-definition (HD) maps for precise environmental information, which is crucial for planning and navigation. While current HD map constructors perform well under ideal conditions, their resilience to real-world challenges, \eg, adverse weather and sensor failures, is not well understood, raising safety concerns. This work introduces MapBench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the robustness of HD map construction methods against various sensor corruptions. Our benchmark encompasses a total of 29 types of corruptions that occur from cameras and LiDAR sensors. Extensive evaluations across 31 HD map constructors reveal significant performance degradation of existing methods under adverse weather conditions and sensor failures, underscoring critical safety concerns. We identify effective strategies for enhancing robustness, including innovative approaches that leverage multi-modal fusion, advanced data augmentation, and architectural techniques. These insights provide a pathway for developing more reliable HD map construction methods, which are essential for the advancement of autonomous driving technology. The benchmark toolkit and affiliated code and model checkpoints have been made publicly accessible.

paragraphs: High-definition maps supply detailed environmental information used in driving-system planning and navigation. Strong map-construction performance under ideal conditions leaves an important question unanswered: how well do these methods work when their sensors are affected by adverse weather or failures? This paper makes that question the focus of a dedicated evaluation.

MapBench tests robustness against 29 corruption types involving cameras and LiDAR. The authors evaluate 31 HD map constructors, providing a broad comparison of how existing methods behave when their inputs deteriorate. The evaluations reveal substantial performance losses under adverse weather and sensor failures, highlighting a gap between ideal-condition capability and dependable operation.

The study also identifies strategies that improve robustness, including combining sensing modalities, using advanced data augmentation, and changing architectural designs. These findings offer directions for building more reliable map constructors rather than merely documenting failures. The publicly available toolkit, code, and model checkpoints support further evaluation of this problem. The practical message is that sensor-corruption robustness needs explicit measurement alongside standard map-construction performance.
summary.tldr: MapBench evaluates 31 HD map constructors under 29 sensor corruptions, revealing substantial degradation and identifying strategies for improving robustness.

title: Is Your HD Map Constructor Reliable under Sensor Corruptions?

abstract: When learning in strategic environments, a key question is whether agents can overcome uncertainty about their preferences to achieve outcomes they could have achieved absent any uncertainty. Can they do this solely through interactions with each other? We focus this question on the ability of agents to attain the value of their Stackelberg optimal strategy and study the impact of information asymmetry. We study repeated interactions in fully strategic environments where players' actions are decided based on learning algorithms that take into account their observed histories and knowledge of the game. We study the pure Nash equilibria (PNE) of a meta-game where players choose these algorithms as their actions. We demonstrate that if one player has perfect knowledge about the game, then any initial informational gap persists. That is, while there is always a PNE in which the informed agent achieves her Stackelberg value, there is a game where no PNE of the meta-game allows the partially informed player to achieve her Stackelberg value. On the other hand, if both players start with some uncertainty about the game, the quality of information alone does not determine which agent can achieve her Stackelberg value. In this case, the concept of information asymmetry becomes nuanced and depends on the game's structure. Overall, our findings suggest that repeated strategic interactions alone cannot facilitate learning effectively enough to earn an uninformed player her Stackelberg value.

paragraphs: Can repeated interaction let a strategic player overcome incomplete knowledge of a game? This paper studies that question using the player's Stackelberg value as the target outcome. Players choose learning algorithms that respond to observed histories and their existing knowledge, so learning behavior is itself part of strategic decision-making.

The authors analyze pure Nash equilibria of a meta-game whose actions are those algorithms. When one player knows the game perfectly, there is always such an equilibrium where that player obtains her Stackelberg value. However, they exhibit a game where no pure Nash equilibrium lets the partially informed player obtain her own Stackelberg value. Repeated interaction therefore does not guarantee that the informational disadvantage disappears.

When both players begin with uncertainty, information quality alone no longer determines who can attain the target value. The answer also depends on the game's structure. These results show why learning from another strategic learner can differ from simply collecting more observations: the other player's algorithm is also chosen to serve that player's interests.
summary.tldr: Repeated strategic interaction need not let a partially informed player attain her Stackelberg value, and information advantages depend on game structure.

title: Is Knowledge Power? On the (Im)possibility of Learning from Strategic Interactions

abstract: With the blossom of large language models (LLM), inference efficiency becomes increasingly important. Various approximate methods are proposed to reduce the cost at inference time. Contextual Sparsity (CS) is appealing for its training-free nature and its ability to reach a higher compression ratio seemingly without significant performance degradation. However, after a comprehensive evaluation of contextual sparsity methods on various complex generation tasks, we find that although CS succeeds in prompt-understanding tasks, it significantly degrades the model performance for reasoning, deduction, and knowledge-based tasks. Despite the gap in end-to-end accuracy, we observed that sparse models and original models often share the general problem-solving logic and require only a few token corrections to recover the original model performance. This paper introduces SIRIUS, an efficient correction mechanism, which significantly boosts CS models on reasoning tasks while maintaining its efficiency gain. SIRIUS is evaluated on 6 models with 8 difficult generation tasks in reasoning, deduction, and coding and shows consistent effectiveness and efficiency. Also, we carefully develop a system implementation for SIRIUS and show that SIRIUS delivers theoretical latency reduction with roughly a 20% reduction in latency for 8B model on-chip and a 35% reduction in latency for 70B model offloading. We open-source our implementation of Sirius at https://github.com/Infini-AI-Lab/Sirius.git.

paragraphs: Contextual sparsity reduces language-model inference costs without additional training, but its effects depend on the task. The authors find that methods performing well on prompt understanding can substantially degrade reasoning, deduction, and knowledge-based generation. This motivates examining where sparse generation goes wrong.

Their key observation is that sparse and original models often follow similar overall problem-solving logic. In those cases, correcting only a few tokens can recover the original model's performance. SIRIUS introduces an efficient correction mechanism built around this observation, improving reasoning performance while preserving efficiency gains from sparsity.

These results show how targeted corrections can help turn sparsity's computational savings into usable generation speedups on demanding tasks.
summary.tldr: SIRIUS corrects sparse language-model generation to improve difficult-task performance while retaining inference speedups.

title: SIRIUS : Contexual Sparisty with Correction for Efficient LLMs

abstract: Recent studies have put into question the belief that emergent abilities in language models are exclusive to large models. This skepticism arises from two observations: 1) smaller models can also exhibit high performance on emergent abilities and 2) there is doubt on the discontinuous metrics used to measure these abilities. In this paper, we propose to study emergent abilities in the lens of pre-training loss, instead of model size or training compute. We demonstrate that the Transformer models with the same pre-training loss, but different model and data sizes, generate the same performance on various downstream tasks, with a fixed data corpus, tokenization, and model architecture. We also discover that a model exhibits emergent abilities on certain tasks—regardless of the continuity of metrics—when its pre-training loss falls below a specific threshold. Before reaching this threshold, its performance remains at the level of random guessing. This inspires us to redefine emergent abilities as those that manifest in models with lower pre-training losses, highlighting that these abilities cannot be predicted by merely extrapolating the performance trends of models with higher pre-training losses.

The authors find that Transformers reaching the same pretraining loss achieve the same performance on various downstream tasks despite differences in model and training-data size. Those conditions matter because they define the setting in which loss aligns downstream performance across different scales.

The authors observe this regardless of whether the evaluation metric is continuous. They therefore propose defining emergence through lower pretraining loss: performance after the threshold cannot be predicted merely by extending trends seen among models with higher loss.
summary.tldr: Under fixed training conventions, pretraining loss aligns downstream performance across model scales and reveals thresholds for certain emergent abilities.

title: Understanding Emergent Abilities of Language Models from the Loss Perspective

abstract: Knowledge in materials science is widely dispersed across extensive scientific literature, posing significant challenges for efficient discovery and integration of new materials. Traditional methods, often reliant on costly and time-consuming experimental approaches, further complicate rapid innovation. Addressing these challenges, the integration of artificial intelligence with materials science has opened avenues for accelerating the discovery process, though it also demands precise annotation, data extraction, and traceability of information. To tackle these issues, this article introduces the Materials Knowledge Graph (MKG), which utilizes advanced natural language processing techniques, integrated with large language models to extract and systematically organize a decade's worth of high-quality research into structured triples, contains 162,605 nodes and 731,772 edges. MKG categorizes information into comprehensive labels such as Name, Formula, and Application, structured around a meticulously designed ontology, thus enhancing data usability and integration. By implementing network-based algorithms, MKG not only facilitates efficient link prediction but also significantly reduces reliance on traditional experimental methods. This structured approach not only streamlines materials research but also lays the groundwork for more sophisticated materials knowledge graphs.

The paper addresses this organization problem by constructing a Materials Knowledge Graph from a decade of high-quality research. Its aim is to turn dispersed textual information into a structured resource that supports integration and further analysis.

A designed ontology specifies how the extracted knowledge is organized, including labels such as Name, Formula, and Application. The resulting graph contains 162,605 nodes and 731,772 edges, giving the extracted literature a shared relational structure.

The authors apply network-based algorithms to support link prediction and report reduced reliance on traditional experimental methods. The practical significance lies in making relationships across the literature available for computational exploration. Organizing names, formulas, applications, and their connections in a common framework also provides a foundation for more sophisticated materials knowledge graphs.
summary.tldr: A language-model-assisted knowledge graph organizes materials literature into structured relationships for integration and link prediction.

title: Construction and Application of Materials Knowledge Graph in Multidisciplinary Materials Science via Large Language Model

abstract: It is commonplace to produce application-specific models by fine-tuning large pre-trained models using a small bespoke dataset. The widespread availability of foundation model checkpoints on the web poses considerable risks, including the vulnerability to backdoor attacks. In this paper, we unveil a new vulnerability: the privacy backdoor attack. This black-box privacy attack aims to amplify the privacy leakage that arises when fine-tuning a model: when a victim fine-tunes a backdoored model, their training data will be leaked at a significantly higher rate than if they had fine-tuned a typical model. We conduct extensive experiments on various datasets and models, including both vision-language models (CLIP) and large language models, demonstrating the broad applicability and effectiveness of such an attack. Additionally, we carry out multiple ablation studies with different fine-tuning methods and inference strategies to thoroughly analyze this new threat. Our findings highlight a critical privacy concern within the machine learning community and call for a re-evaluation of safety protocols in the use of open-source pre-trained models.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a publicly available pretrained model is a common way to build a specialized system from a small dataset. This paper identifies a privacy threat in that workflow: a pretrained model can be deliberately altered so that later fine-tuning exposes more information about the victim’s training data. The authors call this a privacy backdoor.

The attack aims to strengthen black-box membership inference, which concerns determining whether data participated in training through access to the model’s behavior. Its defining feature is the timing: the attacker poisons the pretrained model before the victim uses private data for fine-tuning. The resulting model leaks membership information at a significantly higher rate than a typical fine-tuned model in the reported experiments.

The authors test the attack across datasets and model types, including CLIP vision-language models and large language models. Ablations examine different fine-tuning methods and inference strategies. These findings support the threat’s applicability across multiple evaluated workflows. The contribution is identifying how the starting checkpoint can influence the privacy leakage of a later training stage, even though the sensitive dataset enters only during that later stage.
summary.tldr: Poisoned pretrained checkpoints can amplify membership leakage from private data used in subsequent fine-tuning.

title: Privacy Backdoors: Enhancing Membership Inference through Poisoning Pre-trained Models

abstract: Detection of face forgery videos remains a formidable challenge in the field of digital forensics, especially the generalization to unseen datasets and common perturbations. In this paper, we tackle this issue by leveraging the synergy between audio and visual speech elements, embarking on a novel approach through audio-visual speech representation learning. Our work is motivated by the finding that audio signals, enriched with speech content, can provide precise information effectively reflecting facial movements. To this end, we first learn precise audio-visual speech representations on real videos via a self-supervised masked prediction task, which encodes both local and global semantic information simultaneously. Then, the derived model is directly transferred to the forgery detection task. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of cross-dataset generalization and robustness, without the participation of any fake video in model training.

Its motivation is that speech-rich audio provides precise information about the movements a face makes during speech.

The method first learns audio-visual speech representations from real videos through a self-supervised masked prediction task. This training encodes both local and global semantic information, giving the representation access to speech structure at different scales. The resulting model is then transferred directly to forgery detection. No fake videos participate in model training.

Extensive experiments report stronger cross-dataset generalization and robustness than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods. These findings support learning the relationship between authentic speech and facial movement as a useful basis for detecting forged faces. The contribution is both the audio-visual representation strategy and the demonstrated transfer from real-video training to forgery detection, addressing the challenge of performance beyond the datasets a detector initially encounters.
summary.tldr: SpeechForensics learns audio-visual speech representations from real videos and transfers them to robust face-forgery detection.

title: SpeechForensics: Audio-Visual Speech Representation Learning for Face Forgery Detection

abstract: Blended-target domain adaptation (BTDA), which implicitly mixes multiple sub-target domains into a fine domain, has attracted more attention in recent years. Most previously developed BTDA approaches focus on utilizing a single source domain, which makes it difficult to obtain sufficient feature information for learning domain-invariant representations. Furthermore, different feature distributions derived from different domains may increase the uncertainty of models. To overcome these issues, we propose a style adaptation and uncertainty estimation (SAUE) approach for multi-source blended-target domain adaptation (MBDA). Specifically, we exploit the extra knowledge acquired from the blended-target domain, where a similarity factor is adopted to select more useful target style information for augmenting the source features. \!Then, to mitigate the negative impact of the domain-specific attributes, we devise a function to estimate and mitigate uncertainty in category prediction. Finally, we construct a simple and lightweight adversarial learning strategy for MBDA, effectively aligning multi-source and blended-target domains without the requirements of domain labels of the target domains. Extensive experiments conducted on several challenging DA benchmarks, including the ImageCLEF-DA, Office-Home, VisDA 2017, and DomainNet datasets, demonstrate the superiority of our method over the state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches.

paragraphs: Blended-target domain adaptation handles target data containing multiple mixed domains. Learning from only one source can provide insufficient information for representations that work across those domains. Differences in feature distributions also introduce prediction uncertainty. This paper addresses both issues by combining multiple source domains with style adaptation and uncertainty estimation.

The proposed SAUE method draws style information from the blended target data and uses a similarity factor to select useful information for augmenting source features. It also estimates and mitigates uncertainty in category predictions to reduce the negative influence of domain-specific attributes. A lightweight adversarial learning strategy aligns the source and target domains.

The alignment does not require labels identifying which target domain each example belongs to. Experiments on ImageCLEF-DA, Office-Home, VisDA 2017, and DomainNet report improvements over leading approaches. These results support combining selective target-style augmentation with uncertainty handling, so the model can use multiple sources while accounting for the mixed and unlabeled domain structure of the target data.
summary.tldr: SAUE combines target-style augmentation, uncertainty estimation, and adversarial alignment for adaptation from multiple sources to mixed target domains.

title: Style Adaptation and Uncertainty Estimation for Multi-Source Blended-Target Domain Adaptation

abstract: We characterized the generalization capabilities of deep neural network encoding models when predicting neuronal responses from the visual cortex to flashed images. We collected MacaqueITBench, a large-scale dataset of neuronal population responses from the macaque inferior temporal (IT) cortex to over $300,000$ images, comprising $8,233$ unique natural images presented to seven monkeys over $109$ sessions. Using MacaqueITBench, we investigated the impact of distribution shifts on models predicting neuronal activity by dividing the images into Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) train and test splits. The OOD splits included variations in image contrast, hue, intensity, temperature, and saturation. Compared to the performance on in-distribution test images---the conventional way in which these models have been evaluated---models performed worse at predicting neuronal responses to out-of-distribution images, retaining as little as $20\\%$ of the performance on in-distribution test images. Additionally, the relative ranking of different models in terms of their ability to predict neuronal responses changed drastically across OOD shifts. The generalization performance under OOD shifts can be well accounted by a simple image similarity metric---the cosine distance between image representations extracted from a pre-trained object recognition model is a strong predictor of neuronal predictivity under different distribution shifts. The dataset of images, neuronal firing rate recordings, and computational benchmarks are hosted publicly at: https://github.com/Spandan-Madan/benchmarking_ood_generalization_visual_cortex.
