paragraphs: This paper tests whether neural networks that predict visual brain responses remain accurate when the images change from those used for training. The researchers collected MacaqueITBench, containing neuronal population recordings from the inferior temporal cortex of seven monkeys across 109 sessions. Its more than 300,000 image presentations cover 8,233 unique natural images.

The benchmark separates training and test images using shifts in contrast, hue, intensity, temperature, and saturation. These splits expose weaknesses that conventional evaluation on images from the training distribution can miss. Under some shifts, models retained as little as 20% of their original predictive performance, and their relative rankings changed substantially.

The researchers also found that a simple measure of image similarity strongly predicted performance under these shifts. Specifically, cosine distance between representations from a pretrained object recognition model helped account for neuronal prediction quality. The findings show why evaluating these encoding models across multiple visual distributions can change conclusions about which models best predict brain activity.
summary.tldr: MacaqueITBench reveals substantial accuracy losses and changing model rankings when visual brain-response predictors encounter shifted image distributions.

title: Benchmarking Out-of-Distribution Generalization Capabilities of DNN-based Encoding Models for the Ventral Visual Cortex.

abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal foundation models have showcased impressive capabilities in understanding and reasoning with visual and textual information. Adapting these foundation models trained for general usage to specialized domains like biomedicine requires large-scale domain-specific instruction datasets. While existing works have explored curating such datasets automatically, the resultant datasets are not explicitly aligned with domain expertise. In this work, we propose a data-centric framework, Biomedical Visual Instruction Tuning with Clinician Preference Alignment (BioMed-VITAL), that incorporates clinician preferences into both stages of generating and selecting instruction data for tuning biomedical multimodal foundation models. First, during the generation stage, we prompt the GPT-4V generator with a diverse set of clinician-selected demonstrations for preference-aligned data candidate generation. Then, during the selection phase, we train a separate selection model, which explicitly distills clinician and policy-guided model preferences into a rating function to select high-quality data for medical instruction tuning. Results show that the model tuned with the instruction-following data from our method demonstrates a significant improvement in open visual chat (18.5% relatively) and medical VQA (win rate up to 81.73%). Our instruction-following data and models are available at https://BioMed-VITAL.github.io.

First, during the generation stage, we prompt the GPT-4V generator with a diverse set of clinician-selected demonstrations for preference-aligned data candidate generation. Then, during the selection phase, we train a separate selection model, which explicitly distills clinician and policy-guided model preferences into a rating function to select high-quality data for medical instruction tuning. Results show that the model tuned with the instruction-following data from our method demonstrates a significant improvement in open visual chat (18.5% relatively) and medical VQA (win rate up to 81.73%). Our instruction-following data and models are available at https://BioMed-VITAL.github.io.

paragraphs: BioMed-VITAL addresses how to adapt general multimodal models to biomedical tasks using instruction data that reflects clinical expertise. Automatically generated medical training examples can provide scale, but their generation alone does not explicitly align them with clinician preferences. The paper makes those preferences part of both producing candidate examples and deciding which examples enter training.

During generation, GPT-4V receives a diverse collection of demonstrations selected by clinicians. These demonstrations guide the creation of candidate instruction data. During selection, a separate model learns a rating function from clinician preferences and preferences supplied by a policy-guided model. That function then selects high-quality examples for tuning the biomedical multimodal model.

The resulting instruction data improves the evaluated model's performance on open visual chat and medical visual question answering. The abstract reports an 18.5% relative improvement in open visual chat and a medical question-answering win rate reaching 81.73%. These findings support the value of incorporating domain preferences into the construction of training data, with guidance operating at two distinct stages.
summary.tldr: BioMed-VITAL uses clinician preferences to generate and select instruction data, improving evaluated biomedical visual conversations and question answering.

title: Biomedical Visual Instruction Tuning with Clinician Preference Alignment

abstract: We present a novel multimodal preference dataset for creative tasks, consisting of over 250 million human votes on more than 2.2 million captions, collected through crowdsourcing rating data for The New Yorker's weekly cartoon caption contest over the past eight years. This unique dataset supports the development and evaluation of multimodal large language models and preference-based fine-tuning algorithms for humorous caption generation. We propose novel benchmarks for judging the quality of model-generated captions, utilizing both GPT4 and human judgments to establish ranking-based evaluation strategies. Our experimental results highlight the limitations of current fine-tuning methods, such as RLHF and DPO, when applied to creative tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even state-of-the-art models like GPT4 and Claude currently underperform top human contestants in generating humorous captions. As we conclude this extensive data collection effort, we release the entire preference dataset to the research community, fostering further advancements in AI humor generation and evaluation.

This paper provides a large source of human preferences for studying that combination: more than 250 million votes covering over 2.2 million captions from eight years of The New Yorker’s weekly caption contest.

The dataset supports both training and evaluation of models that work with images and text. The authors also introduce benchmarks that rank generated captions using GPT4 judgments and human judgments. Ranking makes preferences between captions central to evaluation, connecting the assessment of generated humor to the kind of feedback collected in the contest.

The experiments reveal limitations in applying preference-based fine-tuning methods, including RLHF and DPO, to this creative task. GPT4 and Claude also fall short of top human contestants in the reported caption-generation comparisons. Releasing the complete preference dataset gives researchers material for investigating that gap and testing new methods. The findings establish a demanding evaluation setting rather than suggesting that large quantities of preference feedback already solve humor generation.
summary.tldr: A massive cartoon-caption preference dataset and new ranking benchmarks expose gaps between AI-generated humor and top human captions.

title: Humor in AI: Massive Scale Crowd-Sourced Preferences and Benchmarks for Cartoon Captioning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now available from cloud API providers in various sizes and configurations. While this diversity offers a broad spectrum of choices, effectively leveraging the options to optimize computational cost and performance remains challenging. In this work, we present AutoMix, an approach that strategically routes queries to larger LMs, based on the approximate correctness of outputs from a smaller LM. Central to AutoMix are two key technical contributions. First, it has a few-shot self-verification mechanism, which estimates the reliability of its own outputs without requiring extensive training. Second, given that self-verification can be noisy, it employs a POMDP based router that can effectively select an appropriately sized model, based on answer confidence. Experiments across five language models and five challenging datasets show that Automix consistently surpasses strong baselines, reducing computational cost by over 50\% for comparable performance.

Experiments across five language models and five challenging datasets show that Automix consistently surpasses strong baselines, reducing computational cost by over 50\% for comparable performance.

paragraphs: AutoMix addresses a practical question when several language models are available: which queries justify the cost of a larger model? Its approach uses a smaller model’s answer and an estimate of that answer’s correctness to decide whether a query should move to a larger model. This makes model selection depend on the apparent difficulty of each case.

The first component is few-shot self-verification. Using a small number of examples, the system estimates the reliability of its own outputs without extensive training. Those estimates can be noisy, so AutoMix does not treat confidence as a perfectly trustworthy signal. Its router uses a partially observable Markov decision process, a framework for making decisions when relevant information is uncertain.

Experiments spanning five language models and five challenging datasets show that AutoMix consistently outperforms the strong baselines evaluated. It reduces computational cost by more than 50% while maintaining comparable performance. The finding supports combining inexpensive initial answers with uncertainty-aware routing as a way to make a collection of models more economical.
summary.tldr: AutoMix uses answer self-verification and uncertainty-aware routing to reduce language-model computation costs while preserving comparable performance.

title: AutoMix: Automatically Mixing Language Models

abstract: This paper presents innovative enhancements to diffusion models by integrating a novel multi-resolution network and time-dependent layer normalization.Diffusion models have gained prominence for their effectiveness in high-fidelity image generation.While conventional approaches rely on convolutional U-Net architectures, recent Transformer-based designs have demonstrated superior performance and scalability.However, Transformer architectures, which tokenize input data (via "patchification"), face a trade-off between visual fidelity and computational complexity due to the quadratic nature of self-attention operations concerning token length.While larger patch sizes enable attention computation efficiency, they struggle to capture fine-grained visual details, leading to image distortions.To address this challenge, we propose augmenting the **Di**ffusion model with the **M**ulti-**R**esolution network (DiMR), a framework that refines features across multiple resolutions, progressively enhancing detail from low to high resolution.Additionally, we introduce Time-Dependent Layer Normalization (TD-LN), a parameter-efficient approach that incorporates time-dependent parameters into layer normalization to inject time information and achieve superior performance.Our method's efficacy is demonstrated on the class-conditional ImageNet generation benchmark, where DiMR-XL variants surpass previous diffusion models, achieving FID scores of 1.70 on ImageNet $256 \times 256$ and 2.89 on ImageNet $512 \times 512$. Our best variant, DiMR-G, further establishes a state-of-the-art 1.63 FID on ImageNet $256 \times 256$.

Our best variant, DiMR-G, further establishes a state-of-the-art 1.63 FID on ImageNet $256 \times 256$.

paragraphs: Transformer diffusion models divide images into patches, creating a tension between computation and detail. Larger patches reduce the number of tokens processed by attention, whose cost grows quadratically with token count. However, those larger patches can struggle to represent fine visual structure, contributing to distorted generated images. This paper addresses that architectural trade-off.

The proposed DiMR framework refines features at multiple resolutions, progressively developing detail from coarse representations to finer ones. The authors also introduce Time-Dependent Layer Normalization, which incorporates parameters that vary with diffusion time into the normalization operation. This provides a parameter-efficient way to supply time information while supporting the model’s image-generation performance.

On class-conditional ImageNet generation, the DiMR-XL variants achieve FID scores of 1.70 at 256 × 256 resolution and 2.89 at 512 × 512. The strongest reported variant, DiMR-G, reaches 1.63 at 256 × 256, described as state of the art. These results support the combined architecture’s effectiveness on the evaluated benchmark.
summary.tldr: DiMR combines progressive multi-resolution refinement with time-dependent normalization to improve diffusion image generation.

title: Alleviating Distortion in Image Generation via Multi-Resolution Diffusion Models and Time-Dependent Layer Normalization

abstract: Most of existing federated learning (FL) formulation is treated as a point-estimate of models, inherently prone to overfitting on scarce client-side data with overconfident decisions. Though Bayesian inference can alleviate this issue, a direct posterior inference at clients may result in biased local posterior estimates due to data heterogeneity, leading to a sub-optimal global posterior. From an information-theoretic perspective, we propose FedMDMI, a federated posterior inference framework based on model-data mutual information (MI). Specifically, a global model-data MI term is introduced as regularization to enforce the global model to learn essential information from the heterogeneous local data, alleviating the bias caused by data heterogeneity and hence enhancing generalization. To make this global MI tractable, we decompose it into local MI terms at the clients, converting the global objective with MI regularization into several locally optimizable objectives based on local data. For these local objectives, we further show that the optimal local posterior is a Gibbs posterior, which can be efficiently sampled with stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics methods. Finally, at the server, we approximate sampling from the global Gibbs posterior by simply averaging samples from the local posteriors. Theoretical analysis provides a generalization bound for FL w.r.t. the model-data MI, which, at different levels of regularization, represents a federated version of the bias-variance trade-off. Experimental results demonstrate a better generalization behavior with better calibrated uncertainty estimates of FedMDMI.

paragraphs: Federated learning can overfit when individual clients have little data, producing predictions that are too confident. Representing uncertainty through posterior inference can help, but differences between clients' data can bias local posteriors and weaken the combined global result. FedMDMI addresses this tension through a global model-data mutual-information regularizer.

The regularizer is intended to help the global model learn essential information from heterogeneous client data. To make the objective manageable, the authors decompose the global information term into locally optimizable terms. They show that each resulting optimal local posterior has a Gibbs form and can be sampled using stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. The server approximates global posterior sampling by averaging local posterior samples.

The theoretical analysis provides a generalization bound expressed through model-data mutual information. Changing the regularization level yields a federated version of the bias-variance trade-off. Experiments report improved generalization and better-calibrated uncertainty estimates. Together, these findings connect an information-based training objective with both predictive performance and the reliability of the model's expressed uncertainty.
summary.tldr: FedMDMI regularizes federated posterior inference with model-data mutual information to improve generalization and uncertainty calibration.

title: Improving Generalization in Federated Learning with Model-Data Mutual Information Regularization: A Posterior Inference Approach

abstract: Controlling the spatial and semantic structure of diffusion-generated images remains a challenge. Existing methods like ControlNet rely on handcrafted condition maps and retraining, limiting flexibility and generalization. Inversion-based approaches offer stronger alignment but incur high inference cost due to dual-path denoising. We present \textbf{FreeControl}, a training-free framework for semantic structural control in diffusion models. Unlike prior methods that extract attention across multiple timesteps, FreeControl performs \textit{one-step attention extraction} from a single, optimally chosen timestep and reuses it throughout denoising. This enables efficient structural guidance without inversion or retraining. To further improve quality and stability, we introduce \textit{Latent-Condition Decoupling (LCD)}: a principled separation of the timestep condition and the noised latent used in attention extraction. LCD provides finer control over attention quality and eliminates structural artifacts. FreeControl also supports compositional control via reference images assembled from multiple sources, enabling intuitive scene layout design and stronger prompt alignment. FreeControl introduces a new paradigm for test-time control—enabling structurally and semantically aligned, visually coherent generation directly from raw images, with the flexibility for intuitive compositional design and compatibility with modern diffusion models at ~5\% additional cost.

The paper instead builds structural guidance from attention extracted at one selected diffusion timestep and reuses that information throughout denoising.

The contribution is an efficient way to reuse reference-derived attention as structural guidance while supporting intuitive composition with modern diffusion models.

title: FreeControl: Efficient, Training-Free Structural Control via One-Step Attention Extraction

abstract: In order to enable fluid and natural human-machine speech interaction, existing full-duplex conversational systems often adopt modular architectures with auxiliary components such as voice activity detectors, interrupters, conversation state predictors, or multiple LLMs. These systems, however, suffer from error accumulation across modules and struggle with key challenges such as context-dependent barge-in and echo cancellation. Recent approaches, most notably Moshi, simplify the pipeline by injecting audio codecs into the token space of a single LLM. However, such methods still incur significant performance degradation when operating on the speech rather than text modality. In this paper, we introduce SALMONN-omni, the first single, standalone full-duplex speech LLM that operates without audio codecs in its token space. It features a novel dynamic thinking mechanism within the LLM backbone, enabling the model to learn when to transition between speaking and listening states. Experiments on widely used benchmarks for spoken question answering and open-domain dialogue show that SALMONN-omni achieves at least 30\% relative performance improvement over existing open-source full-duplex models and performs highly competitively to half-duplex and turn-based systems, despite using substantially less training data. Moreover, SALMONN-omni demonstrates strong performance in complex conversational scenarios, including turn-taking, backchanneling, echo cancellation and context-dependent barge-in, with further improvements achieved through reinforcement learning. Some demo conversations between user and SALMONN-omni are provided in the following repository https://github.com/bytedance/SALMONN.

title: SALMONN-omni: A Standalone Speech LLM without Codec Injection for Full-duplex Conversation

abstract: Despite the success of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP in aligning vision and language, their proficiency in detailed, fine-grained visual comprehension remains a key challenge. We present CLIP-IN, a novel framework that bolsters CLIP's fine-grained perception through two core innovations. Firstly, we leverage instruction-editing datasets, originally designed for image manipulation, as a unique source of hard negative image-text pairs. Coupled with a symmetric hard negative contrastive loss, this enables the model to effectively distinguish subtle visual-semantic differences. Secondly, CLIP-IN incorporates long descriptive captions, utilizing rotary positional encodings to capture rich semantic context often missed by standard CLIP. Our experiments demonstrate that CLIP-IN achieves substantial gains on the MMVP benchmark and various fine-grained visual recognition tasks, without compromising robust zero-shot performance on broader classification and retrieval tasks. Critically, integrating CLIP-IN's visual representations into Multimodal Large Language Models significantly reduces visual hallucinations and enhances reasoning abilities. This work underscores the considerable potential of synergizing targeted, instruction-based contrastive learning with comprehensive descriptive information to elevate the fine-grained understanding of VLMs.

paragraphs: CLIP aligns images and language effectively, but subtle visual distinctions remain challenging. CLIP-IN addresses this through training examples that emphasize small differences and captions that describe images more fully. The work combines these two sources of information to improve detailed visual understanding.

First, it repurposes instruction-based image-editing datasets to create hard negative image–text pairs. A symmetric hard-negative contrastive loss teaches the model to distinguish closely related visual and semantic content. Second, it incorporates long descriptive captions and rotary positional encodings to capture richer context than standard CLIP commonly uses. The two changes jointly target fine detail and descriptive completeness.

The authors report substantial gains on MMVP and other fine-grained recognition tasks while preserving robust zero-shot classification and retrieval performance. When incorporated into multimodal language models, the learned visual representations also significantly reduce visual hallucinations and improve reasoning. These findings indicate that more precise visual representations can benefit both image–text matching and the downstream models that depend on those representations.
summary.tldr: CLIP-IN combines editing-derived hard negatives and long captions to improve fine-grained perception and downstream multimodal reasoning.

title: VITRIX-CLIPIN: Enhancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding in CLIP via Instruction-Editing Data and Long Captions

abstract: Current AIGC detectors often achieve near-perfect accuracy on images produced by the same generator used for training but struggle to generalize to outputs from unseen generators. We trace this failure in part to latent prior bias: detectors learn shortcuts tied to patterns stemming from the initial noise vector rather than learning robust generative artifacts. To address this, we propose \textbf{On-Manifold Adversarial Training (OMAT)}: by optimizing the initial latent noise of diffusion models under fixed conditioning, we generate \emph{on-manifold} adversarial examples that remain on the generator’s output manifold—unlike pixel-space attacks, which introduce off-manifold perturbations that the generator itself cannot reproduce and that can obscure the true discriminative artifacts. To test against state-of-the-art generative models, we introduce GenImage++, a test-only benchmark of outputs from advanced generators (Flux.1, SD3) with extended prompts and diverse styles. We apply our adversarial-training paradigm to ResNet50 and CLIP baselines and evaluate across existing AIGC forensic benchmarks and recent challenge datasets. Extensive experiments show that adversarially trained detectors significantly improve cross-generator performance without any network redesign. Our findings on latent-prior bias offer valuable insights for future dataset construction and detector evaluation, guiding the development of more robust and generalizable AIGC forensic methodologies.

paragraphs: Detectors of AI-generated images can perform extremely well on a familiar generator while struggling with unfamiliar ones. This paper attributes part of that failure to latent prior bias: detectors exploit patterns associated with a generator’s initial noise rather than learning artifacts that transfer reliably across generators. Such shortcuts can make strong training-domain results misleading.

The proposed On-Manifold Adversarial Training method creates difficult examples by optimizing a diffusion model’s initial noise while keeping its conditioning fixed. The resulting images remain outputs that the generator itself can produce. This matters because directly perturbing pixels can create changes outside the generator’s output space and obscure the artifacts that detection should examine.

The authors also introduce GenImage++, a test-only benchmark containing outputs from Flux.1 and SD3 with varied prompts and styles. Applying the training approach to ResNet50 and CLIP detectors improves cross-generator performance across the evaluated benchmarks and challenge datasets. The reported gains require no network redesign, showing that changing the examples used during training can improve generalization.
summary.tldr: Training detectors on adversarial images generated through latent-noise optimization improves detection across unfamiliar image generators.

title: Breaking Latent Prior Bias in Detectors for Generalizable AIGC Image Detection

abstract: State-of-the-art embeddings often capture distinct yet complementary discriminative features: For instance, one image embedding model may excel at distinguishing fine-grained textures, while another focuses on object-level structure. Motivated by this observation, we propose a principled approach to fuse such complementary representations through *kernel multiplication*. Multiplying the kernel similarity functions of two embeddings allows their discriminative structures to interact, producing a fused representation whose kernel encodes the union of the clusters identified by each parent embedding. This formulation also provides a natural way to construct *joint kernels* for paired multi-modal data (e.g., image–text tuples), where the product of modality-specific kernels inherits structure from both domains. We highlight that this kernel product is mathematically realized via the *Kronecker product* of the embedding feature maps, yielding our proposed *KrossFuse* framework for embedding fusion. To address the computational cost of the resulting high-dimensional Kronecker space, we further develop *RP-KrossFuse*, a scalable variant that leverages random projections for efficient approximation. As a key application, we use this framework to bridge the performance gap between cross-modal embeddings (e.g., CLIP, BLIP) and unimodal experts (e.g., DINOv2, E5). Experiments show that RP-KrossFuse effectively integrates these models, enhancing modality-specific performance while preserving cross-modal alignment. The project code is available at https://github.com/yokiwuuu/KrossFuse.

KrossFuse combines these representations by multiplying their similarity kernels. The goal is to let the discriminative structure of each embedding contribute to a fused representation rather than requiring one model to supply every useful distinction.

The same construction also forms joint kernels for paired multimodal examples, allowing the combined similarity to inherit structure from both modalities.

Because the Kronecker representation can become very large, RP-KrossFuse uses random projections to approximate it efficiently. Experiments combine cross-modal models such as CLIP and BLIP with unimodal experts such as DINOv2 and E5. The reported results improve modality-specific performance while preserving cross-modal alignment, supporting kernel multiplication as a principled way to integrate specialized and cross-modal representations.
summary.tldr: KrossFuse multiplies embedding kernels to combine complementary structure, with random projections making the resulting representation more scalable.

title: When Kernels Multiply, Clusters Unify: Fusing Embeddings with the Kronecker Product

abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) enables a single model to learn multiple tasks simultaneously, leveraging knowledge transfer among tasks for enhanced generalization, and has been widely applied across various domains. However, task imbalance remains a major challenge in MTL. Although balancing the convergence speeds of different tasks is an effective approach to address this issue, it is highly challenging to accurately characterize the training dynamics and convergence speeds of multiple tasks within the complex MTL system. To this end, we attempt to analyze the training dynamics in MTL by leveraging Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory and propose a new MTL method, NTKMTL. Specifically, we introduce an extended NTK matrix for MTL and adopt spectral analysis to balance the convergence speeds of multiple tasks, thereby mitigating task imbalance. Based on the approximation via shared representation, we further propose NTKMTL-SR, achieving training efficiency while maintaining competitive performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods achieve state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of benchmarks, including both multi-task supervised learning and multi-task reinforcement learning. Source code is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/NTKMTL.

A persistent difficulty is task imbalance: the tasks do not necessarily progress at comparable rates during training. Balancing their convergence speeds can help, but describing those speeds accurately is difficult when several learning processes interact within one model.

NTKMTL approaches this problem through Neural Tangent Kernel theory. The authors extend the kernel matrix to the multi-task setting and use spectral analysis to study and balance convergence speeds. This supplies a mathematical view of training dynamics that guides how the method mitigates imbalance, connecting the balancing strategy to the behavior of the joint learning system.

The two variants connect theoretical analysis of task progress with practical optimization, including a more efficient approximation for applying the approach.

title: NTKMTL: Mitigating Task Imbalance in Multi-Task Learning from Neural Tangent Kernel Perspective

abstract: Video camouflaged object segmentation (VCOS), aiming at segmenting camouflaged objects that seamlessly blend into their environment, is a fundamental vision task with various real-world applications. With the release of SAM2, video segmentation has witnessed significant progress. However, SAM2's capability of segmenting camouflaged videos is suboptimal, especially when given simple prompts such as point and box. To address the problem, we propose Camouflaged SAM2 (CamSAM2), which enhances SAM2's ability to handle camouflaged scenes without modifying SAM2's parameters. Specifically, we introduce a decamouflaged token to provide the flexibility of feature adjustment for VCOS. To make full use of fine-grained and high-resolution features from the current frame and previous frames, we propose implicit object-aware fusion (IOF) and explicit object-aware fusion (EOF) modules, respectively. Object prototype generation (OPG) is introduced to abstract and memorize object prototypes with informative details using high-quality features from previous frames. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our approach. While CamSAM2 only adds negligible learnable parameters to SAM2, it substantially outperforms SAM2 on three VCOS datasets, especially achieving 12.2 mDice gains with click prompt on MoCA-Mask and 19.6 mDice gains with mask prompt on SUN-SEG-Hard, with Hiera-T as the backbone. The code is available at https://github.com/zhoustan/CamSAM2.

These results show that targeted feature adjustment and temporal information can substantially improve SAM2's performance in the evaluated camouflage settings.
summary.tldr: CamSAM2 adds lightweight feature adjustment and temporal object information to improve camouflage segmentation while keeping SAM2's original parameters fixed.

title: CamSAM2: Segment Anything Accurately in Camouflaged Videos

abstract: The Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem (ATSP) ranks among the most fundamental and notoriously difficult problems in combinatorial optimization. We propose a novel continuous relaxation framework for the Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem (ATSP) by leveraging differentiable constraints that encourage acyclic structures and valid permutations. Our approach integrates a differentiable trace-based Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) constraint with a doubly stochastic matrix relaxation of the assignment problem, enabling gradient-based optimization over soft permutations. We develop a projected exponentiated gradient method with adaptive step size to minimize tour cost while satisfying the relaxed constraints. To recover high-quality discrete tours, we introduce a greedy post-processing procedure that iteratively corrects subtours using cost-aware cycle merging. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard asymmetric TSP benchmarks and demonstrates competitive scalability and accuracy, particularly on large or asymmetric instances where heuristic solvers such as LKH-3 struggle.

paragraphs: The asymmetric traveling salesman problem requires finding a low-cost tour when travel costs can depend on direction. This paper approaches the discrete optimization problem through a continuous relaxation, allowing gradient-based updates over soft permutations. The aim is to make tour construction amenable to differentiable optimization while retaining constraints that guide it toward valid solutions.

The framework combines a trace-based differentiable directed-acyclic-graph constraint with a doubly stochastic relaxation of assignment matrices. It optimizes these soft assignments using projected exponentiated gradients with an adaptive step size. After continuous optimization, a greedy post-processing procedure repairs subtours by merging cycles in a cost-aware way, producing discrete tours from the relaxed representation.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on standard asymmetric TSP benchmarks and competitive accuracy and scalability. They particularly highlight large or asymmetric instances where LKH-3 struggles. The contribution brings together differentiable structural guidance and explicit discrete repair: the relaxation enables gradient-based search, while the merging procedure handles the remaining task of recovering a complete tour.
summary.tldr: The method solves asymmetric tour problems through differentiable soft assignments followed by cost-aware subtour merging.

title: Solving the Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem via Trace-Guided Cost Augmentation

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have shown impressive performance across multi-modal tasks by encoding images into thousands of tokens. However, the large number of image tokens results in significant computational overhead, and the use of dynamic high-resolution inputs further increases this burden. Previous approaches have attempted to reduce the number of image tokens through token pruning, typically by selecting tokens based on attention scores or image token diversity. Through empirical studies, we observe that existing methods often overlook the joint impact of pruning on both the current layer's output (local) and the outputs of subsequent layers (global), leading to suboptimal pruning decisions. To address this challenge, we propose Balanced Token Pruning (BTP), a plug-and-play method for pruning vision tokens. Specifically, our method utilizes a small calibration set to divide the pruning process into multiple stages. In the early stages, our method emphasizes the impact of pruning on subsequent layers, whereas in the deeper stages, the focus shifts toward preserving the consistency of local outputs. Extensive experiments across various LVLMs demonstrate the broad effectiveness of our approach on multiple benchmarks. Our method achieves a 78\% compression rate while preserving 96.7\% of the original models' performance on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/EmbodiedCity/NeurIPS2025-Balanced-Token-Pruning.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can represent an image with thousands of tokens, making visual processing expensive, especially with dynamic high-resolution inputs. Token pruning reduces this burden by removing some image tokens. The paper's empirical analysis finds that existing selection methods often inadequately account for both immediate changes to a layer's output and consequences for later layers.

Balanced Token Pruning addresses this problem by changing its priorities across the model. A small calibration set helps divide pruning into stages. Early stages emphasize how removing tokens affects subsequent layers. Deeper stages place more emphasis on keeping the current layer's output consistent. This makes pruning sensitive to where it happens, rather than treating token importance as an exclusively local decision.

Experiments across multiple vision-language models and benchmarks report a 78% compression rate while retaining, on average, 96.7% of original performance. The result demonstrates a substantial reduction in token representation with a comparatively small average performance loss. As a plug-and-play method, BTP offers a way to incorporate this balance into existing models' visual processing.
summary.tldr: Balanced Token Pruning changes pruning priorities across model depth to compress image tokens while retaining most original performance.

title: Balanced Token Pruning: Accelerating Vision Language Models Beyond Local Optimization

abstract: We study the problem of selecting limited features to observe such that models trained on them can perform well simultaneously across multiple subpopulations. This problem has applications in settings where collecting each feature is costly, e.g. requiring adding survey questions or physical sensors, and we must be able to use the selected features to create high-quality downstream models for different populations. Our method frames the problem as a continuous relaxation of traditional variable selection using a noising mechanism, without requiring backpropagation through model training processes. By optimizing over the variance of a Bayes-optimal predictor, we develop a model-agnostic framework that balances overall performance of downstream prediction across populations. We validate our approach through experiments on both synthetic datasets and real-world data.

paragraphs: Selecting model inputs becomes a practical resource decision when each feature requires a survey question or physical sensor. This paper studies how to choose a limited set of features that supports useful prediction across multiple subpopulations. The objective accounts for the different populations that will depend on the selected information, rather than considering only a single downstream prediction setting.

The method replaces a discrete feature-selection problem with a continuous relaxation built around a noising mechanism. This provides a continuous optimization route for deciding which information to preserve. Its objective uses the variance of a Bayes-optimal predictor, giving the selection process a predictive criterion while avoiding the need to backpropagate through the training of downstream models.

The resulting framework is model-agnostic and aims to balance downstream predictive performance across populations. The authors evaluate it on synthetic datasets and real-world data. The contribution is a way to connect limited information collection with performance across different groups, using an optimization formulation that does not require differentiating through each downstream model's learning procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a model-agnostic method for selecting limited features while balancing predictive performance across subpopulations.

title: Distributionally Robust Feature Selection

abstract: Mobile agents rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to plan and execute tasks on smartphone user interfaces (UIs). While cloud-based LLMs achieve high task accuracy, they require uploading the full UI state at every step, exposing unnecessary and often irrelevant information. In contrast, local LLMs avoid UI uploads but suffer from limited capacity, resulting in lower task success rates. We propose $\textbf{CORE}$, a $\textbf{CO}$llaborative framework that combines the strengths of cloud and local LLMs to $\textbf{R}$educe UI $\textbf{E}$xposure, while maintaining task accuracy for mobile agents. CORE comprises three key components: (1) $\textbf{Layout-aware block partitioning}$, which groups semantically related UI elements based on the XML screen hierarchy; (2) $\textbf{Co-planning}$, where local and cloud LLMs collaboratively identify the current sub-task; and (3) $\textbf{Co-decision-making}$, where the local LLM ranks relevant UI blocks, and the cloud LLM selects specific UI elements within the top-ranked block. CORE further introduces a multi-round accumulation mechanism to mitigate local misjudgment or limited context. Experiments across diverse mobile apps and tasks show that CORE reduces UI exposure by up to 55.6\% while maintaining task success rates slightly below cloud-only agents, effectively mitigating unnecessary privacy exposure to the cloud. The code is available at https://github.com/Entropy-Fighter/CORE.

paragraphs: Mobile agents often send the entire phone interface to a cloud language model at each step. That gives the model useful context but also exposes information unrelated to the task. Running everything locally avoids these uploads, yet smaller local models have lower task success rates. CORE divides the work between local and cloud models.

First, it groups related interface elements into blocks using the screen's XML hierarchy. Local and cloud models then collaborate to identify the current subtask. The local model ranks relevant blocks, and the cloud model chooses a specific element within the highest-ranked block. A mechanism that accumulates information across rounds helps address local ranking errors or insufficient context.

Across the evaluated applications and tasks, CORE reduces interface exposure by up to 55.6%. Task success remains slightly below that of cloud-only agents. The result therefore demonstrates a concrete tradeoff: substantially less interface information reaches the cloud while task performance stays close to the cloud-only approach. It does not imply that all uploads or privacy exposure disappear.
summary.tldr: CORE coordinates local and cloud models to reduce mobile interface exposure by up to 55.6%, with task success slightly below cloud-only agents.

title: CORE: Reducing UI Exposure in Mobile Agents via Collaboration Between Cloud and Local LLMs

abstract: Designing protein binders targeting specific sites, which requires to generate realistic and functional interaction patterns, is a fundamental challenge in drug discovery. Current structure-based generative models are limited in generating nterfaces with sufficient rationality and interpretability. In this paper, we propose **R**etrieval-**A**ugmented **Di**ffusion for **A**lig**n**ed interfa**ce** (**RADiAnce**), a new framework that leverages known interfaces to guide the design of novel binders. By unifying retrieval and generation in a shared contrastive latent space, our model efficiently identifies relevant interfaces for a given binding site and seamlessly integrates them through a conditional latent diffusion generator, enabling cross-domain interface transfer. Extensive exeriments show that **RADiAnce** significantly outperforms baseline models across multiple metrics, including binding affinity and recovery of geometries and interactions. Additional experimental results validate cross-domain generalization, demonstrating that retrieving interfaces from diverse domains, such as peptides, antibodies, and protein fragments, enhances the generation performance of binders for other domains. Our work establishes a new paradigm for protein binder design that successfully bridges retrieval-based knowledge and generative AI, opening new possibilities for drug discovery.

paragraphs: Designing a protein binder for a specific site requires generating a plausible interface: the geometry and interactions through which the binder meets its target. title: Latent Retrieval Augmented Generation of Cross-Domain Protein Binders

abstract: Training data attribution (TDA) provides insights into which training data is responsible for a learned model behavior. Gradient-based TDA methods such as influence functions and unrolled differentiation both involve a computation that resembles an inverse Hessian-vector product (iHVP), which is difficult to approximate efficiently. We introduce an algorithm (ASTRA) which uses the EKFAC-preconditioner on Neumann series iterations to arrive at an accurate iHVP approximation for TDA. ASTRA is easy to tune, requires fewer iterations than Neumann series iterations, and is more accurate than EKFAC-based approximations. Using ASTRA, we show that improving the accuracy of the iHVP approximation can significantly improve TDA performance.

paragraphs: Training data attribution asks which training examples contributed to a particular behavior of a learned model. Several gradient-based approaches, including influence functions and unrolled differentiation, depend on a difficult numerical calculation resembling an inverse Hessian-vector product. This calculation captures information about the training objective’s curvature, and approximating it efficiently is a central obstacle for these attribution methods.

The paper introduces ASTRA, which combines Neumann-series iterations with an EKFAC preconditioner. The preconditioner helps the iterative calculation reach an accurate approximation. This joins two tools that offer different strengths: an iterative refinement procedure and an existing approximation to the curvature information needed by that procedure.

The authors report that ASTRA is easy to tune, needs fewer iterations than ordinary Neumann-series iterations, and is more accurate than EKFAC-based approximations. They also show that greater accuracy in this numerical component can significantly improve attribution performance. The result connects a computational improvement to the substantive goal of identifying training examples responsible for model behavior.
summary.tldr: ASTRA improves training data attribution by combining EKFAC preconditioning with iterative inverse Hessian-vector product approximation.

title: Better Training Data Attribution via Better Inverse Hessian-Vector Products

abstract: Contrastive self-supervised learning based on point-wise comparisons has been widely studied for vision tasks. In the visual cortex of the brain, neuronal responses to distinct stimulus classes are organized into geometric structures known as neural manifolds. Accurate classification of stimuli can be achieved by effectively separating these manifolds, akin to solving a packing problem. We introduce Contrastive Learning As Manifold Packing (CLAMP), a self-supervised framework that recasts representation learning as a manifold packing problem. CLAMP introduces a loss function inspired by the potential energy of short-range repulsive particle systems, such as those encountered in the physics of simple liquids and jammed packings. In this framework, each class consists of sub-manifolds embedding multiple augmented views of a single image. The sizes and positions of the sub-manifolds are dynamically optimized by following the gradient of a packing loss. This approach yields interpretable dynamics in the embedding space that parallel jamming physics, and introduces geometrically meaningful hyperparameters within the loss function. Under the standard linear evaluation protocol, which freezes the backbone and trains only a linear classifier, CLAMP achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art self-supervised models. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that neural manifolds corresponding to different categories emerge naturally and are effectively separated in the learned representation space, highlighting the potential of CLAMP to bridge insights from physics, neural science, and machine learning.

paragraphs: CLAMP approaches self-supervised visual learning as a geometric packing problem. Its inspiration comes from neural manifolds: structures formed by neuronal responses to different stimulus classes. If representations of different categories occupy well-separated structures, classification becomes easier. The paper uses this perspective to move beyond contrastive learning organized around individual point comparisons.

Multiple augmented views of one image form a sub-manifold in the learned representation space. A packing loss adjusts both the sizes and positions of these structures. The loss draws inspiration from the potential energy of particles with short-range repulsion, giving the learning dynamics a connection to packing and jamming physics and making its hyperparameters geometrically interpretable.

The authors also observe that category-level manifolds emerge naturally and become separated. These findings support manifold packing as a useful representation-learning framework while offering a geometric account of how the learned space becomes organized.
summary.tldr: CLAMP learns visual representations by packing and separating geometric structures, achieving competitive self-supervised performance with interpretable learning dynamics.

title: Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning As Neural Manifold Packing

abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method widely used in large language models (LLMs). LoRA essentially describes the projection of an input space into a low-dimensional output space, with the dimensionality determined by the LoRA rank. In standard LoRA, all input tokens share the same weights and undergo an identical input-output projection. This limits LoRA's ability to capture token-specific information due to the inherent semantic differences among tokens. To address this limitation, we propose **Token-wise Projected Low-Rank Adaptation (TopLoRA)**, which dynamically adjusts LoRA weights according to the input token, thereby learning token-wise input-output projections in an end-to-end manner. Formally, the weights of TopLoRA can be expressed as $B\Sigma_X A$, where $A$ and $B$ are low-rank matrices (as in standard LoRA), and $\Sigma_X$ is a diagonal matrix generated from each input token $X$. Notably, TopLoRA does not increase the rank of LoRA weights but achieves more granular adaptation by learning token-wise LoRA weights (i.e., token-wise input-output projections). Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets demonstrate that TopLoRA consistently outperforms LoRA and its variants. The code is available at https://github.com/Leopold1423/toplora-neurips25.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation fine-tunes a language model through a compact set of adjustable weights. Standard LoRA applies the same input-output projection to every token, even though tokens carry different meanings. This paper argues that sharing an identical projection limits how well the adaptation can respond to token-specific information.

TopLoRA makes the adaptation depend on the input token. It retains the two low-rank matrices used by LoRA but inserts a diagonal matrix generated from the current token between them. This token-dependent matrix adjusts the resulting weights, and the entire mechanism is learned end to end.

The added flexibility comes without increasing the rank of the adaptation weights. The approach therefore explores finer control within the low-rank structure rather than relying on a larger rank. Experiments across multiple models and datasets report consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Those findings support token-dependent projections as a useful way to improve parameter-efficient adaptation in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: TopLoRA improves low-rank adaptation by adjusting its projection for each token without increasing the adaptation rank.

title: Beyond Higher Rank: Token-wise Input-Output Projections for Efficient Low-Rank Adaptation

abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) significantly depend on training data drawn from various domains. Optimizing domain-specific mixture ratios can be modeled as a bi-level optimization problem, which we simplify into a single-level penalized form and solve with twin networks: a proxy model trained on primary data and a dynamically updated reference model trained with additional data. Our proposed method, Twin Networks for bi-level DatA mixturE optiMization (TANDEM), measures the data efficacy through the difference between the twin models and up-weights domains that benefit more from the additional data. TANDEM provides theoretical guarantees and wider applicability, compared to prior approaches. Furthermore, our bi-level perspective suggests new settings to study domain reweighting such as data-restricted scenarios and supervised fine-tuning, where optimized mixture ratios significantly improve the performance. Extensive experiments validate TANDEM's effectiveness in all scenarios.

paragraphs: TANDEM addresses how to choose the proportions of different data domains when training a language model. The mixture matters because domains can contribute differently to model capability. The paper frames choosing those proportions as a bi-level optimization problem, in which decisions about the data mixture are tied to the model training they produce.

The authors simplify that formulation into a single-level problem with a penalty and solve it using two networks. A proxy model trains on primary data, while a dynamically updated reference model trains with additional data. Differences between the models estimate how effective the extra data is, and TANDEM increases the weight of domains that benefit more from it.

The method comes with theoretical guarantees and is evaluated across multiple settings. The bi-level perspective also motivates studying mixture optimization when data are restricted and during supervised fine-tuning. Experiments report significant performance improvements from optimized ratios in these settings. The contribution is an adaptive way to allocate training emphasis using observed benefit from additional data.
summary.tldr: TANDEM compares twin training networks to increase the weight of data domains that benefit more from additional examples.

title: TANDEM: Bi-Level Data Mixture Optimization with Twin Networks

abstract: Recent advances in 3D scene reconstruction enable real-time viewing in virtual and augmented reality. To support interactive operations for better immersiveness, such as moving or editing objects, 3D scene inpainting methods are proposed to repair or complete the altered geometry. To support users in interacting (such as moving or editing objects) with the scene for the next level of immersiveness, 3D scene inpainting methods are developed to repair the altered geometry. However, current approaches rely on lengthy and computationally intensive optimization, making them impractical for real-time or online applications. We propose InstaInpaint, a reference-based feed-forward framework that produces 3D-scene inpainting from a 2D inpainting proposal within 0.4 seconds. We develop a self-supervised masked-finetuning strategy to enable training of our custom large reconstruction model (LRM) on the large-scale dataset. Through extensive experiments, we analyze and identify several key designs that improve generalization, textural consistency, and geometric correctness. InstaInpaint achieves a 1000$\times$ speed-up from prior methods while maintaining a state-of-the-art performance across two standard benchmarks. Moreover, we show that InstaInpaint generalizes well to flexible downstream applications such as object insertion and multi-region inpainting.

Existing inpainting approaches rely on expensive optimization, making this repair difficult to integrate into interactive experiences. InstaInpaint targets the delay with a feed-forward framework that produces a repaired 3D scene from a two-dimensional inpainting proposal.

The method uses a custom large reconstruction model trained through self-supervised masked fine-tuning on a large-scale dataset. These findings support the use of learned direct reconstruction for scene editing where a lengthy optimization stage would obstruct interaction.
summary.tldr: InstaInpaint converts a 2D inpainting proposal into a repaired 3D scene in 0.4 seconds using a trained reconstruction model.

title: InstaInpaint: Instant 3D-Scene Inpainting with Masked Large Reconstruction Model

abstract: 3D GAN inversion projects a single image into the latent space of a pre-trained 3D GAN to achieve single-shot novel view synthesis, which requires visible regions with high fidelity and occluded regions with realism and multi-view consistency. However, existing methods focus on the reconstruction of visible regions, while the generation of occluded regions relies only on the generative prior of 3D GAN. As a result, the generated occluded regions often exhibit poor quality due to the information loss caused by the low bit-rate latent code. To address this, we introduce the warping-and-inpainting strategy to incorporate image inpainting into 3D GAN inversion and propose a novel 3D GAN inversion method, WarpGAN. Specifically, we first employ a 3D GAN inversion encoder to project the single-view image into a latent code that serves as the input to 3D GAN. Then, we perform warping to a novel view using the depth map generated by 3D GAN. Finally, we develop a novel SVINet, which leverages the symmetry prior and multi-view image correspondence w.r.t. the same latent code to perform inpainting of occluded regions in the warped image. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms several state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Generating new viewpoints from one image requires preserving visible details while inventing plausible content for previously hidden regions. In 3D GAN inversion, an encoder maps the image into a pretrained generator's latent space. The paper identifies a weakness in relying on that compact latent code and the generator's prior alone to reconstruct unseen content.

Its SVINet component then fills occluded regions using a symmetry prior and correspondences between views associated with the same latent code.

This design gives hidden-region generation additional structure from image relationships and symmetry. It addresses the need for unseen content to look realistic while remaining consistent across viewpoints, alongside faithful reconstruction of visible regions. Quantitative and qualitative experiments report consistent improvements over several state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining geometric transfer of observed content with a dedicated mechanism for completing what the new view exposes.
summary.tldr: WarpGAN combines depth-guided warping with symmetry- and correspondence-based inpainting to improve new views generated from a single image.

title: WarpGAN: Warping-Guided 3D GAN Inversion with Style-Based Novel View Inpainting

abstract: The capacity of deep learning models is often large enough to both learn the underlying statistical signal and overfit to noise in the training set. This noise memorization can be harmful especially for data with a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), leading to poor generalization. Inspired by prior observations that label noise provides implicit regularization that improves generalization, in this work, we investigate whether introducing label noise to the gradient updates can enhance the test performance of neural network (NN) in the low SNR regime. Specifically, we consider training a two-layer NN with a simple label noise gradient descent (GD) algorithm, in an idealized signal-noise data setting. We prove that adding label noise during training suppresses noise memorization, preventing it from dominating the learning process; consequently, label noise GD enjoys rapid signal growth while the overfitting remains controlled, thereby achieving good generalization despite the low SNR. In contrast, we also show that NN trained with standard GD tends to overfit to noise in the same low SNR setting and establish a non-vanishing lower bound on its test error, thus demonstrating the benefit of introducing label noise in gradient-based training.

paragraphs: A neural network can learn meaningful patterns and memorize irrelevant variation in the same training set. When the signal is weak relative to the noise, memorization can dominate and hurt predictions on new data. This paper investigates whether deliberately adding label noise to gradient updates can help prevent that outcome.

The analysis studies a two-layer neural network in an idealized setting that separates signal and noise. The authors prove that their label-noise gradient descent procedure suppresses noise memorization while allowing the signal to grow rapidly. Within this setting, overfitting stays controlled and the network achieves good generalization despite the low signal-to-noise ratio.

The paper also analyzes ordinary gradient descent under the same conditions. It shows a tendency to overfit noise and establishes a test-error lower bound that does not vanish. This comparison identifies a theoretical mechanism for the benefit of injected label noise: it changes the balance between learning useful structure and fitting noise. The guarantee concerns the specified network and data model, making those assumptions integral to interpreting the result.
summary.tldr: In an idealized two-layer network setting, label-noise gradient descent suppresses noise memorization and improves generalization when the signal is weak.

title: How Does Label Noise Gradient Descent Improve Generalization in the Low SNR Regime?

abstract: We marry ideas from deep neural networks and approximate Bayesian inference to derive a generalised class of deep, directed generative models, endowed with a new algorithm for scalable inference and learning. Our algorithm introduces a recognition model to represent an approximate posterior distribution and uses this for optimisation of a variational lower bound. We develop stochastic backpropagation – rules for gradient backpropagation through stochastic variables – and derive an algorithm that allows for joint optimisation of the parameters of both the generative and recognition models. We demonstrate on several real-world data sets that by using stochastic backpropagation and variational inference, we obtain models that are able to generate realistic samples of data, allow for accurate imputations of missing data, and provide a useful tool for high-dimensional data visualisation.

We develop stochastic backpropagation – rules for gradient backpropagation through stochastic variables – and derive an algorithm that allows for joint optimisation of the parameters of both the generative and recognition models. We demonstrate on several real-world data sets that by using stochastic backpropagation and variational inference, we obtain models that are able to generate realistic samples of data, allow for accurate imputations of missing data, and provide a useful tool for high-dimensional data visualisation.

paragraphs: The paper combines deep neural networks with approximate Bayesian inference to construct deep directed generative models. Such models connect hidden variables to observed data, creating a need to learn both how observations are generated and how hidden variables can be inferred from them. The proposed algorithm addresses these linked computations at scale.

A recognition model represents an approximate posterior distribution over hidden variables. Training uses this approximation to optimize a variational lower bound. The authors develop stochastic backpropagation, a set of rules for propagating gradients through stochastic variables, enabling joint optimization of the generative model and the recognition model.

This makes approximate inference a learned component of the overall system. Experiments on several real-world datasets show models that generate realistic samples, accurately fill in missing data, and support visualization of high-dimensional observations. These findings demonstrate several uses of the same framework. The contribution is the combination of a learned posterior approximation with gradient-based joint training through the model’s random variables.
summary.tldr: Stochastic backpropagation jointly trains deep generative and recognition models, enabling useful generation, missing-data imputation, and visualization.

title: Stochastic Backpropagation and Approximate Inference in Deep Generative Models

abstract: Dance Dance Revolution (DDR) is a popular rhythm-based video game. Players perform steps on a dance platform in synchronization with music as directed by on-screen step charts. While many step charts are available in standardized packs, players may grow tired of existing charts, or wish to dance to a song for which no chart exists. We introduce the task of learning to choreograph. Given a raw audio track, the goal is to produce a new step chart. This task decomposes naturally into two subtasks: deciding when to place steps and deciding which steps to select. For the step placement task, we combine recurrent and convolutional neural networks to ingest spectrograms of low-level audio features to predict steps, conditioned on chart difficulty. For step selection, we present a conditional LSTM generative model that substantially outperforms n-gram and fixed-window approaches.

paragraphs: Dance Dance Revolution requires players to follow a sequence of steps synchronized with music. This paper introduces learning to generate those step charts directly from a raw audio track. The motivation is practical: players may want fresh charts for familiar songs or a chart for music that has never had one.

The authors divide choreography into two decisions: when a step should happen and which step should be chosen. For timing, they combine convolutional and recurrent neural networks operating on spectrograms of low-level audio features. The prediction also depends on the requested chart difficulty, so step placement is framed as a difficulty-conditioned task rather than a single fixed interpretation of a song.

For choosing steps, the paper introduces a conditional LSTM generative model and reports that it substantially outperforms n-gram and fixed-window approaches. Separating timing from step identity gives the system a clear structure for turning sound into instructions. The stated comparative finding concerns the step-selection model, while the overall contribution establishes automated chart creation as a learning task.
summary.tldr: The paper generates dance-game charts from audio by learning step timing and step selection as separate tasks.

title: Dance Dance Convolution

abstract: We present an efficient algorithm for learning mixed membership models when the number of variables p is much larger than the number of hidden components k. This algorithm reduces the computational complexity of state-of-the-art tensor methods, which require decomposing an $O(p^3)$ tensor, to factorizing $O(p/k)$ sub-tensors each of size $O(k^3)$. In addition, we address the issue of negative entries in the empirical method of moments based estimators. We provide sufficient conditions under which our approach has provable guarantees. Our approach obtains competitive empirical results on both simulated and real data.
originalAbstract: We present an efficient algorithm for learning mixed membership models when the number of variables p is much larger than the number of hidden components k. This algorithm reduces the computational complexity of state-of-the-art tensor methods, which require decomposing an $O(p^3)$ tensor, to factorizing $O(p/k)$ sub-tensors each of size $O(k^3)$. In addition, we address the issue of negative entries in the empirical method of moments based estimators. We provide sufficient conditions under which our approach has provable guarantees. Our approach obtains competitive empirical results on both simulated and real data.

paragraphs: This paper focuses on learning mixed-membership models when the number of observed variables p greatly exceeds the number of hidden components k. In that setting, tensor methods can become computationally demanding because their intermediate representation scales with the much larger observed-variable count.

The proposed algorithm replaces decomposition of an O(p³)-sized tensor with factorization of O(p/k) smaller tensors, each of size O(k³). This partitioning changes the central computational task from processing one large tensor to handling multiple tensors whose dimensions are governed by the number of hidden components. It directly targets the imbalance between many variables and relatively few components.

The authors also address negative entries in empirical estimators obtained through the method of moments. They provide sufficient conditions for provable guarantees and report competitive results on simulated and real data. The guarantee is therefore conditional on the stated sufficient conditions, while the experiments support practical competitiveness. The main contribution is a more economical tensor-based learning procedure for the regime where p is much larger than k.
summary.tldr: Partitioning a large tensor into smaller component-sized tensors reduces the computational burden of learning mixed-membership models under sufficient guarantee conditions.

title: Partitioned Tensor Factorizations for Learning Mixed Membership Models

abstract: Latent variable models with hidden binary units appear in various applications. Learning such models, in particular in the presence of noise, is a challenging computational problem. In this paper we propose a novel spectral approach to this problem, based on the eigenvectors of both the second order moment matrix and third order moment tensor of the observed data. We prove that under mild non-degeneracy conditions, our method consistently estimates the model parameters at the optimal parametric rate. Our tensor-based method generalizes previous orthogonal tensor decomposition approaches, where the hidden units were assumed to be either statistically independent or mutually exclusive. We illustrate the consistency of our method on simulated data and demonstrate its usefulness in learning a common model for population mixtures in genetics.

paragraphs: Models with hidden binary variables can describe data generated by unobserved on-or-off factors, but estimating their parameters is computationally challenging, particularly with noise. This paper proposes a spectral method that learns from summary statistics of the observations. It uses eigenvectors associated with both a second-order moment matrix and a third-order moment tensor.

The approach extends earlier orthogonal tensor decomposition methods that assumed hidden units were statistically independent or mutually exclusive. Under mild non-degeneracy conditions, the authors prove consistent parameter estimation at the optimal parametric rate. Consistency means that the estimates approach the true parameters as data increase, with the stated conditions remaining essential to the guarantee.

The authors illustrate consistency using simulated data and demonstrate the method on a population-mixture model in genetics. These examples connect the mathematical result to both controlled data and an application. The contribution is a broader tensor-based learning approach whose statistical guarantees do not rely on the particular independence or exclusivity assumptions of the earlier methods.
summary.tldr: A moment-based spectral method learns binary latent-variable models consistently at the optimal parametric rate under mild non-degeneracy conditions.

title: Learning Binary Latent Variable Models: A Tensor Eigenpair Approach

abstract: We present the first computationally-efficient algorithm with $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret for learning in Linear Quadratic Control systems with unknown dynamics. By that, we resolve an open question of Abbasi-Yadkori and Szepesvari (2011) and Dean,Mania, Matni, Recht, and Tu (2018).
originalAbstract: We present the first computationally-efficient algorithm with $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret for learning in Linear Quadratic Control systems with unknown dynamics. By that, we resolve an open question of Abbasi-Yadkori and Szepesvari (2011) and Dean,Mania, Matni, Recht, and Tu (2018).

paragraphs: This paper studies learning to control a linear-quadratic system when its dynamics are unknown. The learner therefore has to choose control actions without already having a complete description of how the system responds. The contribution concerns both the accumulated cost of learning and the computational efficiency of the algorithm used to make those decisions.

The authors present an algorithm with regret bounded at the square-root scale in the time horizon T, with logarithmic factors suppressed by the stated notation. Regret measures accumulated excess cost relative to a comparison controller. A square-root dependence means this excess grows more slowly than the horizon itself, so the corresponding bound on excess cost per step decreases as the horizon grows.

The central achievement is obtaining that regret guarantee with a computationally efficient algorithm for unknown dynamics. The authors identify this combination as a first result and as resolving an existing open question. The stated finding is thus a theoretical advance joining learning performance and tractable computation in linear-quadratic control.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a computationally efficient algorithm with square-root regret, up to logarithmic factors, for linear-quadratic control with unknown dynamics.

title: Learning Linear-Quadratic Regulators Efficiently with only $\sqrtT$ Regret

abstract: Deriving Optimal bounds on Sample Complexity of Latent Variable models is an active area of research. Recently such bounds were obtained for Mixture of Gaussians \cite{HSNCAY18}, no such results are known for Ad-mixtures, a generalization of Mixture distributions. In this paper we show that $O^*(dk/m)$ samples are sufficient to learn each of $k-$ topic vectors of LDA, a popular Ad-mixture model, with vocabulary size $d$ and $m\in \Omega(1)$ words per document, to any constant error in $L_1$ norm. The result is a corollary of the major contribution of this paper: the first sample complexity upper bound for the problem (introduced in \cite{BK20}) of learning the vertices of a Latent $k-$ Polytope in $\RR^d$, given perturbed points from it. The bound, $O^*(dk/\beta)$, is optimal and linear in number of parameters. It applies to many stochastic models including a broad class Ad-mixtures. To demonstrate the generality of the approach we specialize the setting to Mixed Membership Stochastic Block Models(MMSB) and show for the first time that if an MMSB has $k$ blocks, the sample complexity is $O^*(k^2)$ under usual assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many observations are sufficient to recover hidden structure in latent-variable models. Its main contribution concerns a geometric problem: learning the vertices of a latent polytope with k vertices in d dimensions from perturbed points. This framework applies to multiple stochastic models, including a broad class of admixtures.

The authors give the first sample-complexity upper bound for this latent-polytope problem. The stated bound is O*(dk/beta), described as optimal and linear in the number of parameters. By working through a shared geometric formulation, the analysis supplies sample requirements for models whose observed data reflect combinations of hidden components.

For latent Dirichlet allocation, the result implies that O*(dk/m) documents suffice to learn each of k topic vectors to constant L1 error, with vocabulary size d and m words per document in the stated regime. For mixed-membership stochastic block models, the authors obtain O*(k²) sample complexity under the usual assumptions. These applications demonstrate the reach of the geometric bound across topic and network models.
summary.tldr: A sample-complexity bound for learning latent polytope vertices yields guarantees for topic models and mixed-membership network models.

title: Near-optimal sample complexity bounds for learning Latent $k-$polytopes and applications to Ad-Mixtures

abstract: Since the Message Passing (Graph) Neural Networks (MPNNs) have a linear complexity with respect to the number of nodes when applied to sparse graphs, they have been widely implemented and still raise a lot of interest even though their theoretical expressive power is limited to the first order Weisfeiler-Lehman test (1-WL). In this paper, we show that if the graph convolution supports are designed in spectral-domain by a non-linear custom function of eigenvalues and masked with an arbitrary large receptive field, the MPNN is theoretically more powerful than the 1-WL test and experimentally as powerful as a 3-WL existing models, while remaining spatially localized. Moreover, by designing custom filter functions, outputs can have various frequency components that allow the convolution process to learn different relationships between a given input graph signal and its associated properties. So far, the best 3-WL equivalent graph neural networks have a computational complexity in $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ with memory usage in $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$, consider non-local update mechanism and do not provide the spectral richness of output profile. The proposed method overcomes all these aforementioned problems and reaches state-of-the-art results in many downstream tasks.
