paragraphs: Message-passing graph networks are attractive because they scale efficiently on sparse graphs, but their usual expressive power is limited by the first-order Weisfeiler-Lehman test, or 1-WL. This paper investigates whether a different construction of graph convolutions can exceed that limit while keeping the computation spatially localized.

The proposed construction designs convolution supports in the spectral domain using a custom nonlinear function of graph eigenvalues. It then masks those supports with a receptive field that can be arbitrarily large. Under this design, the authors establish expressive power beyond 1-WL. Custom spectral filters also produce different frequency components, allowing the model to learn different relationships between graph signals and their associated properties.

Experiments find performance comparable in expressive power to existing 3-WL models and state-of-the-art results on many downstream tasks. The theoretical claim is specifically stronger-than-1-WL expressiveness; the 3-WL comparison is experimental. The method also addresses the computational, memory, and nonlocal-update drawbacks identified for existing 3-WL-equivalent networks.
summary.tldr: Custom spectral convolutions make localized message-passing networks provably more expressive than 1-WL and competitive with stronger graph models experimentally.

title: Breaking the Limits of Message Passing Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) are a simple yet powerful framework for generative modeling. They are based on a trainable energy function which defines an associated Gibbs measure, and they can be trained and sampled from via well-established statistical tools, such as MCMC. Neural networks may be used as energy function approximators, providing both a rich class of expressive models as well as a flexible device to incorporate data structure. In this work we focus on shallow neural networks. Building from the incipient theory of overparametrized neural networks, we show that models trained in the so-called ’active’ regime provide a statistical advantage over their associated ’lazy’ or kernel regime, leading to improved adaptivity to hidden low-dimensional structure in the data distribution, as already observed in supervised learning. Our study covers both the maximum likelihood and Stein Discrepancy estimators, and we validate our theoretical results with numerical experiments on synthetic data.

In this work we focus on shallow neural networks. Building from the incipient theory of overparametrized neural networks, we show that models trained in the so-called ’active’ regime provide a statistical advantage over their associated ’lazy’ or kernel regime, leading to improved adaptivity to hidden low-dimensional structure in the data distribution, as already observed in supervised learning. Our study covers both the maximum likelihood and Stein Discrepancy estimators, and we validate our theoretical results with numerical experiments on synthetic data.

paragraphs: Energy-based models describe a distribution through a learned energy function and its associated Gibbs measure. Neural networks make that function expressive while providing a way to incorporate structure in the data. This paper focuses on shallow, overparameterized networks and asks how their training regime affects the statistical quality of the resulting generative model.

The authors compare an active training regime with its associated lazy, or kernel, regime. They show a statistical advantage for active training, specifically improved adaptation to hidden low-dimensional structure in the data distribution. This extends a type of advantage already observed in supervised learning to the energy-based generative modeling setting.

The analysis covers both maximum likelihood estimation and estimation based on Stein discrepancy. Numerical experiments on synthetic data validate the theoretical findings. The central implication is that the way a shallow network is trained matters alongside its capacity: active training can better exploit underlying low-dimensional organization than the corresponding kernel regime in the settings analyzed. The work connects overparameterization theory to the statistical behavior of generative models.
summary.tldr: Actively trained shallow neural energy models adapt better to hidden low-dimensional structure than their associated lazy or kernel models.

title: On Energy-Based Models with Overparametrized Shallow Neural Networks

abstract: We study function approximation for episodic reinforcement learning with entropic risk measure. We first propose an algorithm with linear function approximation. Compared to existing algorithms, which suffer from improper regularization and regression biases, this algorithm features debiasing transformations in backward induction and regression procedures. We further propose an algorithm with general function approximation, which features implicit debiasing transformations. We prove that both algorithms achieve a sublinear regret and demonstrate a trade-off between generality and efficiency. Our analysis provides a unified framework for function approximation in risk-sensitive reinforcement learning, which leads to the first sublinear regret bounds in the setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic reinforcement learning with an entropic risk measure, so the learning objective accounts for risk in rewards. It focuses on function approximation, which represents the quantities needed for learning through a chosen function class. The challenge is to combine that approximation with risk-sensitive decision-making while controlling learning performance.

The authors first develop an algorithm using linear function approximation. Existing approaches suffer from inappropriate regularization and biases in regression, so the new method introduces debiasing transformations in both backward induction and regression. They then extend the approach to general function approximation, where the corresponding debiasing transformations are implicit. Both developments address bias within the learning procedure itself.

The paper proves sublinear regret for both algorithms, meaning accumulated regret grows more slowly than the interaction horizon covered by the bounds. It also establishes a trade-off between generality and efficiency. The unified analysis supplies the first reported sublinear regret guarantees for this setting, linking the debiasing approach to a formal account of learning with risk-sensitive objectives.
summary.tldr: Debiasing transformations yield sublinear-regret algorithms for risk-sensitive reinforcement learning with linear and general function approximation.

title: Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation: A Debiasing Approach

abstract: State-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithms tend to overfit due to the model discrepancy between source and target environments. Though applying domain randomization during training can improve the average performance by randomly generating a sufficient diversity of environments in simulator, the worst-case environment is still neglected without any performance guarantee. Since the average and worst-case performance are both important for generalization in RL, in this paper, we propose a policy optimization approach for concurrently improving the policy’s performance in the average and worst-case environment. We theoretically derive a lower bound for the worst-case performance of a given policy by relating it to the expected performance. Guided by this lower bound, we formulate an optimization problem to jointly optimize the policy and sampling distribution, and prove that by iteratively solving it the worst-case performance is monotonically improved. We then develop a practical algorithm, named monotonic robust policy optimization (MRPO). Experimental evaluations in several robot control tasks demonstrate that MRPO can generally improve both the average and worst-case performance in the source environments for training, and facilitate in all cases the learned policy with a better generalization capability in some unseen testing environments.

Randomizing training environments can improve average performance, yet leave difficult environments insufficiently addressed. This paper targets average and worst-case performance together, treating both as relevant to generalization.

The authors derive a lower bound on a policy's worst-case performance in terms of its expected performance. They use this relationship to formulate a joint optimization over the policy and the distribution used to sample training environments. For the iterative solution of that optimization problem, they prove that worst-case performance improves monotonically.

summary.tldr: MRPO jointly optimizes policies and environment sampling to improve robustness, guided by a bound connecting expected and worst-case performance.

title: Monotonic Robust Policy Optimization with Model Discrepancy

abstract: Solving sparse reward tasks through exploration is one of the major challenges in deep reinforcement learning, especially in three-dimensional, partially-observable environments. Critically, the algorithm proposed in this article is capable of using a single human demonstration to solve hard-exploration problems. We train an agent on a combination of demonstrations and own experience to solve problems with variable initial conditions and we integrate it with proximal policy optimization (PPO). The agent is also able to increase its performance and to tackle harder problems by replaying its own past trajectories prioritizing them based on the obtained reward and the maximum value of the trajectory. We finally compare variations of this algorithm to different imitation learning algorithms on a set of hard-exploration tasks in the Animal-AI Olympics environment. To the best of our knowledge, learning a task in a three-dimensional environment with comparable difficulty has never been considered before using only one human demonstration.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards make exploration difficult because an agent may receive little useful feedback until it discovers a successful behavior. The paper addresses this problem in three-dimensional environments where the agent can observe only part of its surroundings. Its central proposal uses a single human demonstration to guide learning on difficult exploration tasks.

The method combines demonstration experience with the agent’s own experience and integrates this training with proximal policy optimization. It is designed to solve tasks with variable initial conditions, so learning involves more than encountering a single fixed starting situation. The agent also replays its previous trajectories, prioritizing them using their obtained reward and maximum trajectory value.

The authors report that this replay mechanism improves performance and enables harder problems to be tackled. They compare algorithm variants with imitation-learning approaches on hard-exploration tasks in the Animal-AI Olympics environment. The stated result shows that one demonstration can provide useful guidance in this setting, especially when paired with continued experience collection and selective reuse of the agent’s own trajectories.
summary.tldr: A PPO-based agent combines one human demonstration with its own experience and prioritized trajectory replay to solve hard-exploration tasks.

title: Guided Exploration with Proximal Policy Optimization using a Single Demonstration

abstract: In real world settings, numerous constraints are present which are hard to specify mathematically. However, for the real world deployment of reinforcement learning (RL), it is critical that RL agents are aware of these constraints, so that they can act safely. In this work, we consider the problem of learning constraints from demonstrations of a constraint-abiding agent’s behavior. We experimentally validate our approach and show that our framework can successfully learn the most likely constraints that the agent respects. We further show that these learned constraints are \textit{transferable} to new agents that may have different morphologies and/or reward functions. Previous works in this regard have either mainly been restricted to tabular (discrete) settings, specific types of constraints or assume the environment’s transition dynamics. In contrast, our framework is able to learn arbitrary \textit{Markovian} constraints in high-dimensions in a completely model-free setting. The code is available at: \url{https://github.com/shehryar-malik/icrl}.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents may need to respect practical restrictions that are difficult to write down mathematically. This paper studies learning those restrictions from demonstrations by an agent that already follows them. The objective is to infer the constraints behind the observed behavior, making them available to guide other agents.

The framework learns in a model-free setting, so it does not assume knowledge of the environment's transition dynamics. It supports high-dimensional problems and arbitrary Markovian constraints within that setting. This broadens the scope beyond earlier approaches described as relying on discrete environments, particular constraint types, or known transition dynamics.

Experiments show that the approach can recover the most likely constraints respected by the demonstrator. The learned constraints also transfer to agents with different morphologies, reward functions, or both. That transfer is central to the contribution: restrictions inferred from one agent's behavior can remain useful when another agent pursues a different objective or has a different physical form.
summary.tldr: The framework learns Markovian constraints from compliant demonstrations and experimentally transfers them to agents with different bodies or rewards.

title: Inverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Missing values arise in most real-world data sets due to the aggregation of multiple sources and intrinsically missing information (sensor failure, unanswered questions in surveys...). In fact, the very nature of missing values usually prevents us from running standard learning algorithms. In this paper, we focus on the extensively-studied linear models, but in presence of missing values, which turns out to be quite a challenging task. Indeed, the Bayes predictor can be decomposed as a sum of predictors corresponding to each missing pattern. This eventually requires to solve a number of learning tasks, exponential in the number of input features, which makes predictions impossible for current real-world datasets. First, we propose a rigorous setting to analyze a least-square type estimator and establish a bound on the excess risk which increases exponentially in the dimension. Consequently, we leverage the missing data distribution to propose a new algorithm, and derive associated adaptive risk bounds that turn out to be minimax optimal. Numerical experiments highlight the benefits of our method compared to state-of-the-art algorithms used for predictions with missing values.

paragraphs: Missing inputs complicate prediction even when the underlying models are linear. The ideal predictor can be decomposed into separate predictors for different patterns of missing features. Because the number of possible patterns grows exponentially with the number of features, treating every pattern as a separate learning problem quickly becomes impractical.

The paper first establishes a rigorous framework for analyzing a least-squares-type estimator in this setting. Its excess-risk bound grows exponentially with dimension, making the statistical difficulty explicit. The authors then use the distribution of missing data to design a new algorithm, allowing the analysis to adapt to how missingness actually occurs.

The resulting adaptive risk bounds are minimax optimal in the studied setting. This connects the algorithm’s guarantees to the best achievable worst-case performance for that setting, while incorporating information about the missing-data distribution. Numerical experiments show benefits over state-of-the-art prediction methods for missing values. The main insight is that the pattern distribution provides useful structure for addressing a problem whose naive formulation contains exponentially many prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: An algorithm that uses the missing-data distribution achieves adaptive, minimax-optimal risk bounds for the studied linear prediction setting.

title: Near-optimal rate of consistency for linear models with missing values

abstract: As real-world images come in varying sizes, the machine learning model is part of a larger system that includes an upstream image scaling algorithm. In this paper, we investigate the interplay between vulnerabilities of the image scaling procedure and machine learning models in the decision-based black-box setting. We propose a novel sampling strategy to make a black-box attack exploit vulnerabilities in scaling algorithms, scaling defenses, and the final machine learning model in an end-to-end manner. Based on this scaling-aware attack, we reveal that most existing scaling defenses are ineffective under threat from downstream models. Moreover, we empirically observe that standard black-box attacks can significantly improve their performance by exploiting the vulnerable scaling procedure. We further demonstrate this problem on a commercial Image Analysis API with decision-based black-box attacks.

paragraphs: Images often need resizing before a machine learning model can process them. This paper treats that scaling procedure as part of the system being attacked. It investigates how weaknesses in resizing interact with weaknesses in the downstream model when an attacker operates in a decision-based black-box setting.

The authors introduce a sampling strategy that allows a black-box attack to exploit the scaling algorithm, scaling defenses, and final model together. This end-to-end view matters because a defense aimed at preprocessing must also withstand attacks that account for the model receiving the processed image. The attack explicitly incorporates these interactions into its search.

Using the scaling-aware attack, the paper finds that most existing scaling defenses are ineffective under the studied downstream-model threat. It also observes that standard black-box attacks can substantially improve their performance by exploiting vulnerable scaling. A demonstration on a commercial Image Analysis API shows the issue in an applied system. The findings support evaluating robustness across the complete image-processing pipeline.
summary.tldr: Scaling-aware black-box attacks expose weaknesses arising from the interaction between image resizing, scaling defenses, and downstream models.

title: Rethinking Image-Scaling Attacks: The Interplay Between Vulnerabilities in Machine Learning Systems

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is important for machine learning models deployed in the wild. Recent methods use auxiliary outlier data to regularize the model for improved OOD detection. However, these approaches make a strong distributional assumption that the auxiliary outlier data is completely separable from the in-distribution (ID) data. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that leverages wild mixture data—that naturally consists of both ID and OOD samples. Such wild data is abundant and arises freely upon deploying a machine learning classifier in their natural habitats. Our key idea is to formulate a constrained optimization problem and to show how to tractably solve it. Our learning objective maximizes the OOD detection rate, subject to constraints on the classification error of ID data and on the OOD error rate of ID examples. We extensively evaluate our approach on common OOD detection tasks and demonstrate superior performance. Code is available at https://github.com/jkatzsam/woods_ood.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection identifies inputs that differ from the data a classifier is intended to handle. Some training approaches use auxiliary outlier data while assuming it is completely separable from in-distribution data. This paper instead uses the mixed stream of familiar and unfamiliar examples that naturally appears during deployment.

The authors formulate learning as a constrained optimization problem. The objective maximizes detection of out-of-distribution examples, while constraints control classification error on in-distribution data and the rate at which those familiar examples are incorrectly flagged as outliers. This formulation explicitly balances detecting unfamiliar inputs with preserving useful behavior on the classifier’s intended inputs.

The paper shows how to solve the optimization problem tractably and evaluates the approach extensively on common out-of-distribution detection tasks. It reports superior performance in those evaluations. The practical significance is that training can use naturally occurring mixture data instead of requiring an auxiliary collection assumed to consist of cleanly separated outliers. The constraints make the competing goals of classification and detection part of the learning objective.
summary.tldr: A constrained training framework learns OOD detection from naturally mixed deployment data while controlling errors on in-distribution examples.

title: Training OOD Detectors in their Natural Habitats

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is indispensable for machine learning models deployed in the open world. Recently, the use of an auxiliary outlier dataset during training (also known as outlier exposure) has shown promising performance. As the sample space for potential OOD data can be prohibitively large, sampling informative outliers is essential. In this work, we propose a novel posterior sampling based outlier mining framework, POEM, which facilitates efficient use of outlier data and promotes learning a compact decision boundary between ID and OOD data for improved detection. We show that POEM establishes state-of-the-art performance on common benchmarks. Compared to the current best method that uses a greedy sampling strategy, POEM improves the relative performance by 42.0% and 24.2% (FPR95) on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, respectively. We further provide theoretical insights on the effectiveness of POEM for OOD detection.

paragraphs: Outlier exposure trains an out-of-distribution detector using auxiliary examples outside its target distribution. Since the possible outlier space is enormous, selecting informative examples can matter as much as simply collecting more of them. POEM addresses this selection problem through posterior-sampling-based outlier mining.

The framework aims to use outlier data efficiently while learning a compact boundary between in-distribution and out-of-distribution examples. Posterior sampling determines which outliers to emphasize, providing an alternative to a greedy selection strategy. The paper also supplies theoretical insights into why this approach can improve detection.

On common benchmarks, POEM reaches state-of-the-art performance. Relative to the strongest compared greedy method, the abstract reports FPR95 improvements of 42.0% on CIFAR-10 and 24.2% on CIFAR-100. Those are relative metric improvements, not percentage-point gains in classification accuracy. The contribution concerns selecting useful exposure data for OOD detection within the evaluated training and benchmark settings.
summary.tldr: Posterior sampling selects more useful outliers for exposure training and improves benchmark out-of-distribution detection.

title: POEM: Out-of-Distribution Detection with Posterior Sampling

abstract: In this work, we study high-dimensional mean estimation under user-level differential privacy, and design an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private mechanism using as few users as possible. In particular, we provide a nearly optimal trade-off between the number of users and the number of samples per user required for private mean estimation, even when the number of users is as low as $O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{1}{\delta})$. Interestingly, this bound on the number of users is independent of the dimension (though the number of samples per user is allowed to depend polynomially on the dimension), unlike the previous work that requires the number of users to depend polynomially on the dimension. This resolves a problem first proposed by Amin et al. (2019). Moreover, our mechanism is robust against corruptions in up to $49%$ of the users. Finally, our results also apply to optimal algorithms for privately learning discrete distributions with few users, answering a question of Liu et al. (2020), and a broader range of problems such as stochastic convex optimization and a variant of stochastic gradient descent via a reduction to differentially private mean estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate a high-dimensional mean while protecting each user through differential privacy. Each user may contribute multiple samples, creating a trade-off between recruiting more users and obtaining more observations from each one. The authors design a mechanism with a nearly optimal trade-off between those two resources.

The required user count can be as low as order log(1/delta) divided by epsilon, independent of dimension. That independence applies to users: the samples required per user may still grow polynomially with dimension. This improves on earlier work whose user requirements grew polynomially with dimension, and resolves a previously posed problem about private estimation with few users.

The mechanism also tolerates corruption affecting up to 49 percent of users. Beyond mean estimation, the results yield optimal algorithms for privately learning discrete distributions with few users. Through reductions to private mean estimation, they also apply to stochastic convex optimization and a variant of stochastic gradient descent. The contribution therefore makes scarce user participation compatible with both privacy and substantial corruption tolerance.
summary.tldr: Private mean estimation can use a dimension-independent number of users, with a nearly optimal sample trade-off and tolerance of up to 49 percent corrupted users.

title: Tight and Robust Private Mean Estimation with Few Users

abstract: Transformers \cite{transformer} have gained increasing popularity in a wide range of applications, including Natural Language Processing (NLP), Computer Vision and Speech Recognition, because of their powerful representational capacity. However, harnessing this representational capacity effectively requires a large amount of data, strong regularization, or both, to mitigate overfitting. Recently, the power of the Transformer has been unlocked by self-supervised pretraining strategies based on masked autoencoders which rely on reconstructing masked inputs, directly, or contrastively from unmasked content. This pretraining strategy which has been used in BERT models in NLP \cite{bert}, Wav2Vec models in Speech \cite{wv2v2} and, recently, in MAE models in Vision \cite{beit, mae}, forces the model to learn about relationships between the content in different parts of the input using autoencoding related objectives. In this paper, we propose a novel, but surprisingly simple alternative to content reconstruction – that of predicting locations from content, without providing positional information for it. Doing so requires the Transformer to understand the positional relationships between different parts of the input, from their content alone. This amounts to an efficient implementation where the pretext task is a classification problem among all possible positions for each input token. We experiment on both Vision and Speech benchmarks, where our approach brings improvements over strong supervised training baselines and is comparable to modern unsupervised/self-supervised pretraining methods. Our method also enables Transformers trained without position embeddings to outperform ones trained with full position information.

paragraphs: Transformer pretraining often asks a model to reconstruct hidden input content. This paper explores a different task: infer where an input token belongs from its content, without supplying its positional information. To succeed, the model must learn relationships among the contents of different parts of the input that reveal their positions.

The task is implemented as classification over the possible positions for each token. This provides a simple training objective for learning positional relationships through content alone. It addresses the broader challenge of using Transformers’ representational capacity effectively, where sufficient data or strong regularization is needed to control overfitting.

The method also enables Transformers without position embeddings to outperform models trained with full positional information in the reported experiments. These findings support position prediction as an effective pretraining signal, without establishing that explicit positional information is unnecessary in every Transformer application.
summary.tldr: Predicting token positions from content provides effective Transformer pretraining on vision and speech benchmarks.

title: Position Prediction as an Effective Pretraining Strategy

abstract: In symbolic regression, the objective is to find an analytical expression that accurately fits experimental data with the minimal use of mathematical symbols such as operators, variables, and constants. However, the combinatorial space of possible expressions can make it challenging for traditional evolutionary algorithms to find the correct expression in a reasonable amount of time. To address this issue, Neural Symbolic Regression (NSR) algorithms have been developed that can quickly identify patterns in the data and generate analytical expressions. However, these methods, in their current form, lack the capability to incorporate user-defined prior knowledge, which is often required in natural sciences and engineering fields. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel neural symbolic regression method, named Neural Symbolic Regression with Hypothesis (NSRwH) that enables the explicit incorporation of assumptions about the expected structure of the ground-truth expression into the prediction process. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed conditioned deep learning model outperforms its unconditioned counterparts in terms of accuracy while also providing control over the predicted expression structure.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression seeks a compact mathematical expression that fits observed data. The difficulty is that possible combinations of operators, variables, and constants form a large search space. Neural approaches can generate expressions quickly, but the paper identifies a missing capability: existing methods do not explicitly incorporate users' prior knowledge about the expected expression.

The proposed method, Neural Symbolic Regression with Hypothesis, adds that knowledge to the prediction process. A user can supply assumptions about the structure of the expression being sought, and the deep learning model conditions its prediction on those assumptions. This makes structural expectations part of how the expression is generated, which is relevant when scientific or engineering knowledge accompanies the measurements.

In the reported experiments, the conditioned model is more accurate than its unconditioned counterparts and also gives users control over the structure of predicted expressions. These are related benefits: the system can use additional information to guide its predictions while making the output more responsive to the user's stated hypothesis. The findings concern the tested conditioned models and comparisons.
summary.tldr: NSRwH incorporates user assumptions about expression structure into neural symbolic regression, improving accuracy and structural control in the reported experiments.

title: Controllable Neural Symbolic Regression

abstract: Policy optimization methods are popular reinforcement learning algorithms in practice and recent works have build theoretical foundation for them by proving $\sqrt{T}$ regret bounds even when the losses are adversarial. Such bounds are tight in the worst case but often overly pessimistic. In this work, we show that by carefully designing the regularizer, bonus terms, and learning rates, one can achieve a more favorable $\text{polylog}(T)$ regret bound when the losses are stochastic, without sacrificing the worst-case guarantee in the adversarial regime. Specifically, we show the first best of both worlds guarantee for policy optimization in tabular MDPs by leveraging either a Tsallis entropy or a Shannon entropy regularizer. Then we show that under known transitions, we can further obtain a first-order regret bound in the adversarial regime by leveraging the log barrier regularizer.

paragraphs: The paper studies policy optimization methods that remain reliable when losses change adversarially but can learn faster when losses are stochastic. Existing square-root-in-T regret guarantees protect against difficult loss sequences. Regret measures the accumulated performance shortfall against a comparison policy, so a smaller growth rate gives a stronger account of how learning improves over time.

The authors show that carefully coordinated choices of regularizer, bonus terms, and learning rates achieve polylogarithmic regret in the stochastic regime while preserving the square-root worst-case guarantee in the adversarial regime. They establish this best-of-both-worlds result for tabular Markov decision processes using either Tsallis entropy or Shannon entropy regularization. The same approach can therefore offer guarantees suited to both regimes.

A further result assumes the transition dynamics are known. Under that assumption, a log-barrier regularizer yields a first-order regret bound in the adversarial setting. Together, these results show that policy optimization guarantees can reflect more favorable problem structure while retaining protection against adversarial losses, with the additional first-order result requiring known transitions.
summary.tldr: Carefully designed policy optimization achieves polylogarithmic stochastic regret while retaining square-root regret guarantees against adversarial losses.

title: Best of Both Worlds Policy Optimization

abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have shown great potential for image synthesis, but there is a lack of research on the security and privacy risks they may pose. In this paper, we investigate the vulnerability of diffusion models to Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs), a common privacy concern. Our results indicate that existing MIAs designed for GANs or VAE are largely ineffective on diffusion models, either due to inapplicable scenarios (e.g., requiring the discriminator of GANs) or inappropriate assumptions (e.g., closer distances between synthetic samples and member samples). To address this gap, we propose Step-wise Error Comparing Membership Inference (SecMI), a query-based MIA that infers memberships by assessing the matching of forward process posterior estimation at each timestep. SecMI follows the common overfitting assumption in MIA where member samples normally have smaller estimation errors, compared with hold-out samples. We consider both the standard diffusion models, e.g., DDPM, and the text-to-image diffusion models, e.g., Latent Diffusion Models and Stable Diffusion. Experimental results demonstrate that our methods precisely infer the membership with high confidence on both of the two scenarios across multiple different datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/jinhaoduan/SecMI.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example was used to train a model. This paper investigates that privacy risk for diffusion models. The authors find that attacks developed for GANs and variational autoencoders are largely ineffective here, because some require unavailable components and others rely on assumptions that do not fit diffusion models.

Their proposed attack, SecMI, queries the model and compares errors associated with estimating the forward-process posterior at individual timesteps. It follows the usual overfitting assumption behind membership inference: training examples tend to have smaller estimation errors than held-out examples. This makes the diffusion process’s own estimation behavior the evidence used to infer membership.

The experiments cover standard diffusion models, including DDPM, and text-to-image systems, including Latent Diffusion Models and Stable Diffusion. Across multiple datasets, the authors report precise membership inference with high confidence in both settings. The findings show that weak performance by attacks transferred from other model families does not establish privacy protection; an attack tailored to diffusion behavior can reveal training membership.
summary.tldr: SecMI exploits timestep-level estimation errors to infer training membership in standard and text-to-image diffusion models.

title: Are Diffusion Models Vulnerable to Membership Inference Attacks?

abstract: We propose a generalizable neural radiance fields - MonoNeRF, that can be trained on large-scale monocular videos of moving in static scenes without any ground-truth annotations of depth and camera poses. MonoNeRF follows an Autoencoder-based architecture, where the encoder estimates the monocular depth and the camera pose, and the decoder constructs a Multiplane NeRF representation based on the depth encoder feature, and renders the input frames with the estimated camera. The learning is supervised by the reconstruction error. Once the model is learned, it can be applied to multiple applications including depth estimation, camera pose estimation, and single-image novel view synthesis. More qualitative results are available at: https://oasisyang.github.io/mononerf.

paragraphs: MonoNeRF learns a generalizable neural radiance-field model from monocular videos recorded as a camera moves through static scenes. Its training does not require ground-truth depth or camera-pose annotations. This makes the observed video frames themselves the learning evidence for quantities that would otherwise need to be supplied as supervision.

The architecture follows an autoencoder design. An encoder estimates depth and camera pose, while a decoder uses features from the depth encoder to construct a Multiplane NeRF representation. The model then renders the input frames using the estimated camera. Reconstruction error between those renderings and the observed frames supplies the training signal, linking scene representation and camera estimation through a shared objective.

Once trained, the model can be used for depth estimation, camera-pose estimation, and novel-view synthesis from a single image. These applications show how the same learned system supports both geometric estimation and image generation. The static-scene setting is an explicit part of the training formulation, while the central contribution is learning the required components together without annotated depth or camera poses.
summary.tldr: MonoNeRF learns depth, camera pose, and a renderable scene representation from monocular static-scene videos using reconstruction supervision.

title: MonoNeRF: Learning Generalizable NeRFs from Monocular Videos without Camera Poses

abstract: We provide an optimization-based framework to perform counterfactual analysis in a dynamic model with hidden states. Our framework is grounded in the “abduction, action, and prediction” approach to answer counterfactual queries and handles two key challenges where (1) the states are hidden and (2) the model is dynamic. Recognizing the lack of knowledge on the underlying causal mechanism and the possibility of infinitely many such mechanisms, we optimize over this space and compute upper and lower bounds on the counterfactual quantity of interest. Our work brings together ideas from causality, state-space models, simulation, and optimization, and we apply it on a breast cancer case study. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to compute lower and upper bounds on a counterfactual query in a dynamic latent-state model.

paragraphs: Counterfactual analysis asks how an outcome would have changed under a different action in a situation that already occurred. This becomes especially difficult when the system evolves over time and its underlying states are hidden. The paper develops an optimization framework that handles these two challenges together, rather than assuming the relevant state is directly observed.

The framework follows an abduction, action, and prediction structure: reason from observations about the underlying situation, change an action, and predict the resulting outcome. A central difficulty is that the causal mechanism is not fully known. There may be infinitely many possible mechanisms, so choosing a single mechanism would leave important uncertainty unresolved.

The authors optimize over the space of mechanisms to obtain lower and upper bounds on the counterfactual quantity of interest. The resulting interval expresses a range of counterfactual answers under that uncertainty. The framework brings together causal reasoning, state-space models, simulation, and optimization, and is applied in a breast cancer case study. The authors describe it as the first such bounding approach for dynamic latent-state models, to their knowledge.
summary.tldr: An optimization framework bounds counterfactual outcomes in evolving systems with hidden states and uncertain causal mechanisms.

title: Counterfactual Analysis in Dynamic Latent State Models

abstract: In this paper, we provide a tighter analysis for ProxSkip, an algorithm that allows fewer proximal operator computations to solve composite optimization problems. We improve the existing decreasing speed of Lyapunov function from $\mathcal{O}(p^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(p)$, when $p$, the frequency of the proximal operators is small enough. Our theoretical analysis also reveals the drawbacks of using large step sizes for gradient descent in ProxSkip when the proximal operator part is the bottleneck. Our main motivation comes from the continuous limit in which the original analysis of ProxSkip fails to guarantee convergence when both the step size $\gamma$ and frequency $p$ tend to zero. We construct a counterexample to demonstrate why such counterintuitive behavior occurs for the original analysis and then propose a novel Lyapunov function variant to construct a tighter analysis, avoiding the problem of the old one. Such a new Lyapunov function can be directly extended to many other variants of ProxSkip. When applied to stochastic gradient setup, our analysis leads to an improved proximal operator complexity for SProxSkip from $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\frac{1}{\varepsilon\mu^2}}\log(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}))$ to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}\log(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}))$.

paragraphs: ProxSkip solves composite optimization problems while reducing how often it computes a proximal operator. This paper revisits its convergence analysis, especially when those computations are infrequent. The motivation comes from a continuous-limit regime: the original analysis cannot guarantee convergence as both the gradient step size and the proximal-computation frequency approach zero.

The authors construct a counterexample explaining this behavior of the old analysis and introduce a different Lyapunov function, a mathematical quantity used to track progress. When the proximal frequency p is sufficiently small, the new analysis improves the stated decrease-rate dependence from order p squared to order p. It also reveals drawbacks of large gradient steps when proximal computations are the bottleneck.

The new Lyapunov construction extends directly to many ProxSkip variants. For stochastic SProxSkip, it improves the proximal-operator complexity bound from a dependence involving the square root of one over epsilon times mu squared to one involving the square root of kappa, with both retaining a logarithmic factor in inverse epsilon. The central advance is a tighter guarantee for the algorithm and its variants.
summary.tldr: A new Lyapunov analysis sharpens ProxSkip's convergence guarantees for sufficiently infrequent proximal computations and improves SProxSkip's proximal-complexity bound.

title: Tighter Analysis for ProxSkip

abstract: Natural data is redundant yet predominant architectures tile computation uniformly across their input and output space. We propose the Recurrent Interface Network (RIN), an attention-based architecture that decouples its core computation from the dimensionality of the data, enabling adaptive computation for more scalable generation of high-dimensional data. RINs focus the bulk of computation (i.e. global self-attention) on a set of latent tokens, using cross-attention to read and write (i.e. route) information between latent and data tokens. Stacking RIN blocks allows bottom-up (data to latent) and top-down (latent to data) feedback, leading to deeper and more expressive routing. While this routing introduces challenges, this is less problematic in recurrent computation settings where the task (and routing problem) changes gradually, such as iterative generation with diffusion models. We show how to leverage recurrence by conditioning the latent tokens at each forward pass of the reverse diffusion process with those from prior computation, i.e. latent self-conditioning. RINs yield state-of-the-art pixel diffusion models for image and video generation, scaling to1024×1024 images without cascades or guidance, while being domain-agnostic and up to 10× more efficient than 2D and 3D U-Nets.

paragraphs: High-dimensional images and videos contain redundancy, yet many architectures distribute computation uniformly across them. The Recurrent Interface Network, or RIN, concentrates its main computation in latent tokens. Cross-attention transfers information between those tokens and the data tokens, separating the central self-attention workload from the dimensionality of the generated data.

Stacked RIN blocks allow information to travel from data to latents and back, creating deeper routing between the two. Learning that routing is challenging, but iterative generation offers a helpful property: the task changes gradually between steps. RIN uses latent self-conditioning, supplying each reverse-diffusion pass with latent information from prior computation so that the recurrent process can carry useful computational context forward.

The authors report state-of-the-art pixel diffusion models for images and videos, including generation at 1024 × 1024 resolution without cascades or guidance. They also report efficiency improvements of up to tenfold over 2D and 3D U-Nets. These findings support adaptive information routing and recurrence as a way to scale generation while concentrating expensive computation in a latent representation.
summary.tldr: RIN routes data through recurrent latent computation, enabling high-resolution pixel diffusion with reported efficiency gains of up to tenfold over U-Nets.

title: Scalable Adaptive Computation for Iterative Generation

abstract: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has demonstrated its effectiveness in learning collaboration, but it often struggles with low-quality reward signals and high non-stationarity. In contrast, Evolutionary Algorithm (EA) has shown better convergence, robustness, and signal quality insensitivity. This paper introduces a hybrid framework, Representation Asymmetry and Collaboration Evolution (RACE), which combines EA and MARL for efficient collaboration. RACE maintains a MARL team and a population of EA teams. To enable efficient knowledge sharing and policy exploration, RACE decomposes the policies of different teams controlling the same agent into a shared nonlinear observation representation encoder and individual linear policy representations. To address the partial observation issue, we introduce Value-Aware Mutual Information Maximization to enhance the shared representation with useful information about superior global states. EA evolves the population using novel agent-level crossover and mutation operators, offering diverse experiences for MARL. Concurrently, MARL optimizes its policies and injects them into the population for evolution. The experiments on challenging continuous and discrete tasks demonstrate that RACE significantly improves the basic algorithms, consistently outperforming other algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/yeshenpy/RACE.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning can struggle with weak reward signals and a changing learning environment created by other agents. Evolutionary methods offer a different route to exploring policies. RACE combines the two approaches so gradient-based learning and population search can exchange useful experience and policy improvements.

The framework maintains a reinforcement-learning team and a population of evolutionary teams. Policies for the same agent share a nonlinear observation encoder but use individual linear policy representations. Value-Aware Mutual Information Maximization enriches the shared representation under partial observability. Agent-level crossover and mutation generate varied experience, while reinforcement-learning policies are periodically introduced into the evolving population.

Experiments on challenging continuous and discrete tasks show improvements over the base algorithms and the compared alternatives. The contribution is a coordinated training framework with a shared representation that makes cross-team knowledge transfer practical. The abstract does not isolate the numerical contribution of each component or establish that the hybrid always uses less total computation.
summary.tldr: RACE combines shared representations, evolutionary policy search, and multi-agent reinforcement learning to improve cooperative learning.

title: RACE: Improve Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Representation Asymmetry and Collaborative Evolution

abstract: $k$-nearest neighbor classification is a popular non-parametric method because of desirable properties like automatic adaption to distributional scale changes. Unfortunately, it has thus far proved difficult to design active learning strategies for the training of local voting-based classifiers that naturally retain these desirable properties, and hence active learning strategies for $k$-nearest neighbor classification have been conspicuously missing from the literature. In this work, we introduce a simple and intuitive active learning algorithm for the training of $k$-nearest neighbor classifiers, the first in the literature which retains the concept of the $k$-nearest neighbor vote at prediction time. We provide consistency guarantees for a modified $k$-nearest neighbors classifier trained on samples acquired via our scheme, and show that when the conditional probability function $\mathbb{P}(Y=y|X=x)$ is sufficiently smooth and the Tsybakov noise condition holds, our actively trained classifiers converge to the Bayes optimal classifier at a faster asymptotic rate than passively trained $k$-nearest neighbor classifiers.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification predicts a label by taking a vote among nearby labeled examples. Its appeal includes adapting automatically to changes in the scale of the data distribution. Active learning introduces another choice: which examples should receive labels? The challenge is to make that choice intelligently while preserving the local voting behavior that makes nearest-neighbor methods useful.

This paper introduces a two-stage active learning algorithm for training these classifiers. Its distinguishing feature is that predictions still use a vote among the k nearest neighbors. The authors describe it as the first active learning approach in this setting to retain that prediction rule, and establish consistency guarantees for a modified classifier trained on the acquired samples.

The stronger rate result requires specific conditions: sufficiently smooth conditional label probabilities and the Tsybakov noise condition. Under those assumptions, the actively trained classifiers approach the Bayes-optimal classifier faster asymptotically than passively trained nearest-neighbor classifiers. This is a conditional advantage in learning rate, rather than a promise of improvement on every dataset.
summary.tldr: A two-stage active learning method preserves nearest-neighbor voting and achieves faster asymptotic convergence under stated smoothness and noise conditions.

title: A Two-Stage Active Learning Algorithm for k-Nearest Neighbors

abstract: Autoencoders are a popular model in many branches of machine learning and lossy data compression. However, their fundamental limits, the performance of gradient methods and the features learnt during optimization remain poorly understood, even in the two-layer setting. In fact, earlier work has considered either linear autoencoders or specific training regimes (leading to vanishing or diverging compression rates). Our paper addresses this gap by focusing on non-linear two-layer autoencoders trained in the challenging proportional regime in which the input dimension scales linearly with the size of the representation. Our results characterize the minimizers of the population risk, and show that such minimizers are achieved by gradient methods; their structure is also unveiled, thus leading to a concise description of the features obtained via training. For the special case of a sign activation function, our analysis establishes the fundamental limits for the lossy compression of Gaussian sources via (shallow) autoencoders. Finally, while the results are proved for Gaussian data, numerical simulations on standard datasets display the universality of the theoretical predictions.

paragraphs: Autoencoders learn compressed representations, but even shallow nonlinear versions raise basic questions about their best possible performance and what gradient training learns. This paper studies two-layer autoencoders in the proportional regime, where input dimension grows linearly with representation size. That setting addresses a gap left by analyses of linear models or regimes with vanishing or diverging compression rates.

The authors characterize the solutions that minimize population risk and show that gradient methods achieve those minimizers. They also describe the structure of the minimizing solutions, connecting optimal performance to the features learned during training. This links questions about what the architecture can achieve with questions about what optimization actually finds.

For sign activation functions, the analysis establishes fundamental limits for lossy compression of Gaussian sources using shallow autoencoders. The proofs apply to Gaussian data. Numerical simulations on standard datasets show behavior consistent with the theoretical predictions beyond that setting, providing empirical evidence of universality while leaving the formal guarantees tied to the stated Gaussian assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal nonlinear two-layer autoencoders for Gaussian data and shows that gradient methods reach those solutions.

title: Fundamental Limits of Two-layer Autoencoders, and Achieving Them with Gradient Methods

abstract: Class incremental learning (CIL) is one of the most challenging scenarios in continual learning. Existing work mainly focuses on strategies like memory replay, regularization, or dynamic architecture but ignores a crucial aspect: mode connectivity. Recent studies have shown that different minima can be connected by a low-loss valley, and ensembling over the valley shows improved performance and robustness. Motivated by this, we try to investigate the connectivity in CIL and find that the high-loss ridge exists along the linear connection between two adjacent continual minima. To dodge the ridge, we propose parameter-saving OPtimizing Connectivity (OPC) based on Fourier series and gradient projection for finding the low-loss path between minima. The optimized path provides infinite low-loss solutions. We further propose EOPC to ensemble points within a local bent cylinder to improve performance on learned tasks. Our scheme can serve as a plug-in unit, extensive experiments on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1K show consistent improvements when adapting EOPC to existing representative CIL methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/HaitaoWen/EOPC.

paragraphs: Class incremental learning introduces new classes over time while requiring a model to retain earlier capabilities. This paper studies the geometry connecting models learned at consecutive stages. It finds that a straight line between adjacent continual-learning minima can cross a high-loss region, making simple interpolation problematic.

The proposed Optimizing Connectivity method searches for a low-loss path around that region using Fourier series and gradient projection. The parameter-saving construction provides a continuous collection of low-loss solutions along the optimized path. The authors then introduce EOPC, which ensembles points within a local bent cylinder to improve performance on previously learned tasks.

The scheme can be added to existing class incremental learning methods. Experiments on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1K report consistent improvements when EOPC is combined with representative approaches. The findings give model connectivity a practical role in continual learning: the route between successive solutions can offer useful models for ensembling, beyond what is available from considering the learned endpoints alone.
summary.tldr: OPC finds low-loss paths between successive class-incremental models, and EOPC uses nearby ensembles to improve existing methods in the reported experiments.

title: Optimizing Mode Connectivity for Class Incremental Learning

abstract: Natural agents can effectively learn from multiple data sources that differ in size, quality, and types of measurements. We study this heterogeneity in the context of offline reinforcement learning (RL) by introducing a new, practically motivated semi-supervised setting. Here, an agent has access to two sets of trajectories: labelled trajectories containing state, action and reward triplets at every timestep, along with unlabelled trajectories that contain only state and reward information. For this setting, we develop and study a simple meta-algorithmic pipeline that learns an inverse dynamics model on the labelled data to obtain proxy-labels for the unlabelled data, followed by the use of any offline RL algorithm on the true and proxy-labelled trajectories. Empirically, we find this simple pipeline to be highly successful — on several D4RL benchmarks (Fu et al., 2020), certain offline RL algorithms can match the performance of variants trained on a fully labelled dataset even when we label only 10% of trajectories which are highly suboptimal. To strengthen our understanding, we perform a large-scale controlled empirical study investigating the interplay of data-centric properties of the labelled and unlabelled datasets, with algorithmic design choices (e.g., choice of inverse dynamics, offline RL algorithm) to identify general trends and best practices for training RL agents on semi-supervised offline datasets.

Here, an agent has access to two sets of trajectories: labelled trajectories containing state, action and reward triplets at every timestep, along with unlabelled trajectories that contain only state and reward information. For this setting, we develop and study a simple meta-algorithmic pipeline that learns an inverse dynamics model on the labelled data to obtain proxy-labels for the unlabelled data, followed by the use of any offline RL algorithm on the true and proxy-labelled trajectories. Empirically, we find this simple pipeline to be highly successful — on several D4RL benchmarks (Fu et al., 2020), certain offline RL algorithms can match the performance of variants trained on a fully labelled dataset even when we label only 10% of trajectories which are highly suboptimal. To strengthen our understanding, we perform a large-scale controlled empirical study investigating the interplay of data-centric properties of the labelled and unlabelled datasets, with algorithmic design choices (e.g., choice of inverse dynamics, offline RL algorithm) to identify general trends and best practices for training RL agents on semi-supervised offline datasets.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning often assumes that recorded trajectories include states, actions, and rewards. This paper studies a mixed-data setting: some trajectories contain all three, while others record states and rewards but omit actions. The goal is to use both collections to train an agent without requiring every trajectory to have action labels.

The proposed pipeline first learns an inverse dynamics model from the fully labeled trajectories. That model supplies proxy action labels for the action-free trajectories. An offline reinforcement learning algorithm then trains on the combined true-labeled and proxy-labeled data. The pipeline is designed as a general wrapper that can work with different offline learning algorithms.

On several D4RL benchmarks, certain algorithms match versions trained with fully labeled data even when only 10% of trajectories have action labels and those labeled trajectories are highly suboptimal. The result is specific to the reported algorithm and dataset combinations. A larger controlled study examines how data properties and choices of inverse dynamics and offline learning method interact, identifying trends and practices for making this semi-supervised approach effective.
summary.tldr: Learning proxy action labels from a small labeled trajectory set lets offline reinforcement learning use additional action-free experience.

title: Semi-Supervised Offline Reinforcement Learning with Action-Free Trajectories

abstract: To make accurate predictions, understand mechanisms, and design interventions in systems of many variables, we wish to learn causal graphs from large scale data. Unfortunately the space of all possible causal graphs is enormous so scalably and accurately searching for the best fit to the data is a challenge. In principle we could substantially decrease the search space, or learn the graph entirely, by testing the conditional independence of variables. However, deciding if two variables are adjacent in a causal graph may require an exponential number of tests. Here we build a scalable and flexible method to evaluate if two variables are adjacent in a causal graph, the Differentiable Adjacency Test (DAT). DAT replaces an exponential number of tests with a provably equivalent relaxed problem. It then solves this problem by training two neural networks. We build a graph learning method based on DAT, DAT-Graph, that can also learn from data with interventions. DAT-Graph can learn graphs of 1000 variables with state of the art accuracy. Using the graph learned by DAT-Graph, we also build models that make much more accurate predictions of the effects of interventions on large scale RNA sequencing data.

summary.tldr: DAT reformulates adjacency testing as a neural optimization problem, enabling scalable causal graph learning and improved reported intervention predictions.

title: Scalable and Flexible Causal Discovery with an Efficient Test for Adjacency

abstract: We consider the effect of temporal aggregation on instantaneous (non-temporal) causal discovery in general setting. This is motivated by the observation that the true causal time lag is often considerably shorter than the observational interval. This discrepancy leads to high aggregation, causing time-delay causality to vanish and instantaneous dependence to manifest. Although we expect such instantaneous dependence has consistency with the true causal relation in certain sense to make the discovery results meaningful, it remains unclear what type of consistency we need and when will such consistency be satisfied. We proposed functional consistency and conditional independence consistency in formal way correspond functional causal model-based methods and conditional independence-based methods respectively and provide the conditions under which these consistencies will hold. We show theoretically and experimentally that causal discovery results may be seriously distorted by aggregation especially in complete nonlinear case and we also find causal relationship still recoverable from aggregated data if we have partial linearity or appropriate prior. Our findings suggest community should take a cautious and meticulous approach when interpreting causal discovery results from such data and show why and when aggregation will distort the performance of causal discovery methods.

paragraphs: Causal effects may unfold faster than the intervals at which observations are recorded. Aggregating measurements over those intervals can hide time delays and create apparently instantaneous dependencies. This paper asks when causal discovery applied to the resulting data still reflects the underlying causal relationships.

The authors formalize two forms of consistency. Functional consistency concerns methods based on functional causal models, while conditional-independence consistency concerns methods that infer structure from conditional independence relationships. They provide conditions under which these connections survive aggregation, giving distinct criteria for assessing the two families of discovery methods.

Theory and experiments show that aggregation can seriously distort causal conclusions, particularly in fully nonlinear settings. The authors also identify circumstances in which recovery remains possible, including partial linearity or suitable prior knowledge. The findings make the measurement interval part of the causal interpretation problem: an apparent instantaneous relationship may reflect aggregated faster dynamics, and whether it remains informative depends on structural conditions. Aggregation can therefore change the meaning of the dependencies a discovery method observes.
summary.tldr: Temporal aggregation can distort causal discovery, but the paper identifies conditions under which causal relationships remain recoverable.

title: On the Recoverability of Causal Relations from Temporally Aggregated I.I.D. Data

abstract: We introduce and study a family of online metric problems with long-term constraints. In these problems, an online player makes decisions $\mathbf{x}_t$ in a metric space $(X,d)$ to simultaneously minimize their hitting cost $f_t(\mathbf{x}_t)$ and switching cost as determined by the metric. Over the time horizon $T$, the player must satisfy a long-term demand constraint $\sum_t c(\mathbf{x}_t) \geq 1$, where $c(\mathbf{x}_t)$ denotes the fraction of demand satisfied at time $t$. Such problems can find a wide array of applications to online resource allocation in sustainable energy/computing systems. We devise optimal competitive and learning-augmented algorithms for the case of bounded hitting cost gradients and weighted $\ell_1$ metrics, and further show that our proposed algorithms perform well in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Some online decisions incur both an immediate operating cost and a cost for changing from the previous decision. They may also need to satisfy an aggregate demand by the end of the horizon. This paper combines these requirements in online metric problems motivated by resource allocation in sustainable energy and computing systems.

At each step, the learner chooses a point in a metric space, pays a hitting cost and a distance-based switching cost, and contributes toward a long-term demand constraint. For bounded hitting-cost gradients and weighted ℓ₁ metrics, the authors design competitive algorithms and versions that incorporate learned predictions.

The paper establishes optimal competitive guarantees in the analyzed setting and reports good numerical performance. The contribution is a framework and algorithmic treatment for balancing immediate efficiency, movement, and eventual demand satisfaction. Its formal scope is defined by the stated metric and gradient conditions; the abstract does not claim the same guarantee for every cost geometry or resource-allocation constraint.
summary.tldr: Online algorithms balance operating and switching costs while meeting aggregate demand, with optimal guarantees in the studied metric setting.

title: Chasing Convex Functions with Long-term Constraints

abstract: The anomaly detection literature is abundant with offline methods, which require repeated access to data in memory, and impose impractical assumptions when applied to a streaming context. Existing online anomaly detection methods also generally fail to address these constraints, resorting to periodic retraining to adapt to the online context. We propose Online-iForest, a novel method explicitly designed for streaming conditions that seamlessly tracks the data generating process as it evolves over time. Experimental validation on real-world datasets demonstrated that Online-iForest is on par with online alternatives and closely rivals state-of-the-art offline anomaly detection techniques that undergo periodic retraining. Notably, Online-iForest consistently outperforms all competitors in terms of efficiency, making it a promising solution in applications where fast identification of anomalies is of primary importance such as cybersecurity, fraud and fault detection.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection methods often assume that stored data can be revisited repeatedly. That assumption is awkward for streams, where observations arrive continuously and the process producing them can change. Even methods described as online may rely on periodic retraining to keep up. Online-iForest is designed explicitly around streaming conditions.

The method tracks the data-generating process as it evolves over time. This addresses adaptation as part of the streaming task itself, where both changing patterns and the speed of detection matter. The paper evaluates whether this design can maintain useful anomaly detection performance while improving the efficiency of processing ongoing data.

On real-world datasets, Online-iForest performs on par with online alternatives and closely approaches leading offline methods that are periodically retrained. It consistently surpasses the evaluated competitors in efficiency. The findings make it promising for settings where identifying unusual events quickly is especially valuable, including cybersecurity, fraud detection, and fault detection, while keeping the accuracy comparison distinct from its stronger efficiency result.
summary.tldr: Online-iForest tracks evolving data streams with competitive anomaly detection performance and consistently better efficiency than the evaluated alternatives.

title: Online Isolation Forest

abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to object completion, with the primary goal of reconstructing a complete object from its partially visible components. Our method, named MaskComp, delineates the completion process through iterative stages of generation and segmentation. In each iteration, the object mask is provided as an additional condition to boost image generation, and, in return, the generated images can lead to a more accurate mask by fusing the segmentation of images. We demonstrate that the combination of one generation and one segmentation stage effectively functions as a mask denoiser. Through alternation between the generation and segmentation stages, the partial object mask is progressively refined, providing precise shape guidance and yielding superior object completion results. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of MaskComp over existing approaches, e.g., ControlNet and Stable Diffusion, establishing it as an effective solution for object completion.

paragraphs: Object completion seeks to reconstruct an entire object when only some of it is visible. MaskComp approaches this task by repeatedly connecting image generation with segmentation. The object mask provides shape information for generation, while segmentation extracts shape information from the generated images. Each stage therefore produces information that can improve the next.

In each iteration, the current object mask becomes an additional condition for generating images. The method then combines segmentations of those images to obtain a more accurate mask. The authors demonstrate that one generation stage followed by one segmentation stage effectively acts as a mask denoiser, refining the shape information available to the process.

Repeating this cycle progressively improves the partial object mask and gives generation more precise guidance about the complete object's shape. Experiments show better object completion than the evaluated existing approaches, including ControlNet and Stable Diffusion. The contribution is the feedback between generating appearance and estimating shape: the two operations cooperate throughout reconstruction instead of serving as isolated steps.
summary.tldr: MaskComp alternates image generation and segmentation to refine partial object masks and improve reconstruction of complete objects.

title: Completing Visual Objects via Bridging Generation and Segmentation

abstract: Second-order methods such as KFAC can be useful for neural net training. However, they are often memory-inefficient since their preconditioning Kronecker factors are dense, and numerically unstable in low precision as they require matrix inversion or decomposition. These limitations render such methods unpopular for modern mixed-precision training. We address them by (i) formulating an inverse-free KFAC update and (ii) imposing structures in the Kronecker factors, resulting in structured inverse-free natural gradient descent (SINGD). On modern neural networks, we show that SINGD is memory-efficient and numerically robust, in contrast to KFAC, and often outperforms AdamW even in half precision. Our work closes a gap between first- and second-order methods in modern low-precision training.

paragraphs: Second-order training methods such as KFAC can be useful, but their implementation creates obstacles for modern neural networks. Dense Kronecker factors consume memory, and matrix inversions or decompositions can become numerically unstable in low precision. These costs make the methods difficult to integrate into mixed-precision training workflows.

The paper addresses both issues through Structured Inverse-Free Natural Gradient Descent, or SINGD. It first reformulates the KFAC update so that it does not require inversion. It then imposes structure on the Kronecker factors, targeting the memory burden associated with storing dense factors. These changes tackle numerical stability and memory use within the same optimization method.

On modern neural networks, the authors show that SINGD is memory-efficient and numerically robust compared with KFAC. They also report that it often outperforms AdamW, including in half precision. The contribution makes second-order optimization more compatible with practical low-precision training, while the qualified performance result indicates an observed advantage across evaluations rather than universal superiority.
summary.tldr: SINGD combines inverse-free updates with structured factors to make second-order training more memory-efficient and stable in low precision.

title: Structured Inverse-Free Natural Gradient Descent: Memory-Efficient & Numerically-Stable KFAC

abstract: Feedback Alignment (FA) methods are biologically inspired local learning rules for training neural networks with reduced communication between layers. While FA has potential applications in distributed and privacy-aware ML, limitations in multi-class classification and lack of theoretical understanding of the alignment mechanism have constrained its impact. This study introduces a unified framework elucidating the operational principles behind alignment in FA. Our key contributions include: (1) a novel conservation law linking changes in synaptic weights to implicit regularization that maintains alignment with the gradient, with support from experiments, (2) sufficient conditions for convergence based on the concept of alignment dominance, and (3) empirical analysis showing better alignment can enhance FA performance on complex multi-class tasks. Overall, these theoretical and practical advancements improve interpretability of bio-plausible learning rules and provide groundwork for developing enhanced FA algorithms.

This paper develops a unified framework for understanding how the alignment mechanism operates.

They also provide a foundation for developing improved algorithms by connecting training performance to the mechanism that keeps updates aligned with the gradient.
summary.tldr: A conservation law explains implicit regularization in Feedback Alignment, alongside sufficient convergence conditions and evidence that better alignment can improve classification.

title: Implicit Regularization in Feedback Alignment Learning Mechanisms for Neural Networks

abstract: Neural Operators that directly learn mappings between function spaces, such as Deep Operator Networks (DONs) and Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs), have received considerable attention. Despite the universal approximation guarantees for DONs and FNOs, there is currently no optimization convergence guarantee for learning such networks using gradient descent (GD). In this paper, we address this open problem by presenting a unified framework for optimization based on GD and applying it to establish convergence guarantees for both DONs and FNOs. In particular, we show that the losses associated with both of these neural operators satisfy two conditions—restricted strong convexity (RSC) and smoothness—that guarantee a decrease on their loss values due to GD. Remarkably, these two conditions are satisfied for each neural operator due to different reasons associated with the architectural differences of the respective models. One takeaway that emerges from the theory is that wider networks benefit optimization convergence guarantees for both DONs and FNOs. We present empirical results on canonical operator learning problems to support our theoretical results and find that larger widths benefit training.
