paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between spaces of functions. Deep Operator Networks and Fourier Neural Operators already have universal approximation guarantees, but representational capability alone does not establish that gradient descent will successfully train them. This paper addresses that optimization question through a unified framework applicable to both architectures.

The authors show that the losses for these neural operators satisfy restricted strong convexity and smoothness, two properties that guarantee loss decreases under gradient descent. Although the same framework covers both models, the architectural reasons supporting these properties differ. This makes the analysis sensitive to how the networks are constructed while still yielding a shared route to convergence guarantees.

A central consequence is that increasing network width benefits the optimization guarantees for both model families. Experiments on canonical operator-learning problems support the theory, with larger widths improving training. The result connects an architectural choice to the behavior of the training algorithm, complementing existing guarantees about which functions these networks can represent.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis gives gradient-descent convergence guarantees for two neural-operator families and shows how greater width can benefit training.

title: Optimization for Neural Operators can Benefit from Width

abstract: Decision-makers often adaptively influence downstream competitive agents’ behavior to minimize their cost, yet in doing so face critical challenges: $(i)$ decision-makers might not a priori know the agents’ objectives; $(ii)$ agents might learn their responses, introducing stochasticity and non-stationarity into the decision-making process; and $(iii)$ there may be additional non-strategic environmental stochasticity. Characterizing convergence of this complex system is contingent on how the decision-maker controls for the tradeoff between the induced drift and additional noise from the learning agent behavior and environmental stochasticity. To understand how the learning agents’ behavior is influenced by the decision-maker’s actions, we first consider a decision-maker that deploys an arbitrary sequence of actions which induces a sequence of games and corresponding equilibria. We characterize how the drift and noise in the agents’ stochastic algorithms decouples from their optimization error. Leveraging this decoupling and accompanying finite-time efficiency estimates, we design decision-maker algorithms that control the induced drift relative to the agent noise. This enables efficient finite-time tracking of game theoretic equilibrium concepts that adhere to the incentives of the players’ collective learning processes.

paragraphs: A decision-maker may try to reduce its own cost by influencing other agents, even without knowing their objectives. The problem becomes harder when those agents learn their responses over time: their behavior changes and contains randomness. Environmental randomness adds another source of uncertainty. This paper studies convergence in systems where these processes interact.

The analysis begins with an arbitrary sequence of actions by the decision-maker, producing a changing sequence of games and equilibria. The authors characterize how movement of the target and noise in the agents’ stochastic learning algorithms separate from their optimization error. This distinction helps explain whether agents are struggling to solve their current problem or to follow a problem that keeps changing.

Using that decomposition and finite-time efficiency estimates, the authors design decision-maker algorithms that regulate induced drift relative to agent noise. The resulting methods efficiently track game-theoretic equilibrium concepts over finite periods. The contribution is a framework for coordinating the pace of intervention with the behavior of learning agents while respecting the incentives of their collective learning processes.
summary.tldr: The paper separates drift, noise, and optimization error to design algorithms that track equilibria when downstream agents learn stochastic responses.

title: Finite-Time Convergence Rates in Stochastic Stackelberg Games with Smooth Algorithmic Agents

abstract: This paper introduces MOTE (MOre Than meets the Eye), a novel multi-object tracking (MOT) algorithm designed to address the challenges of tracking occluded objects. By integrating deformable detection transformers with a custom disocclusion matrix, MOTE significantly enhances the ability to track objects even when they are temporarily hidden from view. The algorithm leverages optical flow to generate features that are processed through a softmax splatting layer, which aids in the creation of a disocclusion matrix. This matrix plays a crucial role in maintaining track consistency by estimating the motion of occluded objects. MOTE’s architecture includes modifications to the enhanced track embedding module (ETEM), which allows it to incorporate these advanced features into the track query layer embeddings. This integration ensures that the model not only tracks visible objects but also accurately predicts the trajectories of occluded ones, much like the human visual system. The proposed method is evaluated on multiple datasets, including MOT17, MOT20, and DanceTrack, where it achieves impressive tracking metrics–82.0 MOTA and 66.3 HOTA on the MOT17 dataset, 81.7 MOTA and 65.8 HOTA on the MOT20 dataset, and 93.2 MOTA and 74.2 HOTA on the DanceTrack dataset. Notably, MOTE excels in reducing identity switches and maintaining consistent tracking in complex real-world scenarios with frequent occlusions, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods across all tested benchmarks.

title: More Than Meets the Eye: Enhancing Multi-Object Tracking Even with Prolonged Occlusions

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in applications requiring long context lengths, but the key-value (KV) cache often becomes a memory bottleneck on GPUs as context grows. To address this, we propose Commutative Vector Quantization (CommVQ) to significantly reduce memory usage for long-context LLM inference. We first introduce additive quantization with a lightweight encoder and codebook to compress the KV cache, which can be decoded via simple matrix multiplication. To further reduce computational costs during decoding, we design the codebook to be commutative with Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) and train it using an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. This enables efficient integration of decoding into the self-attention mechanism. Our approach achieves high accuracy with additive quantization and low overhead via the RoPE-commutative codebook. Experiments on long-context benchmarks and GSM8K show that our method reduces FP16 KV cache size by 87.5% with 2-bit quantization, while outperforming state-of-the-art KV cache quantization methods. Notably, it enables 1-bit KV cache quantization with minimal accuracy loss, allowing a LLaMA-3.1 8B model to run with a 128K context length on a single RTX 4090 GPU. The source code is available at: https://github.com/UMass-Embodied-AGI/CommVQ.

Notably, it enables 1-bit KV cache quantization with minimal accuracy loss, allowing a LLaMA-3.1 8B model to run with a 128K context length on a single RTX 4090 GPU. The source code is available at: https://github.com/UMass-Embodied-AGI/CommVQ.

paragraphs: Long-context language-model inference requires storing a growing key-value cache, which can exhaust GPU memory. CommVQ compresses this cache through additive vector quantization. A lightweight encoder and a learned codebook represent cache contents compactly, while reconstruction can be performed using simple matrix multiplication.

The codebook is designed to commute with Rotary Position Embedding, the model's positional encoding operation. This compatibility lets decoding integrate efficiently into self-attention instead of adding a separate expensive reconstruction process. The authors train the codebook using an Expectation-Maximization algorithm. The design therefore addresses both storage reduction and the computational overhead of using compressed representations.

On long-context benchmarks and GSM8K, the reported 2-bit configuration reduces cache size by 87.5% relative to FP16 and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art quantization methods. The authors also report 1-bit cache quantization with minimal accuracy loss. This enables a LLaMA-3.1 8B model to use a 128K context on a single RTX 4090, illustrating how cache compression can make a demanding inference configuration fit available hardware.
summary.tldr: CommVQ compresses the KV cache with a positional-encoding-compatible codebook, enabling low-bit storage with efficient attention integration.

title: CommVQ: Commutative Vector Quantization for KV Cache Compression

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown promising performance, but at the cost of resource-intensive operations on graph-scale matrices. To reduce computational overhead, previous studies attempt to sparsify the graph or network parameters, but with limited flexibility and precision boundaries. In this work, we propose Unifews, a joint sparsification technique to unify graph and weight matrix operations and enhance GNN learning efficiency. The Unifews design enables adaptive compression across GNN layers with progressively increased sparsity, and is applicable to a variety of architectures with on-the-fly simplification. Theoretically, we establish a novel framework to characterize sparsified GNN learning in view of the graph optimization process, showing that Unifews effectively approximates the learning objective with bounded error and reduced computational overhead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Unifews achieves efficiency improvements with comparable or better accuracy, including 10-20x matrix operation reduction and up to 100x acceleration on graphs up to billion-edge scale.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can require expensive operations on matrices whose scale follows the graph. Earlier efficiency approaches sparsify either the graph or network parameters, with limitations in flexibility and precision. Unifews addresses both sources of computation through a joint sparsification technique that unifies graph and weight matrix operations.

The method adapts compression across layers and progressively increases sparsity. It supports several architectures and simplifies operations on the fly. The authors also develop a theoretical framework that views sparsified learning through graph optimization, showing that Unifews approximates the learning objective with bounded error while reducing computational overhead.

Experiments report comparable or better accuracy alongside substantial efficiency gains. These include a 10–20-fold reduction in matrix operations and acceleration of up to 100 times, with evaluations reaching graphs containing a billion edges. The findings connect coordinated sparsification to practical scalability: reducing work in graph processing and learned transformations together can preserve predictive quality in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Unifews jointly sparsifies graph and weight operations to accelerate graph neural networks while maintaining comparable or better accuracy.

title: Unifews: You Need Fewer Operations for Efficient Graph Neural Networks

abstract: In this work, we design quantum algorithms that are more efficient than classical algorithms to solve time-dependent and finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) in two distinct settings: (1) In the exact dynamics setting, where the agent has full knowledge of the environment’s dynamics (i.e., transition probabilities), we prove that our Quantum Value Iteration (QVI) algorithm QVI-1 achieves a quadratic speedup in the size of the action space $(A)$ compared with the classical value iteration algorithm for computing the optimal policy ($\pi^{\ast}$) and the optimal V-value function ($V_{0}^{\ast}$). Furthermore, our algorithm QVI-2 provides an additional speedup in the size of the state space $(S)$ when obtaining near-optimal policies and V-value functions. Both QVI-1 and QVI-2 achieve quantum query complexities that provably improve upon classical lower bounds, particularly in their dependences on $S$ and $A$. (2) In the generative model setting, where samples from the environment are accessible in quantum superposition, we prove that our algorithms QVI-3 and QVI-4 achieve improvements in sample complexity over the state-of-the-art (SOTA) classical algorithm in terms of $A$, estimation error $(\epsilon)$, and time horizon $(H)$. More importantly, we prove quantum lower bounds to show that QVI-3 and QVI-4 are asymptotically optimal, up to logarithmic factors, assuming a constant time horizon.

paragraphs: This paper develops quantum algorithms for time-dependent decision problems with a finite planning horizon. It studies two access settings separately: full knowledge of transition probabilities, and a generative model that supplies environment samples in quantum superposition. These access assumptions determine what information the algorithms can use and are central to the claimed advantages.

With exact dynamics, QVI-1 computes an optimal policy and value function with a quadratic improvement in action-space dependence over classical value iteration. QVI-2 obtains near-optimal policies and values with an additional improvement in state-space dependence. Both algorithms have quantum query complexities that improve on classical lower bounds, particularly in their dependence on state and action counts.

With quantum-superposition sampling access, QVI-3 and QVI-4 improve sample complexity relative to the state-of-the-art classical algorithm in action count, estimation error, and horizon dependence. Quantum lower bounds show these two algorithms are asymptotically optimal up to logarithmic factors when the horizon is constant. The results establish resource-complexity advantages within the specified quantum access settings.
summary.tldr: Four quantum value-iteration algorithms improve finite-horizon planning complexity under exact-dynamics or quantum-sampling access assumptions.

title: Quantum Algorithms for Finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes

abstract: We introduce a novel generative framework for functions by integrating Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) and Transformer-based hypernetworks into latent variable models. Unlike prior approaches that rely on MLP-based hypernetworks with scalability limitations, our method employs a Transformer-based decoder to generate INR parameters from latent variables, addressing both representation capacity and computational efficiency. Our framework extends latent diffusion models (LDMs) to INR generation by replacing standard decoders with a Transformer-based hypernetwork, which can be trained either from scratch or via hyper-transforming—a strategy that fine-tunes only the decoder while freezing the pre-trained latent space. This enables efficient adaptation of existing generative models to INR-based representations without requiring full retraining. We validate our approach across multiple modalities, demonstrating improved scalability, expressiveness, and generalization over existing INR-based generative models. Our findings establish a unified and flexible framework for learning structured function representations.

paragraphs: This paper develops a generative framework for functions represented by neural networks. It combines Implicit Neural Representations, or INRs, with a Transformer-based hypernetwork: a decoder that produces the parameters of another network from a latent variable. The design addresses representation capacity and computational efficiency challenges associated with earlier MLP-based hypernetworks.

To extend latent diffusion models to INR generation, the authors replace the usual decoder with this Transformer hypernetwork. The resulting system can be trained from scratch. Alternatively, a procedure called hyper-transforming adapts only the decoder while keeping a pretrained latent space frozen, allowing an existing generative model to produce INR representations without full retraining.

Validation across multiple modalities shows improvements in scalability, expressiveness, and generalization over existing INR-based generative models. The significance is both representational and practical: the framework generates structured functions through their network parameters, and the decoder-only adaptation route provides a way to reuse pretrained latent representations. The reported findings support a flexible framework that applies across the tested modalities.
summary.tldr: Transformer hypernetworks adapt latent diffusion models to generate implicit neural representations, including through decoder-only fine-tuning.

title: Hyper-Transforming Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: We empirically investigate how well popular approximate inference algorithms for Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) respect the theoretical properties of Bayesian belief updating. We find strong evidence on synthetic regression and real-world image classification tasks that common BNN algorithms such as variational inference, Laplace approximation, SWAG, and SGLD fail to update in a consistent manner, forget about old data under sequential updates, and violate the predictive coherence properties that would be expected of Bayesian methods. These observed behaviors imply that care should be taken when treating BNNs as true Bayesian models, particularly when using them beyond static prediction settings, such as for active, continual, or transfer learning.

paragraphs: Calling a neural network Bayesian suggests more than attaching uncertainty to a prediction: its beliefs should also change coherently as evidence arrives. This paper empirically tests whether popular approximate inference methods for Bayesian neural networks preserve theoretical properties of Bayesian updating. The question concerns how the models learn from evidence, beyond their behavior on a fixed prediction task.

The authors study variational inference, Laplace approximation, SWAG, and SGLD on synthetic regression and real-world image classification tasks. They find strong evidence of inconsistent updates, forgetting of earlier observations during sequential learning, and violations of expected predictive coherence. These are observed failures of the tested approximation methods to reproduce properties associated with Bayesian inference.

The findings matter especially when a model is repeatedly updated or moved between learning settings. Active learning, continual learning, and transfer learning all go beyond a single static prediction stage, making update behavior consequential. The paper therefore argues for care when treating these approximate Bayesian neural networks as true Bayesian models. Its empirical evidence challenges that interpretation in the studied settings without claiming that every Bayesian neural-network method must fail.
summary.tldr: Common approximate Bayesian neural-network methods empirically violate expected Bayesian updating properties, particularly under sequential learning.

title: Do Bayesian Neural Networks Actually Behave Like Bayesian Models?

abstract: Recent research across mathematical problem solving, proof assistant programming and multimodal jailbreaking documents a striking finding: when (multimodal) language model tackle a suite of tasks with multiple attempts per task – succeeding if any attempt is correct – then the negative log of the average success rate scales a power law in the number of attempts. In this work, we identify an apparent puzzle: a simple mathematical calculation predicts that on each problem, the failure rate should fall exponentially with the number of attempts. We confirm this prediction empirically, raising a question: from where does aggregate polynomial scaling emerge? We then answer this question by demonstrating per-problem exponential scaling can be made consistent with aggregate polynomial scaling if the distribution of single-attempt success probabilities is heavy tailed such that a small fraction of tasks with extremely low success probabilities collectively warp the aggregate success trend into a power law - even as each problem scales exponentially on its own. We further demonstrate that this distributional perspective explains previously observed deviations from power law scaling, and provides a simple method for forecasting the power law exponent with an order of magnitude lower relative error, or equivalently, ${\sim}2-4$ orders of magnitude less inference compute. Overall, our work contributes to a better understanding of how neural language model performance improves with scaling inference compute and the development of scaling-predictable evaluations of (multimodal) language models.

paragraphs: Giving a language model several attempts can improve the chance that at least one succeeds. Across collections of tasks, prior observations found power-law scaling in the negative logarithm of average success. Yet a simple calculation predicts an exponential decline in failure for each individual problem. This paper investigates how those two patterns can coexist.

The authors confirm the individual-problem exponential pattern empirically. They then show that aggregation can produce polynomial scaling when single-attempt success probabilities have a heavy-tailed distribution containing extremely difficult tasks. A small fraction of problems with very low success probabilities can reshape the overall trend, even while each problem separately follows exponential scaling.

This distributional account also explains previously observed departures from power laws. It supports a forecasting method that predicts the power-law exponent with an order of magnitude lower relative error, or approximately two to four orders of magnitude less inference computation. The findings connect aggregate scaling to the mixture of task difficulties, helping explain and forecast the benefits of repeated attempts.
summary.tldr: A heavy-tailed distribution of task success probabilities can reconcile exponential improvement on individual problems with aggregate power-law scaling.

title: How Do Large Language Monkeys Get Their Power (Laws)?

abstract: Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is a cornerstone approach in computational pathology for distilling embeddings from gigapixel tissue images into patient-level representations to predict clinical outcomes. However, MIL is frequently challenged by the constraints of working with small, weakly-supervised clinical datasets. Unlike fields such as natural language processing and computer vision, which effectively use transfer learning to improve model quality in data-scarce environments, the transferability of MIL models remains largely unexplored. We conduct the first comprehensive investigation into transfer learning capabilities of pretrained MIL models, evaluating 11 MIL models across 19 pretraining tasks spanning tissue subtyping, cancer grading, and molecular subtype prediction. We observe a substantial performance boost with finetuning pretrained models over training from randomly initialized weights, even with domain differences between pretraining and target tasks. Pretraining on pan-cancer datasets enables consistent generalization across organs and task types compared to single-disease pretraining. Remarkably, this pan-cancer pretraining leads to better transfer than that of a state-of-the-art slide-level foundation model, while using only 6.5% of the training data. These findings indicate that MIL architectures exhibit robust adaptability, offering insights into the benefits of leveraging pretrained models to enhance performance in computational pathology.

paragraphs: Computational pathology often uses multiple instance learning to combine embeddings from enormous tissue images into patient-level representations. Training these models is difficult when clinical datasets are small and supervision is weak. This paper investigates whether pretrained multiple instance learning models can provide a useful starting point for new prediction tasks.

The study evaluates 11 models across 19 pretraining tasks covering tissue subtyping, cancer grading, and molecular subtype prediction. Fine-tuning pretrained models substantially improves performance over starting from random weights, including when the pretraining and target domains differ. Pretraining across multiple cancers also produces more consistent generalization across organs and task types than pretraining on a single disease.

In the reported comparison, this pan-cancer pretraining transfers better than a state-of-the-art slide-level foundation model while using only 6.5% as much training data. These findings support the adaptability of multiple instance learning architectures. They also indicate that the breadth of pretraining tasks and diseases can matter when building reusable models for pathology settings with limited labeled data.
summary.tldr: Pretrained multiple instance learning models transfer well across pathology tasks, with pan-cancer pretraining providing especially consistent benefits.

title: Do Multiple Instance Learning Models Transfer?

abstract: Can the relative performance of a pre-trained large multimodal model (LMM) be predicted without access to labels? As LMMs proliferate, it becomes increasingly important to develop efficient ways to choose between them when faced with new data or tasks. The usual approach does the equivalent of giving the models an exam and marking them. We opt to avoid marking and the associated labor of determining the ground-truth answers. Instead, we explore other signals elicited and ascertain how well the models know their own limits, evaluating the effectiveness of these signals at unsupervised model ranking. We evaluate 47 state-of-the-art LMMs (e.g., LLaVA) across 9 visual question answering benchmarks, analyzing how well uncertainty-based metrics can predict relative model performance. Our findings show that uncertainty scores derived from softmax distributions provide a robust and consistent basis for ranking models across various tasks. This facilitates the ranking of LMMs on unlabeled data, providing a practical approach for selecting models for diverse target domains without requiring manual annotation.

paragraphs: Choosing a multimodal model for new data usually requires labeled examples against which to score its answers. This paper investigates whether models can instead be ranked using signals available from their own outputs. The intended benefit is to support model selection when obtaining correct reference answers would require manual annotation.

The authors evaluate forty-seven large multimodal models across nine visual question answering benchmarks. They examine uncertainty-based metrics and ask how well those signals predict relative performance. In particular, they study uncertainty scores derived from softmax distributions, using the models’ output probabilities as evidence about how they compare.

The reported results identify these scores as a robust and consistent basis for ranking models across the evaluated tasks. This supports choosing among pretrained models using unlabeled target data. The object being predicted is relative model performance: which model is likely to perform better. The empirical finding is that internal uncertainty contains useful comparative information across the studied benchmarks, reducing reliance on manually marked answers for model selection.
summary.tldr: Softmax-derived uncertainty scores provide a consistent empirical signal for ranking multimodal models on unlabeled visual question answering data.

title: Ranked from Within: Ranking Large Multimodal Models Without Labels

abstract: Code Agent development is an extremely active research area, where a reliable performance metric is critical for tracking progress and guiding new developments. This demand is underscored by the meteoric rise in popularity of SWE-Bench – a benchmark that challenges code agents to generate patches addressing GitHub issues given the full repository as context. The correctness of generated patches is then evaluated by executing a human-written test suite extracted from the repository after the issue’s resolution. However, constructing benchmarks like SWE-Bench requires substantial manual effort to set up historically accurate execution environments for testing. Crucially, this severely limits the number of considered repositories, e.g., just 12 for SWE-Bench. Considering so few repositories, selected for their popularity runs the risk of leading to a distributional mismatch, i.e., the measured performance may not be representative of real-world scenarios running the riks of misguiding development efforts. In this work, we address this challenge and introduce SetUpAgent, a fully automated system capable of historically accurate dependency setup, test execution, and result parsing. Using SetUpAgent, we generate two new datasets: (i) SWEE-Bench an extended version of SWE-Bench encompassing hundreds of repositories, and (ii) SWA-Bench a benchmark focusing on applications rather than libraries. Comparing these datasets to SWE-Bench with respect to their characteristics and code agent performance, we find significant distributional differences, including lower issue description quality and detail level, higher fix complexity, and most importantly up to 60% lower agent success rates.

Its proposed patch must run in an environment consistent with the repository's historical dependencies, and tests must be executed and interpreted. That setup work has restricted benchmark coverage: the abstract identifies just 12 repositories in SWE-Bench.

The findings indicate that benchmark composition can strongly affect apparent capability. Broader repository coverage therefore matters both for measuring progress and for deciding which coding-agent weaknesses deserve attention.
summary.tldr: SetUpAgent automates repository benchmark construction, revealing broader coding tasks on which evaluated agents have substantially lower success rates.

title: Automated Benchmark Generation for Repository-Level Coding Tasks

abstract: In aligning large language models (LLMs), reward models have played an important role, but are standardly trained as discriminative models and rely only on labeled human preference data. In this paper, we explore methods that train reward models using both unlabeled and labeled data. Building on the generative models in LLMs, we develop a generative reward model that is first trained via large-scale unsupervised learning and then fine-tuned via supervised learning. We also show that by using label smoothing, we are in fact optimizing a regularized pairwise ranking loss. This result, in turn, provides a new view of training reward models, which links generative models and discriminative models under the same class of training objectives. The outcome of these techniques is a foundation reward model, which can be applied to a wide range of tasks with little or no further fine-tuning effort. Extensive experiments show that this model generalizes well across several tasks, including response ranking, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and task adaptation with fine-tuning, achieving significant performance improvements over several strong baseline models.

paragraphs: Reward models help align language models by evaluating their responses. Standard training commonly treats this as a discriminative problem and relies on labeled human preferences. GRAM explores a broader training route: use unlabeled data as well as preference labels to build a reward model that can transfer across tasks.

The method starts with large-scale unsupervised training of a generative reward model and then applies supervised fine-tuning. The paper also analyzes label smoothing, showing that its use corresponds to optimizing a regularized pairwise ranking loss. This connects the generative formulation to discriminative reward modeling through a shared class of objectives, providing a theoretical interpretation of how the model learns to compare responses.

The resulting foundation reward model is intended to serve many tasks with little or no additional fine-tuning. Experiments demonstrate generalization in response ranking, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and adaptation through fine-tuning, with significant gains over several strong baselines. These findings support combining broad unsupervised learning with targeted supervision to improve the reach of reward models.
summary.tldr: GRAM combines unsupervised generative training and supervised preference learning to produce a reward model that generalizes across several tasks.

title: GRAM: A Generative Foundation Reward Model for Reward Generalization

abstract: Node equivalence is common in graphs, such as computing networks, encompassing automorphic equivalence (preserving adjacency under node permutations) and attribute equivalence (nodes with identical attributes). Despite their importance for learning node representations, these equivalences are largely ignored by existing graph models. To bridge this gap, we propose a GrAph self-supervised Learning framework with Equivalence (GALE) and analyze its connections to existing techniques. Specifically, we: 1) unify automorphic and attribute equivalence into a single equivalence class; 2) enforce the equivalence principle to make representations within the same class more similar while separating those across classes; 3) introduce approximate equivalence classes with linear time complexity to address the NP-hardness of exact automorphism detection and handle node-feature variation; 4) analyze existing graph encoders, noting limitations in message passing neural networks and graph transformers regarding equivalence constraints; 5) show that graph contrastive learning are a degenerate form of equivalence constraint; and 6) demonstrate that GALE achieves superior performance over baselines.
originalAbstract: Node equivalence is common in graphs, such as computing networks, encompassing automorphic equivalence (preserving adjacency under node permutations) and attribute equivalence (nodes with identical attributes). Despite their importance for learning node representations, these equivalences are largely ignored by existing graph models. To bridge this gap, we propose a GrAph self-supervised Learning framework with Equivalence (GALE) and analyze its connections to existing techniques. Specifically, we: 1) unify automorphic and attribute equivalence into a single equivalence class; 2) enforce the equivalence principle to make representations within the same class more similar while separating those across classes; 3) introduce approximate equivalence classes with linear time complexity to address the NP-hardness of exact automorphism detection and handle node-feature variation; 4) analyze existing graph encoders, noting limitations in message passing neural networks and graph transformers regarding equivalence constraints; 5) show that graph contrastive learning are a degenerate form of equivalence constraint; and 6) demonstrate that GALE achieves superior performance over baselines.

paragraphs: This paper builds self-supervised graph learning around the idea that some nodes are equivalent. Such equivalence can come from graph structure, when swapping nodes preserves adjacency, or from identical node attributes. The authors argue that these relationships provide useful constraints on learned representations but receive insufficient attention in existing graph models.

Their framework, GALE, unifies structural and attribute equivalence into a shared class-based treatment. It encourages representations of nodes within a class to become more similar while separating representations across classes. Because exact structural equivalence is computationally difficult and node features can vary, the method uses approximate equivalence classes that can be constructed in linear time.

The paper also analyzes how message passing networks and graph transformers relate to these constraints, identifying limitations in both. It interprets graph contrastive learning as a degenerate form of the broader equivalence constraint. Reported improvements over baselines support the proposed framework. The contribution combines a practical training principle with a unified perspective on what relationships self-supervised graph representations should preserve.
summary.tldr: GALE uses approximate structural and attribute equivalence classes to guide self-supervised graph representations.

title: Equivalence is All: A Unified View for Self-supervised Graph Learning

abstract: Optimizing high-dimensional and complex black-box functions is crucial in numerous scientific applications. While Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful method for sample-efficient optimization, it struggles with the curse of dimensionality and scaling to thousands of evaluations. Recently, leveraging generative models to solve black-box optimization problems has emerged as a promising framework. However, those methods often underperform compared to BO methods due to limited expressivity and difficulty of uncertainty estimation in high-dimensional spaces. To overcome these issues, we introduce DiBO, a novel framework for solving high-dimensional black-box optimization problems. Our method iterates two stages. First, we train a diffusion model to capture the data distribution and deep ensembles to predict function values with uncertainty quantification. Second, we cast the candidate selection as a posterior inference problem to balance exploration and exploitation in high-dimensional spaces. Concretely, we fine-tune diffusion models to amortize posterior inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across synthetic and real-world tasks. Our code is publicly available https://github.com/umkiyoung/DiBO.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization searches for good inputs when the objective function must be evaluated rather than directly analyzed. High-dimensional problems make this search difficult, and Bayesian optimization can struggle with both dimensionality and large evaluation histories. DiBO combines generative modeling with uncertainty estimation to guide candidate selection in this setting.

The framework repeatedly alternates between two stages. First, a diffusion model learns the data distribution, while deep ensembles predict objective values and quantify uncertainty. Second, candidate selection becomes a posterior inference problem. This formulation balances exploitation of inputs that appear promising with exploration of regions where predictions remain uncertain.

DiBO fine-tunes its diffusion model to amortize posterior inference, placing the work of learning to generate candidates into the model. The design addresses both the expressiveness of the candidate generator and the uncertainty information needed to direct search. Experiments across synthetic and real-world tasks report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. These results support coupling diffusion generation with uncertainty-aware selection for the evaluated high-dimensional optimization problems.
summary.tldr: DiBO combines diffusion generation with ensemble uncertainty estimates to select promising candidates for high-dimensional black-box optimization.

title: Posterior Inference with Diffusion Models for High-dimensional Black-box Optimization

abstract: Machine learning community is discovering Contextual Integrity (CI) as a useful framework to assess the privacy implications of large language models (LLMs). This is an encouraging development.The CI theory emphasizes sharing information in accordance with *privacy norms* and can bridge the social, legal, political, and technical aspects essential for evaluating privacy in LLMs. However, this is also a good point to reflect on use of CI for LLMs. *This position paper argues that existing literature inadequately applies CI for LLMs without embracing the theory’s fundamental tenets.*Inadequate applications of CI could lead to incorrect conclusions and flawed privacy-preserving designs. We clarify the four fundamental tenets of CI theory, systematize prior work on whether they deviate from these tenets, and highlight overlooked issues in experimental hygiene for LLMs (e.g., prompt sensitivity, positional bias).

paragraphs: Contextual Integrity is a privacy framework centered on whether information is shared according to the norms of its context. This position paper welcomes its growing use in language model research because it can connect social, legal, political, and technical aspects of privacy. The concern is whether researchers are applying the framework faithfully.

The authors argue that existing work often uses Contextual Integrity without adopting its fundamental commitments. They clarify four core tenets and organize prior research according to whether it departs from those tenets. This makes the paper a structured examination of how a privacy theory is being translated into language model evaluation and design.

The paper also highlights experimental issues, including sensitivity to prompts and positional bias, that can undermine the interpretation of evaluations. Its central warning is that an incomplete application of the theory could produce mistaken conclusions or flawed privacy protections. The contribution is therefore both conceptual and methodological: clarify what the framework requires, then examine whether research designs and experiments support conclusions made in its name.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that language model privacy research often misapplies Contextual Integrity and needs stronger theoretical and experimental discipline.

title: Position: Contextual Integrity is Inadequately Applied to Language Models

abstract: Text-to-image generation models have achieved remarkable progress in preference optimization, yet achieving robust alignment across diverse reward models remains a significant challenge. Existing multi-reward fusion approaches rely on weighted summation, which is costly to tune and insufficient for balancing conflicting objectives. More critically, optimization with reward models is highly susceptible to reward hacking, where reward scores increase while the perceived quality of generated images deteriorates. We demonstrate that optimizing against a unified global target under heterogeneous reward upper bounds can induce reward hacking, a risk further exacerbated by the inherent instability of weak reward models. To mitigate this, we propose a Pareto Frontier-Guided Optimal Transport (PG-OT) framework. Our method constructs a prompt-specific Pareto frontier and maps dominated samples toward it via distribution-aware optimal transport. Furthermore, we develop both online and offline optimization strategies tailored to diverse reward signal characteristics. To provide a more rigorous assessment, we introduce the Joint Domination Rate (JDR) and Joint Collapse Rate (JCR) as principled metrics to quantify multi-reward synergy and reward hacking. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms strong baselines with an 11% gain in JDR and achieves a near 80% win rate in human evaluations.

paragraphs: Aligning image generators with several reward models is difficult when their objectives conflict. Weighted sums require tuning, and rising reward scores can accompany declining perceived image quality. The paper shows that a shared global target can induce this reward hacking when reward upper bounds differ, with weak reward models adding instability.

Pareto Frontier-Guided Optimal Transport constructs a separate Pareto frontier for each prompt. This frontier captures reward trade-offs among samples that are not dominated by others. The method then uses distribution-aware optimal transport to move dominated samples toward that frontier. It provides both online and offline optimization strategies for different reward-signal characteristics.

The authors introduce Joint Domination Rate and Joint Collapse Rate to assess multi-reward synergy and reward hacking. Their experiments report an 11% gain in Joint Domination Rate over strong baselines and a human-evaluation win rate near 80%. These findings support using prompt-specific reward trade-offs to guide optimization, rather than forcing heterogeneous rewards toward one global target.
summary.tldr: PG-OT aligns image generators using prompt-specific Pareto frontiers to balance rewards and mitigate reward hacking.

title: Pareto-Guided Optimal Transport for Multi-Reward Alignment

abstract: Inference-time compute has re-emerged as a practical way to improve LLM reasoning. Most test-time scaling (TTS) algorithms rely on autoregressive decoding, which is ill-suited to discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) due to their parallel decoding over the entire sequence. As a result, developing effective and efficient TTS methods to unlock dLLMs’ full generative potential remains an underexplored challenge. To address this, we propose LLaDA-S, an efficient TTS framework for dLLMs that (i) performs Hierarchical Trajectory Search (HTS) which dynamically prunes and reallocates compute in an early-to-mid denoising window, (ii) replaces external verifiers with Self-Verified Feedback (SVF) obtained via self-evaluation prompts on intermediate completions, and (iii) introduces Local branching with partial remasking to explore diverse implementations while preserving a high-confidence tokens. Across four mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks on three dLLMs, including LLaDA 8B Instruct, Dream 7B Instruct, and LLaDA 2.0-mini, our LLaDA-S achieves a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off, matching best-of-$N$ performance with substantially fewer function evaluations (NFE). The code will be released.

paragraphs: Spending more computation during inference can improve language-model reasoning, but many search strategies assume tokens are generated sequentially. Discrete diffusion language models instead decode across the sequence in parallel. This paper introduces LLaDA-S, a framework that allocates additional inference computation around that different generation process.

Its hierarchical trajectory search prunes candidates and reallocates computation during an early-to-middle portion of denoising. Intermediate completions are assessed through self-evaluation prompts, providing feedback without an external verifier. The framework also branches locally by partially remasking a candidate, preserving high-confidence tokens while exploring alternatives in other parts of the sequence.

The evaluation spans four mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks and three diffusion language models: LLaDA 8B Instruct, Dream 7B Instruct, and LLaDA 2.0-mini. The authors report performance matching best-of-N selection with substantially fewer function evaluations. The result supports adapting search to diffusion trajectories, using selective branching and self-verification to obtain useful reasoning gains without fully exploring every candidate.
summary.tldr: LLaDA-S combines hierarchical search, self-verification, and partial remasking to improve diffusion-language-model inference efficiency.

title: PRISM: Efficient Test-Time Scaling via Hierarchical Search and Self-Verification for Discrete Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Many striking phenomena in deep learning, such as linear mode connectivity and the structured behavior of training dynamics, are closely tied to parameter symmetries: transformations that leave the realized function unchanged. Despite growing attention to parameter symmetries, the exact interplay between parameters, data, and representations remains underexplored. To investigate this, we develop a theoretical framework of effective function classes, i.e., the set of functions a neuron can realize on its input support, and the norm cost of realizing them. We then formalize effective symmetry breaking via neuron identifiability across independent training runs. Our analysis shows that neural networks can admit large families of approximately equivalent solutions even in structurally asymmetric models. We further show that neuron identifiability enables representation merging without prior alignment, and characterize when such merging admits a linear low-loss path. These findings highlight the role of effective function classes in affecting the loss landscape.

paragraphs: Different neural-network parameter settings can represent the same function, making parameter symmetry relevant to how training behaves and how solutions connect. This paper investigates that relationship beyond symmetries visible in the network’s architecture. Its focus is how the data a neuron receives and the representations it learns affect which solutions are effectively equivalent.

The authors introduce effective function classes: the functions a neuron can realize on its input support, together with the norm cost of realizing them. They use this framework to formalize effective symmetry breaking through neuron identifiability across independent training runs. Their analysis shows that even structurally asymmetric networks can contain large families of approximately equivalent solutions.

The framework also connects identifiability to model merging. The authors show that identifiable neurons enable representations to be merged without a separate prior alignment step, and characterize when the merge admits a straight path through parameter space with low loss. This is a conditional characterization of linear connectivity. It explains why architectural symmetry alone does not determine the structure of the loss landscape.
summary.tldr: A theory of neuron function classes explains approximate solution equivalence and identifies when representations can merge along a linear low-loss path without prior alignment.

title: Beyond Structural Symmetries: Linear Mode Connectivity via Neuron Identifiability

abstract: While scaling laws guide compute allocation for LLM pre-training, analogous prescriptions for reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of LLMs remain poorly understood. We study the compute-optimal allocation of sampling compute for on-policy RL methods in LLMs, framing scaling as a compute-constrained optimization over three resources: parallel rollouts per problem, number of problems per batch, and number of update steps. We find that the compute-optimal number of parallel rollouts per problem increases predictably with compute budget and then saturates. This trend holds across both easy and hard problems, though driven by different mechanisms: solution sharpening on easy problems and coverage expansion on hard problems. We further show that increasing the number of parallel rollouts mitigates interference across problems, while the number of problems per batch primarily affects training stability and can be chosen within a broad range. Validated across base models and data distributions, our results recast RL scaling laws as prescriptive allocation rules and provide practical guidance for compute-efficient LLM RL post-training.

paragraphs: A fixed sampling budget for language-model reinforcement learning can be spent on more attempts per problem, more problems per batch, or more update steps. This paper studies how to allocate that budget for on-policy training. It frames these choices as a constrained optimization problem, seeking useful allocation rules rather than simply recommending more computation.

The authors find that the compute-optimal number of parallel rollouts per problem rises predictably with the available budget and eventually saturates. The pattern appears for both easy and hard problems, but with different explanations: sharpening solutions on easy problems and expanding solution coverage on hard ones. These distinctions connect the allocation rule to what additional samples accomplish.

More parallel rollouts also reduce interference across problems, while the number of problems in a batch mainly influences training stability and can vary over a broad range. Validation across base models and data distributions supports the practical usefulness of these findings. The resulting guidance treats rollout count as a budget-dependent decision and batch problem count as a comparatively flexible stability choice.
summary.tldr: The study finds budget-dependent rules for allocating RL sampling compute, with optimal rollouts per problem increasing and then saturating.

title: IsoCompute Playbook: Optimally Scaling Sampling Compute for LLM RL

abstract: To define a steepest descent method over a neural network, we need to choose a norm for each layer, a way to aggregate these norms across layers, and whether to use normalization. We systematically explore different alternatives for aggregating norms across layers, both formalizing existing combinations of Adam and the recently proposed Muon as a type of non-Euclidean gradient descent, and deriving new variants of the Muon optimizer. Through a comprehensive experimental evaluation of the optimizers within our framework, we find that Muon is sensitive to the choice of learning rate, whereas a new variant we call MuonMax is significantly more robust. We then show how to combine any non-Euclidean gradient method with model based momentum (known as Momo). The new Momo variants of Muon are significantly more robust to hyperparameter tuning, and often achieve a better validation score. Thus for new tasks, where the optimal hyperparameters are not known, we advocate for using Momo in combination with MuonMax to save on costly hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: Defining the steepest update for a neural network requires choices about how to measure changes within each layer and how to combine those measurements across layers. This paper systematically studies those choices, including normalization. Its framework interprets existing Adam–Muon combinations as forms of non-Euclidean gradient descent and generates additional optimizer variants.

The experiments find that Muon's performance is sensitive to the learning rate. A newly derived variant, MuonMax, is substantially more robust to that choice. This result connects an abstract design decision about combining layer norms to a practical training concern: how much performance depends on selecting the right optimization settings.

The authors also show how to combine non-Euclidean gradient methods with model-based momentum, called Momo. Their Momo versions of Muon are more robust to hyperparameter tuning and often obtain better validation scores. They consequently recommend Momo with MuonMax for new tasks where good settings are unknown. The recommendation rests on the reported robustness findings and aims to reduce costly tuning, rather than guaranteeing the best score for every task.
summary.tldr: A unified view of non-Euclidean optimizers yields MuonMax and momentum variants that reduce sensitivity to hyperparameter choices.

title: An Exploration of Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent: Muon and its Many Variants

abstract: While decoders have rapidly scaled, encoders have remained largely unchanged since BERT. We revisit this disparity by frozen backbone evaluation via probing. Under this lens, the representations of BERT encoders become increasingly unexploitable by frozen probes, despite improved perplexity. The misalignment originates in BERT’s flat design, which couples representation learning to the token reconstruction loss. We propose CrossBERT, a two-part architecture that separates the learning of high-quality encoded representations from the rigid grounding of token reconstruction. This design further enables high masking ratios ($\geq 50$%) and gradient collection over all tokens via a Complementary Masking Strategy, respectively increasing throughput by $1.5$ to $2\times$ and sample efficiency by $2\times$. Overall, CrossBERT demonstrates monotonic scaling and superior performance on MTEB(eng, v2) and frozen GLUE benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why text encoders have not scaled like decoders. Using probes with frozen backbones, the authors find that BERT representations become harder for those probes to exploit even as perplexity improves. This exposes a mismatch between improving token reconstruction and producing representations useful under the frozen evaluation setup.

CrossBERT addresses the mismatch with a two-part architecture that separates representation learning from token reconstruction. The design allows masking ratios of at least 50%, while a Complementary Masking Strategy gathers gradients across all tokens. These mechanisms target training throughput and sample efficiency alongside the quality of the encoded representations.

The abstract reports throughput gains of 1.5–2 times and a twofold improvement in sample efficiency from these respective mechanisms. CrossBERT also shows monotonic scaling and superior results on MTEB English version 2 and frozen GLUE evaluations. The findings support separating the two learning roles when scaling encoders, with the original diagnosis specifically grounded in how usable representations are to frozen-backbone probes.
summary.tldr: CrossBERT separates representation learning from token reconstruction, improving encoder scaling, throughput, and sample efficiency in the reported evaluations.

title: Separating Representation from Reconstruction Enables Scalable Text Encoders

abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) to heterogeneous and rapidly evolving safety requirements remains a critical challenge. Existing instruction-tuned LLMs and standalone safety classifiers often fail to generalize to new safety configurations, motivating the need for Reward Models (RMs) that are explicitly configurable to changing specifications. We introduce the Configurable Safety Reward Model (CSRM), which is jointly optimized for calibrated safety compliance and reward modeling. Our approach is supported by configuration-targeted data augmentation that enforces instruction adherence while preserving relative severity structure. The resulting RM is sensitive to fine-grained safety configurations and conversational nuances, substantially improving generalization to previously unseen safety configurations. CSRM achieves state-of-the-art performance on recent configurable safety benchmarks, including CoSApien (94.6% F1) and DynaBench (75.8% F1), without requiring additional human annotation. When used for downstream safety alignment, CSRM yields LLMs with a significantly improved helpfulness–safety tradeoff compared to existing baselines.

paragraphs: Safety requirements differ across applications and can change over time, making a fixed judgment of acceptable behavior insufficient for some alignment tasks. This paper introduces the Configurable Safety Reward Model, or CSRM, to score responses according to supplied safety specifications. The goal is to support changing requirements while retaining the ability to provide useful training rewards.

CSRM is trained jointly for calibrated safety compliance and reward modeling. Its data augmentation targets particular configurations, encouraging the model to follow their instructions while preserving distinctions in the severity of violations. This connects sensitivity to the requested rules with sensitivity to conversational context, rather than treating every safety decision as an isolated, uniform classification.

The authors report improved generalization to unseen safety configurations and state-of-the-art results of 94.6% F1 on CoSApien and 75.8% F1 on DynaBench, without additional human annotation. Using CSRM for downstream alignment also improves the helpfulness–safety tradeoff against the evaluated baselines. The findings indicate that configurable reward judgments can translate into better aligned model behavior.
summary.tldr: CSRM learns configurable safety rewards that generalize to unseen specifications and improve the helpfulness–safety tradeoff in downstream alignment.

title: Configurable Reward Model for Balanced Safety Alignment

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled rapid progress in automatic heuristic discovery (AHD), yet most existing methods are predominantly limited by static evaluation against fixed instance distributions, leading to potential overfitting and poor generalization under distributional shifts. We propose Algorithm Space Response Oracles (ASRO), a game-theoretic framework that reframes heuristic discovery as a program level co-evolution between solver and instance generator. ASRO models their interaction as a two-player zero-sum game, maintains growing strategy pools on both sides, and iteratively expands them via LLM-based best-response oracles against mixed opponent meta-strategies, thereby replacing static evaluation with an adaptive, self-generated curriculum. Across multiple combinatorial optimization domains, ASRO consistently outperforms static-training AHD baselines built on the same program search mechanisms, achieving substantially improved generalization and robustness on diverse and out-of-distribution instances.

paragraphs: LLMs can help discover programs that solve optimization problems, but evaluating every candidate against a fixed distribution of instances can encourage overfitting. A heuristic may become effective on familiar instances while generalizing poorly when the distribution changes. Algorithm Space Response Oracles, or ASRO, addresses this by making the training challenges evolve alongside the solver.

The framework represents solver programs and instance-generator programs as opposing players in a two-player zero-sum game. It maintains growing collections of strategies for both sides. LLM-based response oracles propose new programs against mixtures of the opponent’s existing strategies, allowing the interaction to create an adaptive curriculum instead of relying on a static evaluation set.

Across multiple combinatorial optimization domains, ASRO consistently outperforms static-training heuristic-discovery baselines that use the same underlying program-search mechanisms. The authors report substantially better generalization and robustness on diverse and out-of-distribution instances. This comparison supports the value of changing how candidate programs encounter challenges, while keeping the underlying search machinery comparable.
summary.tldr: ASRO co-evolves solver and instance-generator programs to improve the generalization of LLM-discovered optimization heuristics.

title: Game-Theoretic Co-Evolution for LLM-Based Heuristic Discovery

abstract: We propose a unified framework to enhance the power of online multiple hypothesis testing procedures based on $e$-values. While $e$-value-based methods offer robust online False Discovery Rate (FDR) control under minimal assumptions, they often suffer from power loss by discarding evidence that exceeds the rejection threshold. We address this inefficiency via the Sequential Control with Overshoot Refund for E-values (SCORE) framework, which leverages the inequality $\mathbb{I}(y \ge 1) \le y - (y-1)_+$, valid for all $y\ge 0$, to reclaim this otherwise “wasted” evidence. This simple yet powerful insight yields a unified principle for improving a broad class of online testing algorithms. Building on this framework, we develop SCORE-enhanced versions of several state-of-the-art procedures, including SCORE-LOND, SCORE-LORD, and SCORE-SAFFRON, all of which strictly dominate their original counterparts while preserving valid finite-sample FDR control. Furthermore, under mild assumptions, SCORE permits retroactive updates of alpha-wealth by using the latest decision twice: first to determine its reward or loss, and then to refresh past wealth. Such a mechanism enables more aggressive testing strategies while maintaining valid FDR control, thereby further improving statistical power. The effectiveness of the proposed methods is validated through extensive simulation and real-data experiments.

paragraphs: Online multiple testing makes a sequence of decisions while controlling the false discovery rate. Methods based on e-values provide this control under minimal assumptions, but they can lose power by discarding evidence beyond the rejection threshold. SCORE introduces a shared accounting principle for recovering that excess evidence and using it to support subsequent testing.

The framework uses an inequality that separates the contribution needed for a rejection from the amount by which evidence exceeds the threshold. This overshoot becomes a refund rather than being wasted. The authors develop SCORE versions of LOND, LORD, and SAFFRON, proving that these procedures strictly dominate their original counterparts while retaining valid finite-sample false discovery rate control.

Under mild assumptions, SCORE also permits retroactive updates to alpha-wealth, the accounting resource governing testing aggressiveness. The latest decision first determines a reward or loss and then refreshes past wealth. This enables more aggressive tests while preserving error control. Simulations and real-data experiments validate the proposed methods, complementing the theoretical guarantees with evidence of improved statistical power.
summary.tldr: SCORE recovers excess e-value evidence to improve online testing power while preserving finite-sample false discovery rate control.

title: SCORE: A Unified Framework for Overshoot Refund in Online FDR Control

abstract: Parity functions are fundamental Boolean operations with critical applications across machine learning, cryptography, and error correction. Yet, learning high-dimensional parity functions poses significant challenges: in a general setting, standard neural network architectures typically require exponential sample complexity, making gradient-based optimization intractable for large number of inputs $N$. We demonstrate that compact product-based neural architectures combined with stochastic data sparsity (Bernoulli inputs with $p_e \leq 1/N$) and appropriate hyperparameter choice enable efficient parity learning, with theoretical guarantees of convergence. Experiments validate our theory across dimensions up to $N = 100{,}000$, with empirical evidence showing optimal hyperparameter choices for $p_e$ and learning rate $\alpha$, as well as polynomial complexity scaling laws. This work establishes fundamental connections between architectural inductive bias and data sparsity, opening new possibilities for neural arithmetic, structured reasoning, binary neural networks, and machine learning applied to automated protocol discovery.

The architectural choice and input distribution work together: the claim concerns this combination of product structure, stochastic sparsity, and suitable training settings.

The work connects architectural inductive bias with data sparsity and suggests possible applications in neural arithmetic, structured reasoning, binary networks, and automated protocol discovery.
summary.tldr: Compact product networks can learn high-dimensional parity efficiently under sparse Bernoulli inputs and suitable hyperparameter choices.

title: Learning High-Dimensional Parity Functions with Product Networks using Gradient Descent

abstract: This paper studies causal discovery in irregularly sampled time series—a key challenge in risk-sensitive domains like finance, healthcare, and climate science, where missing data and inconsistent sampling frequencies distort causal mechanisms. The main challenge comes from the interdependence between missing data imputation and causal structure recovery: errors in imputation and structure learning can reinforce each other, leading to an inaccurate causal graph. Existing methods either impute first and then discover, or jointly optimize both via neural representation learning, but lack explicit mechanisms to ensure mutual consistency of imputation and structure learning. We address this challenge with ReTimeCausal, an EM-based framework that alternates between imputation and structure learning, which encourages structural consistency throughout the optimization process. Our framework provides theoretical consistency guarantees for structure recovery and extends classical results to settings with irregular sampling and high missingness. ReTimeCausal combines kernel-based sparse regression and structural constraints in an alternating process that updates the completed data and the causal graph in turn. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that ReTimeCausal is more effective than existing methods under challenging irregular sampling and missing data.

paragraphs: Learning causal relationships from time series becomes harder when observations arrive at uneven intervals or are missing. Filling gaps requires assumptions about how variables relate, while discovering those relationships depends on the filled values. Errors can reinforce each other: an inaccurate completion can suggest a misleading causal graph, which can then encourage further inaccurate completions.

ReTimeCausal addresses this dependence through an expectation-maximization framework that alternates between completing the data and learning causal structure. It combines kernel-based sparse regression with structural constraints, updating each part in light of the other. The aim is to encourage agreement between the completed observations and the relationships inferred from them throughout optimization.

The paper provides theoretical consistency guarantees for structure recovery, extending classical results to irregular sampling and substantial missingness. It also reports better performance than existing methods on synthetic and real-world datasets under challenging sampling conditions. The contribution connects the two estimation problems explicitly, with theoretical and empirical support for the resulting recovery process.
summary.tldr: ReTimeCausal alternates missing-data completion and causal graph learning to encourage consistency when time series are irregularly sampled.

title: Causal Discovery for Irregularly Time Series with Consistency Guarantees

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show promise for Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) but often remain unreliable because sparse emotional cues could be easily overwhelmed and affected by redundant context. While fine-tuning is effective, it is usually costly when using large models. Training-free methods like chain-of-thought reasoning provide a practical alternative, but they mostly rely on heuristic prompting to influence the model behaviors and do not explicitly focus on emotion relevant tokens internally, which would allow decision-relevant emotional tokens to be diluted by environmental noise, resulting in unstable predictions. To address this limitation without training, we rethink MER from a world-model perspective that treats emotion as a latent state inferred from noisy and redundant multimodal observations. Under frozen parameters, this view suggests that robustness depends on constraining why and how tokens contribute to inference. Based on this insight, we propose WETR (World-Model inspired Emotion-aware Token Refinement), a training-free, plug-and-play regulator that reshapes token usage through two mechanisms: Noise-suppressed Token Selection (NTS), which suppresses redundant intra-modal noise, and State-strengthened Token Reweighting (STR), which amplifies decision-relevant emotional tokens. Experiments on multiple MER benchmarks demonstrate that WETR consistently improves accuracy and stability under frozen parameters, which also improves token-level interpretability.

paragraphs: Emotional signals can occupy only a small part of a multimodal input, leaving them vulnerable to being overwhelmed by irrelevant context. This paper approaches emotion recognition as inference about a hidden emotional state from noisy observations. That perspective motivates controlling which tokens contribute to a prediction while leaving the model’s parameters frozen.

World-Model inspired Emotion-aware Token Refinement, or WETR, implements that control through two mechanisms. Noise-suppressed Token Selection reduces redundant information within each modality. State-strengthened Token Reweighting increases the influence of tokens relevant to the emotional decision. Together, they reshape how the existing model uses its input without requiring additional training.

Experiments on multiple emotion-recognition benchmarks report consistent improvements in accuracy and stability, alongside better token-level interpretability. The contribution goes beyond prompting the model to reason more carefully: it directly regulates token selection and weighting so sparse emotional evidence receives more useful attention. The findings support this as a practical way to improve frozen models when costly fine-tuning is undesirable and irrelevant context would otherwise dilute the evidence.
summary.tldr: WETR improves emotion recognition without training by suppressing noisy tokens and strengthening emotionally relevant ones.

title: World-Model Inspired Emotion-aware Token Refinement for Training-Free Multimodal Emotion Recognition

abstract: We study optimization over non-convex constraint sets that are homeomorphic to a ball, encompassing important problem classes such as star-shaped sets that frequently arise in machine learning and engineering applications. We propose Hom-PGD$^+$, a learning-based and projection-efficient first-order method that efficiently solves such problems without requiring expensive projection or optimization oracles. Our approach leverages an invertible neural network (INN) to learn the homeomorphism between the non-convex constraint set and a unit ball, transforming the original problem into an equivalent ball-constrained optimization where projections admit efficient solutions. We establish that Hom-PGD$^+$ achieves an $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ convergence rate to an ($\epsilon + \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{inn}}})$)-approximate stationary solution, where $\epsilon_{\text{inn}}$ denotes the homeomorphism learning error. This rate significantly improves upon existing methods for optimization over non-convex sets, while maintaining a per-iteration complexity of only $\mathcal{O}(W)$ for $W$ INN parameters. Extensive experiments, including QCQP, chance-constrained power-system optimization, and non-uniform adversarial attacks, demonstrate that Hom-PGD$^+$ achieves competitive solution quality while delivering speedups of up to one order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Optimization becomes expensive when keeping each update inside a complicated constraint set requires a difficult projection. Hom-PGD+ studies non-convex sets that are homeomorphic to a ball: their geometry permits a continuous, reversible correspondence with a ball. This class includes star-shaped sets encountered in machine learning and engineering.

The method trains an invertible neural network to learn that correspondence. It then expresses the optimization problem in ball coordinates, where projecting an update back into the allowed region is efficient. This reparameterization replaces expensive projection or optimization oracles with computations through the learned network, with per-iteration complexity linear in its number of parameters.

The convergence rate is O(ε⁻²) to an approximately stationary solution, with accuracy ε plus a term proportional to the square root of the mapping’s learning error. Thus mapping quality directly affects the guarantee. Experiments on quadratically constrained quadratic programs, chance-constrained power systems, and non-uniform adversarial attacks report competitive solution quality and speedups of up to an order of magnitude.
summary.tldr: Hom-PGD+ learns an invertible mapping to a ball to make constrained optimization faster, with accuracy depending on mapping error.

title: Hom-PGD$^+$: Fast Reparameterized Optimization over Non-convex Ball-Homeomorphic Set

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly acquiring capabilities relevant to biological research, from literature synthesis to interpretation of experimental data. Increasingly, LLM agents can also perform in silico biology tasks that previously required experienced human biologists. These emerging AI capabilities offer new opportunities for scientific discovery and biomedical advances, but they also shift the landscape of biosecurity risks. To address this, we introduce the Agentic Bio-Capabilities Benchmark (ABC-Bench), a suite of tasks to measure agentic biosecurity-relevant capabilities. ABC-Bench evaluates LLM agents on both benign and dual-use biology tasks: writing code to operate liquid handling robots, designing DNA fragments for in vitro assembly, and evading DNA synthesis screening. These tasks require a combination of biology and software expertise. All tested LLM agents outperformed the median expert human baseliner on all three tasks. Agents performed highly on tasks drawing on published knowledge and well-documented protocols, and more weakly on a task requiring novel bioinformatics reasoning. In three wet-lab validation experiments, we found that OpenAI’s o4-mini-high produced scripts that, when run on an OpenTrons liquid handling robot, successfully assembled DNA with expected sequences.

These results connect benchmark performance to demonstrated laboratory execution, while the weaker novel-reasoning result distinguishes established-knowledge use from more original problem solving.
summary.tldr: ABC-Bench finds that tested agents exceed median expert baselines on three biosecurity-relevant tasks, with selected robot-control outputs validated in the laboratory.

title: ABC-Bench: An Agentic Bio-Capabilities Benchmark for Biosecurity

abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) is inherently multi-dimensional, yet existing reward models are typically limited to a single task and become unstable when extended to multi-task settings. In particular, heterogeneous reward scales and variances across tasks can lead to conflicting optimization signals during reinforcement learning. We propose VisualScore, a unified visual evaluation framework that formulates multi-task IQA as structured, task-aware reasoning followed by continuous reward optimization. VisualScore produces interpretable rationales together with scalar quality scores under explicit evaluation principles. We construct a reasoning-enhanced reward modeling dataset via rejection sampling and initialize the model through supervised fine-tuning. VisualScore is then optimized with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using a Gaussian-based continuous reward. To address multi-task reward conflicts and stabilize training, we introduce standard deviation filtering and entropy gating to normalize task-wise reward signals and suppress noisy updates. Experiments on technical quality, aesthetic quality, and text–image alignment show that VisualScore improves robustness, generalization, and interpretability, and can effectively guide text-to-image generation at test time without retraining.
