summary.tldr: VisualScore learns explanations and numerical image-quality scores across tasks while controlling reward conflicts during reinforcement learning.

title: VisualScore: Learning Holistic Visual Quality Scores via Multi-Task Reasoning

abstract: Self-attention is often viewed as probabilistic query-key lookup, motivating designs that preserve normalized attention scores and fixed positional semantics. We advocate a simpler and more unified perspective: an autoregressive attention head can be viewed as a dynamic two-layer MLP whose weights are instantiated from the context history. From this view, attention scores form an ever-growing hidden representation, and standard MLP activations such as ReLU or GLU naturally implement input-conditioned selection over a context-dependent memory pool rather than a probability distribution. Based on this formulation, we introduce HyperMLP and HyperGLU, which learn dynamic mixing in both feature space and sequence space, using a reverse-offset (lag) layout to align temporal mixing with autoregressive semantics. We provide theoretical characterizations of the expressivity and implications of this structure, and empirically show that HyperMLP/HyperGLU consistently outperform strong softmax-attention baselines under matched parameter budgets.

paragraphs: Self-attention is usually described as a query looking up keys through normalized scores. This paper develops another interpretation: an autoregressive attention head acts like a two-layer neural network whose weights are constructed from the preceding context. As the context grows, so does the intermediate representation associated with attention scores.

Under this view, standard activations such as ReLU or GLU can select information from context-dependent memory without making the selection weights a probability distribution. HyperMLP and HyperGLU build on this formulation by learning dynamic mixing across both features and sequence positions. A reverse-offset layout organizes temporal mixing by lag, aligning it with the autoregressive use of preceding context.

The paper provides theoretical characterizations of this structure’s expressive capacity and implications. Empirically, both models consistently outperform strong softmax-attention baselines with matched parameter budgets. These findings support the proposed interpretation as an architectural design principle: viewing attention through familiar neural-network operations leads to alternatives that improve sequence modeling in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: HyperMLP and HyperGLU reinterpret attention as a context-generated neural network and outperform matched-budget softmax-attention baselines in reported experiments.

title: HyperMLP: An Integrated Perspective for Sequence Modeling

abstract: We propose CRAFT, a red-teaming alignment framework that leverages model reasoning capabilities and hidden representations to improve robustness against jailbreak attacks. Unlike prior defenses that operate primarily at the output level, CRAFT aligns large reasoning models to generate safety-aware reasoning traces by explicitly optimizing objectives defined over the hidden state space. Methodologically, CRAFT integrates contrastive representation learning with reinforcement learning to separate safe and unsafe reasoning trajectories, yielding a latent-space geometry that supports robust, reasoning-level safety alignment. Theoretically, we show that incorporating latent–textual consistency into GRPO eliminates superficially aligned policies by ruling them out as local optima. Empirically, we evaluate CRAFT on multiple safety benchmarks using two strong reasoning models, Qwen3-4B-Thinking and R1-Distill-Llama-8B, where it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art defenses such as IPO and SafeKey. Notably, CRAFT delivers an average 79.0% improvement in reasoning safety and 87.7% improvement in final-response safety over the base models, demonstrating the effectiveness of hidden-space reasoning alignment.

paragraphs: CRAFT aims to make reasoning models more robust to jailbreak attacks by training the internal representations associated with their reasoning. Its objectives operate in hidden-state space as well as addressing safety-aware reasoning traces. The motivation is to align the reasoning process that leads to a response, extending safety training beyond the final text a model produces.

The framework combines contrastive representation learning with reinforcement learning. It separates representations of safe and unsafe reasoning trajectories, shaping the model’s internal geometry around that distinction. The theoretical analysis shows that adding consistency between latent representations and text to GRPO rules out superficially aligned policies as local optima. This is a statement about the optimization formulation, rather than an unconditional guarantee against every attack.

summary.tldr: CRAFT combines contrastive learning and reinforcement learning in hidden-state space to improve reasoning-model safety against jailbreaks.

title: Contrastive Reasoning Alignment: Reinforcement Learning from Hidden Representations

abstract: Current repository agents encounter a reasoning disconnect due to fragmented representations, as existing methods rely on isolated API documentation or dependency graphs that lack semantic depth. We consider repository comprehension and generation to be inverse processes within a unified cycle: generation expands intent into implementation, while comprehension compresses implementation back into intent. To address this, we propose RPG-Encoder, a framework that generalizes the Repository Planning Graph (RPG) from a static generative blueprint into a unified, high-fidelity representation. RPG-Encoder closes the reasoning loop through three mechanisms: (1) Encoding raw code into the RPG that combines lifted semantic features with code dependencies; (2) Evolving the topology incrementally to decouple maintenance costs from repository scale, reducing overhead by 95.7%; and (3) Operating as a unified interface for structure-aware navigation. In evaluations, RPG-Encoder establishes state-of-the-art repository understanding on SWE-bench Verified with 93.7% Acc@5 and exceeds the best baseline by over 10% on SWE-bench Live. These results highlight our superior fine-grained localization accuracy in complex codebases. Furthermore, it achieves 98.5% reconstruction coverage on RepoCraft, confirming RPG’s high-fidelity capacity to mirror the original codebase and closing the loop between intent and implementation. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/microsoft/RPG-ZeroRepo.

title: Closing the Loop: Universal Repository Representation with RPG-Encoder

abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improves large language models (LLMs) on difficult reasoning tasks, but it often incurs long natural-language rationales that are poorly aligned with efficient machine reasoning. We propose Communicative Language Symbolism Routing (CLSR), a test-time framework in which multiple LLM agents autonomously invent, evolve, and share compact Language Symbolism Frameworks (LSFs), while a latent-free router adaptively selects and composes these languages per query to optimize the accuracy–token trade-off. Unlike prompt optimization that refines surface instructions, CLSR treats each LSF as a reusable symbolic protocol with compact symbols, usage rules, and a message-passing contract, and improves it through an evolutionary loop driven by correctness and token cost. At inference time, the router may invoke a single low-cost LSF call, ensemble multiple LSFs, or execute a multi-round LSF composition protocol on harder queries. Across challenging benchmarks, CLSR reduces latency-oriented generated token completion by $3\sim 6\times$ compared to standard CoT while maintaining accuracy. We further derive an information-theoretic lower bound on token cost under arbitrary symbolism and show that, under an interpreter-realizability premise, multi-round LSF protocols conditionally subsume program-execution pipelines.

paragraphs: Natural-language reasoning traces can become lengthy even when they help solve difficult problems. CLSR investigates whether multiple language-model agents can communicate through compact symbolic protocols instead. Each protocol includes symbols, usage rules, and a message-passing contract that can be reused across queries.

Its claim that multiround protocols subsume program-execution pipelines is conditional on an interpreter-realizability premise. The empirical and theoretical results therefore address both practical compression and the conditions governing symbolic protocol capabilities.
summary.tldr: CLSR evolves and routes compact symbolic communication protocols, reducing reported reasoning-token use three- to sixfold while maintaining accuracy.

title: When LLMs Develop Languages: Symbolic Communication for Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning

abstract: This paper introduces a rigorous framework for defining generative diffusion models in infinite dimensions via Doob’s h-transform. Rather than relying on time reversal of a noising process, a reference diffusion is forced towards the target distribution by an exponential change of measure. Compared to existing methodology, this approach readily generalises to the infinite-dimensional setting, hence offering greater flexibility in the diffusion model. The construction is derived rigorously under verifiable conditions, and bounds with respect to the target measure are established. We show that the forced process under the changed measure can be approximated by minimising a score-matching objective and validate our method on both synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical foundation for generative diffusion models in infinite-dimensional settings. Its starting point is a reference diffusion process whose behavior is modified to move toward a target distribution. The construction uses Doob's h-transform rather than building generation through time reversal of a process that adds noise.

The key operation is an exponential change of measure: it changes how possible trajectories of the reference process are weighted. Under the new measure, the process is directed toward the desired distribution. The authors derive this construction under verifiable conditions and establish bounds relative to the target measure, connecting the proposed dynamics to their intended statistical outcome.

The paper also shows that the modified process can be approximated by minimizing a score-matching objective, providing a route from the mathematical construction to a learnable model. Validation uses synthetic and real data. The contribution is a rigorous alternative formulation that extends readily to infinite dimensions and allows greater flexibility in the diffusion model.
summary.tldr: Doob's h-transform provides a rigorous, score-matchable construction of generative diffusions that extends to infinite dimensions.

title: Infinite-Dimensional Generative Diffusions via Doob’s h-Transform

abstract: Conventional practice assumes that online reinforcement learning for flow-matching models requires sampling full denoising trajectories to compute rewards. This assumption underlies methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), where the policy must traverse the entire reverse process before receiving a delayed, trajectory-level reward. We observe, however, that while such terminal rewards provide feedback, they are neither necessary nor optimal for effective learning. In this work, we introduce iGRPO (Instant-reward GRPO), which replaces GRPO’s full-trajectory rollouts with a single-step mapping that assigns rewards instantly at each denoising step. Because the flow matching model behaves differently across timesteps, our step-local instant rewards which are inherently time-dependent, overcome prior approaches that rely on a single, time-independent terminal reward. By evaluating each action locally rather than relying on a final terminal score, iGRPO eliminates the need for multi-step SDE rollouts and offers more precise credit assignment. Across standard benchmarks, iGRPO converges 10.2$\times$ faster than FlowGRPO while achieving higher final alignment quality. We hope this work motivates more efficient and scalable online RL methods for flow-matching generative models.

paragraphs: Online reinforcement learning for flow-matching models commonly waits for an entire denoising trajectory before assigning a reward. This makes feedback expensive to obtain and ties individual actions to a score for the completed generation. The paper challenges the assumption that effective learning requires this full-trajectory evaluation.

Its method, iGRPO, replaces full rollouts with a single-step mapping that supplies an immediate reward at each denoising step. These rewards depend on the timestep, reflecting that the model behaves differently at different stages of generation. This is evidence that reducing the delay and cost of reward computation can improve both efficiency and the learned result in the tested setting. The contribution centers on changing where feedback is assigned, making individual denoising decisions directly evaluable during online learning.
summary.tldr: iGRPO assigns timestep-dependent rewards to individual denoising actions, achieving faster convergence and better final alignment than FlowGRPO on evaluated benchmarks.

title: iGRPO: Fast Online RL for Flow Matching Model with Instant Reward

abstract: Current Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit remarkable general capabilities but significantly underperform in spatial reasoning tasks. Existing approaches treat this gap as a knowledge deficit, relying on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to ingest labeled data from external vision sources or synthetic engines. In contrast, we argue that for many tasks, spatial capabilities are already present in pre-trained LRMs but require alignment through principles of internal logical coherence. In this work, we propose a self-supervised reinforcement learning (RL) framework that targets the internal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process without requiring ground-truth annotations. By formalizing the notion of consistency verifiers—reward functions that check for geometric and semantic consistency under transformations like flipping or swapping the order of objects in the question—and optimizing them via our new OT-GRPO strategy, a minimal-consistency matching variant of group relative policy optimization, we demonstrate that models can self-correct their spatial logic. Our results show that this label-free consistency training approaches the accuracy of models trained with ground-truth supervision and achieves similar generalization across diverse tasks and domains.

paragraphs: Large reasoning models can struggle with spatial tasks despite their broad capabilities. This paper argues that, for many tasks, relevant spatial abilities already exist in pretrained models but need better internal alignment. It investigates whether logical consistency can provide a training signal without ground-truth spatial annotations.

The proposed self-supervised reinforcement learning framework targets the chain-of-thought process. Consistency verifiers check geometric and semantic relationships under transformations such as flipping a scene or swapping the order of objects in a question. The authors optimize these rewards with OT-GRPO, a minimal-consistency matching variant of group relative policy optimization. The reported results show that models can improve their spatial logic through this label-free training. These findings support internal consistency as a useful source of supervision for spatial reasoning. They also give empirical backing to the claim that some observed failures reflect how existing capabilities are expressed, rather than solely a lack of spatial knowledge.
summary.tldr: Training reasoning models for geometric and semantic consistency improves spatial reasoning without ground-truth labels.

title: The Art of Interrogation: Consistency Amplifies Factuality in Spatial Reasoning

abstract: Open-Vocabulary Segmentation(OVS) aims to achieve pixel-level semantic recognition from arbitrary text queries. Existing large-scale visual-linguistic models, such as CLIP, perform well in zero-shot generalization, but their image-level training objectives and real-valued cross-modal alignment mix amplitude and phase information, limiting fine-grained segmentation and often causing blurred boundaries and fragmented structures. Inspired by the ability of electromagnetic wave phase to control interference independently of amplitude, we propose PhaseAlign, an OVS framework based on Complex Phase Alignment (CPA). CPA explicitly decouples the magnitude and phase of visual and textual embeddings in the complex domain, refining effective features for stable cross-modal alignment. To further enhance structural awareness, we introduce spatial-aware cross-modal projection, which models local neighborhood relations via multi-scale spatial contrast normalization, and attention-guided affinity modeling, which leverages pre-trained ViT self-attention to propagate category activations, improving boundary clarity and region integrity. Experiments show that PhaseAlign achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple OVS benchmarks.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary segmentation assigns semantic labels to individual pixels using arbitrary text queries. Image-text models can generalize to unfamiliar categories, but image-level training does not necessarily support precise boundaries or coherent regions. The paper also argues that real-valued alignment mixes magnitude and phase information, limiting the quality of fine-grained correspondence between language and image features.

PhaseAlign represents visual and textual embeddings in a complex domain and explicitly separates their magnitude and phase. Inspired by phase-controlled interference in electromagnetic waves, this design seeks more stable alignment between the modalities. The framework also models local neighborhoods through multi-scale spatial contrast normalization. A further component uses self-attention from a pretrained vision transformer to propagate category activations and improve spatial coherence.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across multiple open-vocabulary segmentation benchmarks. The design links two sources of improvement: refining the representation used for image-text matching and strengthening the spatial relationships used to turn those matches into pixel labels. The stated gains in boundary clarity and region integrity address the blurred and fragmented outputs that motivate the approach.
summary.tldr: PhaseAlign separates embedding magnitude and phase while modeling spatial relationships to improve open-vocabulary segmentation.

title: PhaseAlign: Complex Phase Alignment for Stable Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation

abstract: We introduce Native Parallel Reasoner (NPR), a teacher-free framework that enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to self-evolve genuine parallel reasoning capabilities. NPR transforms the model from sequential emulation to native parallel cognition through three key innovations: (1) a self-distilled progressive training paradigm that transitions from cold-start format discovery to strict topological constraints without external supervision; (2) a novel Parallel-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO) algorithm that optimizes branching policies directly within the execution graph, allowing the model to learn adaptive decomposition via trial and error; and (3) a robust NPR Engine that refactors memory management and flow control of SGLang to enable stable, large-scale parallel RL training. Across eight reasoning benchmarks, NPR trained on Qwen3-4B achieves performance gains of up to 24.5% and inference speedups up to 4.6$\times$. Unlike prior baselines that often fall back to autoregressive decoding, NPR demonstrates 100% genuine parallel execution, establishing a new standard for self-evolving, efficient, and scalable agentic reasoning.

paragraphs: Parallel reasoning requires a model to organize work into branches that can actually execute concurrently. Native Parallel Reasoner trains this capability without an external teacher. Its progressive self-distillation process begins with discovering a usable format and moves toward strict constraints on the structure of the reasoning execution graph.

The training algorithm, Parallel-Aware Policy Optimization, learns branching policies directly within that graph. Through trial and error, the model learns how to decompose reasoning adaptively. A supporting execution engine modifies SGLang’s memory management and flow control to make large-scale parallel reinforcement learning stable, connecting the learning procedure to infrastructure capable of running its branches.

Across eight reasoning benchmarks, NPR trained on Qwen3-4B achieves gains of up to 24.5% and inference speedups of up to 4.6 times. The authors report 100% genuine parallel execution in their evaluation, whereas prior baselines often revert to autoregressive decoding. These findings support the joint design of training objectives, branching behavior, and execution infrastructure for improving both reasoning performance and inference efficiency.
summary.tldr: NPR trains language models to execute reasoning branches in parallel through self-distillation, graph-aware reinforcement learning, and supporting runtime changes.

title: Native Parallel Reasoner: Reasoning in Parallelism via Self-Distilled Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Masked diffusion language models decode by iteratively unmasking tokens, where the unmasking order defines an “order of thought” that strongly influences generation quality yet is typically chosen heuristically. We derive a tractable upper bound on the sequential decoding mismatch, measured by the Kullback–Leibler divergence and expressed in terms of the model’s pathwise log-likelihood, with tightness under sufficient model expressivity. This bound induces a dense self-aware reward for a target sequence $x$ and unmasking order $\sigma$, over ordered paths, casting order selection as a principled policy optimization problem with a frozen denoiser. We instantiate this idea as Self-Aware Scheduling (SAS), which learns a lightweight order policy using Group Relative Policy Optimization and applies seamlessly to both sequential and semi-autoregressive decoding. On Sudoku with 1B MDM, SAS improves puzzle accuracy from $82.0%$ (best heuristic schedule) to $91.8%$, and reaches $97.9%$ with second-stage fine-tuning along learned trajectories. On LLaDA-8B, SAS improves pass@1 on GSM8K from $64%$ to $76%$ (full diffusion) and on MBPP from $39.5%$ to $41%$, while consistently matching or exceeding heuristic schedules across generation lengths and block sizes.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models generate text by repeatedly revealing hidden tokens. The order of those reveals affects output quality, yet schedules are often chosen by heuristics. This paper turns schedule selection into a learning problem, asking which sequence of token decisions best suits the model's own predictive behavior.

title: Scheduling Thoughts: Learning the Order of Thought in Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have emerged as a powerful backbone for image generation, offering superior scalability over U-Nets. However, their practical deployment is hindered by significant computational costs. While Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) shows promise, its application to DiTs is challenged by the high sensitivity and complex distributions of activations. Identifying activation quantization as the primary bottleneck for low-bit settings, we propose RobuQ, a systematic QAT framework. We first establish a strong ternary weight (W1.58A4) baseline. Building on this, we introduce RobustQuantizer, which utilizes the Hadamard transform to convert unknown per-token distributions into normal distributions. Furthermore, we propose AMPN, the first Activation-only Mixed-Precision Network pipeline, applying ternary weights globally while allocating layer-specific activation precisions to eliminate information bottlenecks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RobuQ achieves state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet-1K, representing the first stable image generation with activations quantized to an average of 2 bits. Code is available at https://github.com/racoonykc/RobuQ.

paragraphs: Diffusion transformers are powerful image generators, but their computational demands complicate deployment. RobuQ studies how to train them with very low numerical precision. The paper identifies activation quantization as the main obstacle in low-bit settings, because activations are sensitive to approximation and have complicated distributions.

The framework first establishes a baseline with ternary weights and four-bit activations. Its RobustQuantizer then applies a Hadamard transform to convert unknown per-token distributions into normal distributions. An activation-only mixed-precision pipeline keeps ternary weights throughout the network while assigning different activation precisions to different layers, addressing information bottlenecks where they occur.

The average is significant: the approach allocates precision across layers rather than requiring every layer to use exactly two bits. The findings support treating activation distribution and layer-specific precision as central design choices for pushing diffusion transformers into extremely low-bit operation.
summary.tldr: RobuQ combines activation distribution transforms and layer-specific precision to achieve stable image generation with ternary weights and average two-bit activations.

title: RobuQ: Pushing DiTs to W1.58A2 via Robust Activation Quantization

abstract: While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures substantially bolster the expressive power of large-language models, their prohibitive memory footprint severely impedes the practical deployment on resource-constrained edge devices, especially when model behavior must be preserved without relying on lossy quantization. In this paper, we present ZipMoE, an efficient and semantically lossless on-device MoE serving system. ZipMoE exploits the synergy between the hardware properties of edge devices and the statistical redundancy inherent to MoE parameters via a caching-scheduling co-design with provable performance guarantee. Fundamentally, our design shifts the paradigm of on-device MoE inference from an I/O-bound bottleneck to a compute-centric workflow that enables efficient parallelization. We implement a prototype of ZipMoE and conduct extensive experiments on representative edge computing platforms using popular open-source MoE models and real-world workloads. Our evaluation reveals that ZipMoE achieves up to 72.77% inference latency reduction and up to $6.76\times$ higher throughput than the state-of-the-art systems. Our code is available at: https://github.com/npnothard/ZipMoE-ICML26.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts language models offer substantial expressive power but require enough memory to make deployment on constrained devices difficult. ZipMoE tackles this serving problem while preserving model behavior, using lossless compression rather than relying on lossy quantization. The goal is to make existing MoE models more practical to run locally.

The system jointly designs caching and scheduling around edge-device hardware and statistical redundancy in model parameters. Its design includes a provable performance guarantee. By coordinating how parameters are retained and work is scheduled, ZipMoE shifts inference away from an input/output bottleneck toward a computation-centered workflow that supports efficient parallel execution.

The authors implement a prototype and evaluate it on representative edge platforms with popular open-source MoE models and real workloads. They report up to 72.77% lower inference latency and up to 6.76 times higher throughput than state-of-the-art systems. These are best reported improvements, rather than uniform gains across all settings. The findings demonstrate the potential of coordinated compression, caching, and scheduling for behavior-preserving on-device inference.
summary.tldr: ZipMoE combines lossless compression with coordinated caching and scheduling to accelerate on-device MoE inference while preserving model behavior.

title: ZipMoE: Efficient On-Device MoE Serving via Lossless Compression and Cache-Affinity Scheduling

abstract: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) offers a promising paradigm for improving reinforcement learning generalization by adaptively shaping training environments, but it requires reliable environment evaluation to remain effective. However, existing UED methods evaluate environments using indirect proxy signals such as regret, value-based errors, or Monte Carlo, which suffer from bias, high variance, or substantial computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose Parameter Change Environment Design (PACE), a general framework for adaptive level selection in UED. PACE evaluates a level by performing a provisional policy update on it and scoring it with the squared $\ell_2$ norm of the induced parameter change, which directly reflects realized learning progress. This score then guides level selection: levels enter a staleness-aware buffer based on their score, and are replayed via rank-based prioritization, inducing a curriculum that adapts to the agent’s evolving capability. By grounding environment evaluation in intrinsic optimization progress, PACE provides a low-variance evaluation signal and avoids the need for additional environment rollouts. Experiments on MiniGrid and Craftax demonstrate that PACE consistently outperforms established UED baselines in zero-shot generalization across diverse out-of-distribution evaluation protocols.

paragraphs: Unsupervised environment design chooses training situations for a reinforcement-learning agent as its abilities develop. Its effectiveness depends on recognizing which environments offer useful learning opportunities. Existing approaches often estimate this through indirect signals that can be biased, noisy, or expensive to calculate. PACE evaluates environments through the parameter changes they induce during learning.

For a candidate level, PACE performs a provisional policy update and measures the squared Euclidean size of the resulting parameter change. That score determines entry into a buffer that accounts for staleness, and rank-based prioritization controls replay. The resulting curriculum changes with the agent because an environment's score depends on its effect on the current policy.

The authors describe this optimization-based score as a low-variance measure of realized learning progress that requires no additional environment rollouts. Experiments on MiniGrid and Craftax show consistent improvements over established environment-design baselines in zero-shot generalization across multiple out-of-distribution evaluation protocols. The results support using the agent's actual update behavior to guide adaptive training-level selection.
summary.tldr: PACE selects reinforcement-learning environments using the parameter changes caused by provisional updates, improving reported zero-shot generalization.

title: PACE: Parameter Change for Unsupervised Environment Design

abstract: With the rapid development of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and the growing demand for their applications, efficient compression of the image inputs has become increasingly important. Existing VLMs predominantly digest and understand high-bitrate compressed images, while their ability to interpret low-bitrate compressed images has yet to be explored by far. In this paper, we introduce the first comprehensive benchmark to evaluate the ability of VLM against compressed images, varying existing widely used image codecs and diverse set of tasks, encompassing over one million compressed images in our benchmark. Next, we analyse the source of performance gap, by categorising the gap from a) the information loss during compression and b) generalisation failure of VLM. We visualize these gaps with concrete examples and identify that for compressed images, only the generalization gap can be mitigated. Finally, we propose a universal VLM adaptor to enhance model performance on images compressed by existing codecs. Consequently, we demonstrate that a single adaptor can improve VLM performance across images with varying codecs and bitrates by 10%-30%. We believe that our benchmark and enhancement method provide valuable insights and contribute toward bridging the gap between VLMs and compressed images. The source code is available at https://github.com/bblgbr/CompressVLMBench.

paragraphs: Compressing image inputs can make vision-language applications more efficient, but stronger compression changes the information available to the model. This paper investigates how vision-language models handle low-bitrate images through a benchmark containing over one million compressed images. It varies widely used image codecs and evaluates a diverse collection of tasks.

The analysis separates two sources of reduced performance. Compression can remove information from the image, and the model can also fail to generalize to the compressed appearance of information that remains. Concrete visual examples illustrate this distinction. The authors identify the generalization component as the part that can be mitigated for compressed inputs.

The paper then introduces a universal adaptor intended to improve understanding across existing codecs. A single adaptor produces reported performance improvements of 10%–30% across varying codecs and bitrates. The findings connect evaluation with a targeted remedy: understanding compression failures requires distinguishing lost content from a model’s difficulty interpreting the content that survives.
summary.tldr: A large benchmark separates compression information loss from model generalization failures, and a shared adaptor improves compressed-image understanding.

title: Benchmarking and Enhancing VLM for Compressed Image Understanding

abstract: Schema Linking serves as the foundational perception layer in Text-to-SQL, tasked with grounding natural language queries into relevant schema elements. However, existing retrieval-based approaches suffer from a critical structural blindness: by prioritizing elements with high textual similarity, they inadvertently prune semantically-thin but topologically-critical bridge tables, thereby severing relational pathways necessary for multi-hop joins. To bridge this gap, we propose Graph-Link, a novel framework that reformulates schema linking from an independent retrieval task into a constrained subgraph induction problem. We argue that generating executable SQL necessitates a connected subgraph that satisfies both semantic relevance and structural constraints. Accordingly, Graph-Link employs a hierarchical schema graph to model the search space across multiple granularities, and then applies a Steiner-tree-based optimization for subgraph induction that guarantees the topological connectivity while maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio for downstream LLMs. Extensive experiments on BIRD and Spider 2.0 demonstrate that Graph-Link achieves state-of-the-art schema linking performance, improving recall and hit rates by up to 7.0% over competitive baselines, and boosts downstream SQL generation accuracy on complex queries by 13.8%.

However, existing retrieval-based approaches suffer from a critical structural blindness: by prioritizing elements with high textual similarity, they inadvertently prune semantically-thin but topologically-critical bridge tables, thereby severing relational pathways necessary for multi-hop joins. paragraphs: Text-to-SQL systems must identify which database tables and columns are relevant to a user's question. Selecting elements mainly by textual similarity can discard bridge tables whose names seem unimportant but whose relationships are essential for joining data. Graph-Link treats this as a structural problem in addition to a language-matching problem.

The framework represents the schema as a hierarchical graph and selects a constrained subgraph rather than retrieving elements independently. A Steiner-tree-based optimization preserves connections among relevant schema elements while aiming to give the downstream language model a focused selection. Accuracy on downstream SQL generation for complex queries improves by 13.8%. These results indicate that preserving relational structure during schema selection can help the later generation stage construct successful multi-hop queries.
summary.tldr: Graph-Link selects connected schema subgraphs so text-to-SQL systems retain bridge tables needed for complex joins.

title: Graph-Link: Bridging the Semantic-Structural Gap in Text-to-SQL via Constrained Subgraph Induction

abstract: Scaling language models to long contexts is often bottlenecked by the size of the key-value (KV) cache. In deployed settings, long contexts are typically managed through compaction in token space via summarization. However, summarization can be highly lossy, substantially harming downstream performance. Recent work on Cartridges (Eyuboglu et al., 2025) has shown that it is possible to train highly compact KV caches in latent space that closely match full-context performance, but at the cost of slow and expensive end-to-end optimization. This work describes an approach for fast context compaction in latent space through Attention Matching, which constructs compact keys and values to reproduce attention outputs and preserve attention mass at a per-KV-head level. We show that this formulation naturally decomposes into simple subproblems, some of which admit efficient closed-form solutions. Within this framework, we develop a family of methods that significantly push the Pareto frontier of compaction time versus quality, achieving up to $50\times$ compaction in seconds on some datasets with little quality loss.

paragraphs: Long contexts require large key-value caches, which store information used by a language model’s attention mechanism. Compressing context into a text summary can discard information needed later. Earlier work showed that directly training a compact cache can preserve full-context performance, but its end-to-end optimization is slow and expensive.

This paper proposes Attention Matching, which constructs compact keys and values by matching what attention produces. At the level of individual key-value heads, it aims to reproduce attention outputs while preserving attention mass. This formulation breaks the compaction problem into simpler subproblems, some with efficient closed-form solutions, reducing the need for costly optimization.

The authors develop several methods within this framework and report an improved tradeoff between compaction time and retained quality. On some datasets, they achieve up to 50-fold compaction in seconds with little quality loss. Those qualifiers matter: the finding demonstrates substantial compression in evaluated settings, while the central methodological contribution is a faster way to preserve attention behavior.
summary.tldr: Attention Matching builds compact KV caches quickly, achieving up to 50-fold compaction in seconds with little quality loss on some datasets.

title: Fast KV Compaction via Attention Matching

abstract: Algorithmic fairness research has largely framed unfairness as discrimination along sensitive attributes. However, this approach limits visibility into unfairness as structural injustice instantiated through social determinants, which are contextual variables that shape attributes and outcomes without pertaining to specific individuals. This position paper argues that the field should quantify structural injustice via social determinants, beyond sensitive attributes. Drawing on cross-disciplinary insights, we argue that prevailing technical paradigms fail to adequately capture unfairness as structural injustice, because contexts are potentially treated as noise to be normalized rather than signal to be audited. We further demonstrate the practical urgency of this shift through a theoretical model of college admissions, a demographic study using U.S. census data, and a high-stakes domain application regarding breast cancer screening within an integrated U.S. healthcare system. Our results indicate that mitigation strategies centered solely on sensitive attributes can introduce new forms of structural injustice. We contend that auditing structural injustice through social determinants must precede mitigation, and call for new technical developments that move beyond sensitive-attribute-centered notions of fairness as non-discrimination.

paragraphs: This paper argues that fairness research needs to measure structural injustice alongside discrimination associated with sensitive attributes. It focuses on social determinants: contextual conditions that shape attributes and outcomes without belonging to particular individuals. These conditions can reveal forms of unfairness that an analysis organized solely around individual group membership may fail to capture.

Drawing on multiple disciplines, the authors argue that existing technical approaches can treat social context as unwanted variation to remove, although that context may be the very evidence an audit needs. They develop their case through a theoretical college admissions model, a demographic analysis using U.S. census data, and an application involving breast cancer screening in an integrated U.S. healthcare system.

Their results indicate that mitigation focused only on sensitive attributes can introduce additional structural injustice. The claim is therefore about how fairness interventions are defined and assessed, as well as what they measure. The authors advocate auditing social determinants before selecting mitigation strategies and developing technical methods capable of representing these contextual sources of unfairness.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that fairness audits should measure structural injustice through social determinants before choosing mitigation strategies.
